note: Separates shared training text from convergence. The study found Qwen3-1.7B agreed with Qwen3-8B no better than Llama did (median 0.40 in both, `study/results/phylo.json.gz`). Gemma or Mistral at 4 bits fit the laptop. Same held-out and word-matched nulls as UN21.

title: Where the two models disagree
question: Are the units with no twin in the other model concentrated in culturally or politically loaded content?
note: Jiralerspong and Bricken 2026 report Chinese-state-aligned features exclusive to Qwen3-8B and American-exceptionalism features exclusive to Llama. Compare twinless units on neutral plots against history or news text. Rival: topic words. Tells users when the choice of reference model matters.

title: Story memes in generated scenes
question: Does one unit fire for a story meme stated in text and shown in a generated image with decoys and masked lettering?
note: Follow-up to UN26 for narrative memes such as a secret identity. Ground truth by construction, with a human check of a sample. Rivals: CLIP zero-shot, a captioner plus TF-IDF, the model asked directly.

title: Two languages, one photograph, no translator
question: Do units agree between English and German captions that two people wrote separately for the same photograph?
note: Crossmodal-3600 has captions written independently in 36 languages for 3,600 images (CC BY 4.0). A check on UN22 that is free of machine-translation artefacts, with Qwen reading German against Llama reading English as the cross-model step. Rivals: multilingual sentence embeddings, TF-IDF after translation, caption length. Concrete scenes only. Hours.

title: Scrambled sentences
question: How much twin agreement survives when the words of each sentence are shuffled, so that only the bag of words is left?
note: Reread UN21's film sentences with word order shuffled inside each sentence. Agreement that survives is carried by vocabulary alone; the drop is the share that needs word order. A check on UN21's word control that fits no model. Rival: TF-IDF, which shuffling leaves unchanged. Under a day.

title: Reference memome: which units pass admission?
question: For one public checkpoint, how many of 150 story motifs get a neuron entry that passes a fixed admission test on held-out, reworded passages, compared with control units and rival detectors put through the same test?
hypothesis: At least 30 of 150 motifs (20%) gain an admitted single-neuron entry and at least 60 (40%) an admitted set of up to eight neurons; the sets admit at least half as many motifs as a probe on the same model's averaged hidden state. Permuted motif labels admit 3 or fewer; a random-weights copy of the model 5 or fewer.
falsifier: Fewer than 15 single-neuron entries admitted; a count inside the permuted-label null's 95% range; a random-weights copy yielding half as many; or neuron sets admitting under half the hidden-state probe's count. With 24 test passages per cell a chance-level unit is admitted under 1% of the time; 150 motifs separate a 20% yield from 10% at z = 4.
data: 150 motifs: 100 drawn by seed from the 307 Thompson motifs tied to ten or more tales in Hagedorn's trilogy data (CC BY-SA 4.0), 50 from TiMoS's 95 film tropes. Per motif, 192 new 120-word passages: motif present or absent (absent: a twin with another event of equal stakes), usual words present or absent. 28,800 passages, CC BY. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, pinned.
method: Units are neurons read on one side (917,504). On 96 development passages per motif, pick the best unit, best eight-unit set and threshold; freeze. Admit if, on 96 test passages by a second writer model, AUC (0.5 is chance) for motif-without-words against words-without-motif has a 90% lower bound of 0.70 and other motifs trigger it under 10% of the time.
rivals: Keyword lists; a TF-IDF (weighted word count) classifier; e5 and Qwen3-Embedding sentence vectors; a probe (simple classifier) on the model's hidden state; Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features (learned units); the neuron whose Transluce description best fits the definition; passage length; a zero-shot LLM reader. The LLM reader will probably admit most; the census still gives every method error rates and cost.
premise: P1. A yield at the permuted-label or random-weights level means single neurons are not usable meme units in this model. A yield of 20% or more turns P1 into a bounded claim: these named units, with these error rates, and no others. If the hidden-state probe admits twice as many, the atlas's unit should be a direction.
bio: Reference genome with evidence codes; mock community
cost: M. About 28,800 short passages by API (under 150 US dollars), six hours of laptop extraction on a 4-bit model, a three-hour human audit of 300 passages; about ten days in all.
payoff: The first citable list of meme units with measured sensitivity and false-fire rates, from which later experiments draw frozen units. It also sizes the memome: how many of 150 human-named motifs one neuron, a small set, or no unit can read.
risk: Passages written by language models share house styles, so a unit can learn a writer's habit for one cell and pass. A second writer family for test passages and the human audit reduce this; they do not remove it. AT-27 then checks the entries on real tales.
review: Changed: motifs come from sources checked to exist and tied to real tales; motif-absent passages are twins; a hidden-state comparison joined the falsifier. Remaining: every admission passage is machine-written, so AT-27 must follow. IN21 is the natural pilot. The TiMoS download was not re-checked.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 9). A public catalogue of meme units with measured hit and false-alarm rates for 150 human-named motifs would be the lasting, citable asset of the programme; run it only after IN-21 shows the yield is not zero.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as IN-21, which the judges would run instead.
update: Give each entry the fields Goodfire's atlas gives a pole: a firing threshold from the unit's own range on general text, cases it does not fire on, and its roles. Add one admission test: a blind judge counts how many of 100 strong firings sampled from general text match the motif. The companion paper's Colorado neuron read as places on ordinary text and as a code library on code.
sources: Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean; Choi et al. 2024, Scaling automatic neuron description (Transluce); Heap et al. 2025, arXiv:2501.17727; Hagedorn and Darányi 2022, doi:10.5334/johd.78; Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: What inside the model copies a meme?
question: When a model retells a story in its own words, is a planted meme carried into the retelling by one neuron, by a small set of neurons, or only by a direction spread across thousands of them?
hypothesis: Silencing 64 chosen neurons cuts a motif's survival in retellings by 30 points or more on average across 20 motifs, at least 20 points more than 64 matched random neurons, while the other planted motifs lose under 10 points. Silencing the single best detector neuron cuts under 10 points.
falsifier: The 64-neuron cut averages under 15 points, or is within 10 points of 64 random neurons matched on layer and activation (bootstrap over motifs, 95% interval includes zero), or the other motifs fall as far as the target. With 25 test stories per motif and arm (500 per arm), a pooled drop has a standard error near 4 points.
data: 800 new stories of 200 words (20 motifs, each with 15 development and 25 test stories), each carrying its target motif plus two others and paired with a twin lacking the target; written by an LLM from a different family, released CC BY. Motif definitions as in AT-21. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 4-bit, which reads the story and writes the retelling.
method: Arms: untouched; best detector neuron; top 8, 64 and 512 neurons, ranked on development stories by how much setting each to its twin-story value changes the retelling, and silenced the same way; one difference-of-means direction removed. The 64-neuron arm is rerun for reading only and writing only. Keywords are blocked from output. A blind cross-family reader scores survival; 150 hand-checked.
rivals: A plain instruction to leave the motif out; the keyword block alone; deleting the motif's sentences from the input; silencing the neurons that best detect the motif's keywords. The instruction will probably remove the motif most cleanly. The design still locates the carrier, which an instruction cannot; the bar to beat is random and keyword neurons.
premise: P1. If one neuron or a few dozen are necessary for copying, P1 gains the causal footing it lacks. If only a dense direction works, the atlas's unit should be a direction, and a neuron is at best an index into it. If only deleting the sentences works, memes are not copied as units here.
bio: Hershey and Chase, then Watson and Crick; gene knock-out
cost: M. Ablation hooks for the 4-bit model, about 7,000 short generations (roughly 30 laptop hours), judge calls under 50 US dollars; two weeks including code.
payoff: The size of the thing that copies a meme in one model: one neuron, dozens, hundreds or a direction, and whether it acts at reading or at writing. That decides what an atlas entry should be and whether editing a meme by neuron is realistic. It is a mechanism for machine culture, not for human minds.
risk: A retelling can copy through attention straight from the source words, with no motif-level carrier to silence, so a null may mean 'no carrier' and not 'spread out'; the direction and sentence-deletion arms help tell these apart. Silencing can also damage the model in ways the collateral checks miss.
review: Changed: per-motif pass counts became a pooled drop; added a 512-neuron arm, twin-story silencing and a reading-only against writing-only split. Remaining: in Cammarata's own example, removing 20 labelled neurons left a concept at 76%, so 64 may be too few; damage and removal stay hard to separate. Neighbours: IN24, EN-27.
ranking: 2 of 3 judges thought the area reviewer rated this too high.
update: Add a 2,048-neuron arm. In the companion paper's circuit tracing, half of the push toward one place name came from 155 neurons and 80% from 2,299, so 64 or 512 may be too few to carry a motif. Silence the chosen neurons only on tokens where they are in their own strong range, and report whether that does as much as silencing them everywhere.
sources: Arora et al. 2026, arXiv:2601.22594; Liu, Joshi, Dawson and Piper 2026, arXiv:2610.12989; Wu et al. 2025, AxBench, arXiv:2501.17148; Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean; Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: Mendel test: particles or blends in two-source works?
question: When a work has two documented sources that differ on a meme, does the work carry that meme at full parental strength or not at all, as particles would, or at an in-between strength, as blending would?
hypothesis: Of memes passed on from the one parent that has them, at most 15% arrive diluted: 25% to 75% of the way between the two parents' readings, beyond test-retest noise. A blind LLM reader's 0 to 4 ratings of the same motifs give a diluted share within 10 points of that.
falsifier: The diluted share for units is 30% or more, or the reader's ratings give a share 20 points higher than the units do, across 150 or more trios (bootstrap over trios; expected standard error about 4 points). If the method cannot tell built blends from built copies at AUC 0.75, the result is void.
data: Wikidata items with two 'based on' sources, all with English Wikipedia articles: 1,620 (counted 8 November 2026; CC0), among them 341 films, 124 television series, 96 video games; many others are not stories. Plots from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0); expect 150 to 250 usable trios. Noise from Tell Me Again: 96,831 summaries of 29,505 stories. 120 constructed crosses, CC BY.
method: Frozen AT-21 entries; names masked; equal-length summaries. For each unit present in one parent only, place the child's reading between the parents'. Fit two clusters at the parents (width from two summaries of one story) against a middle component. Nulls: children swapped for unrelated works matched on medium, decade, genre and length; crosses built to copy or fuse.
rivals: Same fit, with each work read by its three strongest sentences, on TF-IDF weights of one-parent words, sentence-embedding dimensions, the residual stream, random non-meme units, and an LLM reader's 0 to 4 ratings of motifs. The reader is the danger: if it sees blends the units miss, the particles are a thresholding artefact; if it agrees, neurons were not needed.
premise: Assumes P1 for admitted units and tests whether they behave like genes. Particles support treating memes as countable and presence grids as sufficient. Blending supports Sperber's view that ideas are rebuilt, and means thresholded presence throws information away.
bio: Mendel's crosses; particulate against blending inheritance
cost: M. About 600 plot sections fetched and name-masked by script, 120 constructed crosses, one extraction pass, a spot-check by hand; one to two weeks and under 50 US dollars.
payoff: A measured answer to the oldest objection to memetics, that ideas blend and so cannot be counted. It also says whether a set of memes per work is the right data type, or whether readings must be kept as amounts.
risk: A plot summary either mentions an event or does not, so particles may reflect how editors summarise, not how authors combine sources. The constructed crosses test the method's resolution; they cannot test that. In 458 of the 1,620 items one source is based on the other; such chains are analysed apart, and crosses of unrelated stories are few.
review: Changed: the 1,620 count includes non-stories and 458 chains, now stated and split; all bases are pooled alike, because reading the strongest sentences makes units look particulate by construction; the reader's graded rating now decides. Remaining: one generation cannot separate blending from particles with partial dominance (see the two-generation seed).
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as CE-23, which the judges would run instead.
update: Do not read an in-between score as dilution without a check. The companion paper says a neuron's weaker firings tend to fall on related but different content. Class each child reading by the unit's own bands on general text, and have a blind reader judge the firing passage in every in-between case: same motif, neighbouring motif, or neither.
sources: Wikidata property P144 (based on); Hatzel and Biemann 2024, Tell Me Again; Claidière, Scott-Phillips and Sperber 2014, doi:10.1098/rstb.2013.0368; Mesoudi and Whiten 2008, doi:10.1098/rstb.2008.0129; Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: Which kind of meme name reproduces across labs?
question: Given only a published name, can an independently built second pipeline reproduce the first one's presence calls, and which kind of name is both reproducible and valid: a neuron address, a family cluster, a cross-model twin or a written definition?
hypothesis: Neuron addresses: at least 90 of 100 names reach kappa 0.80 between pipelines (4-bit against 8-bit weights, different runtimes). Family clusters rebuilt from the published rule on a second corpus: under 60. Twin names in a second model, on name-free text: under 30. No fewer addresses than written definitions are both reproducible and valid (AUC 0.70 on reworded passages).
falsifier: Fewer than 70 of 100 address names reach kappa 0.80, or rebuilt family names reproduce as often as addresses (a difference under 10 names), or written definitions give 10 or more additional names that are both reproducible and valid. With 2,000 passages per name, kappa is known to about 0.05, and 100 names fix each share to within 10 points.
data: 2,000 passages: plots of the 1,000 accepted random films in preregistration/sources/t3_random_films.jsonl.gz (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0) and 1,000 reworded AT-21 test passages with known motifs. Names: the best entry for each of 100 AT-21 motifs; the 31 labelled units in study/results/labels.json are reported separately. Checkpoints: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, pinned revisions.
method: A name is checkpoint revision, layer, neuron, sign, readout rule and threshold corpus, each hashed. A second pipeline is written from the specification alone, on another runtime and precision. Statistic: Cohen's kappa (agreement beyond chance) per name; validity: AUC on reworded passages. Null: kappa between different units matched on firing rate. Wording cannot confound kappa: both pipelines read identical text.
rivals: A keyword pattern (reproduces perfectly by construction, at chance on reworded passages), an embedding prototype with a named encoder, a Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder feature index, and a written definition read by two different LLMs on a 500-passage sample. The written definition is the danger: probably more valid, and if two readers agree at kappa 0.80 it is the better name.
premise: Both. A stable address is the one practical advantage of raw neurons over learned features (P1). The twin name is P2 stated as a naming rule: if it fails on name-free text, a meme name is good in one checkpoint only.
bio: Exact sequence variants against clustered OTUs; accession numbers
cost: M. Two extraction passes per checkpoint on one laptop (8-bit weights of an 8B model fit in 24 GB), a second pipeline written from the specification, two LLM readers on 500 passages (under 30 US dollars); about four days.
payoff: A written naming standard with a reproducibility and a validity figure for each kind of name, and the first check that 4-bit weights do not move the units. Two labs could then cite one meme and know how far their readings will agree.
risk: Both pipelines come from one person and one family of coding assistants, so shared habits inflate agreement. This is a rehearsal; only a real second lab tests the standard. Address agreement is close to guaranteed, so most of the information sits in the family, twin and definition rows.
review: Changed: every name now carries a motif, so it is scored for validity as well as reproducibility, and the written definition must be beaten on both; cost raised to M. Remaining: IN29 already tests precision, address agreement is near-certain by construction, and the study showed twins failing on name-free text.
update: Extend the name with what the companion paper shows a reading depends on: the band (a percentile, and the reference corpus that fixed it), whether the gate was open, the role that fired, and for models with experts the expert index. Add a reproducibility row: recompute each unit's threshold on a second, disjoint sample of general text and report agreement of the presence calls.
sources: Callahan, McMurdie and Holmes 2017, doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.119; Paulo and Belrose 2025, arXiv:2501.16615; Gurnee et al. 2024, arXiv:2401.12181; study/results/robustness/nulls.json (f2_agreement); Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: Linnaean key: named units against the folktale index
question: Can a short identification key made of named meme units place folktales of unseen tale types into the right division of the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index better than a key of the same length made of words?
hypothesis: A key of 15 units puts tales of held-out types in the right division 35% of the time or better (the largest division holds 11% of tales), at least 8 points above a 15-word key and within 15 points of nearest-neighbour search on e5 sentence embeddings.
falsifier: The unit key is under 3 points above the word key (bootstrap over tale types, 95% interval includes zero), or falls inside the range of keys trained on permuted division labels. Five-fold testing over 159 types (1,359 tales) gives a standard error near 3 points on the paired difference.
data: Hagedorn's trilogy data: 1,518 English folktale texts of 182 tale types; median 543 words (Zenodo 6575263, CC BY-SA 4.0; counted 8 November 2026). Divisions are set from the type number, because the file's division column is blank for 20 types and its chapter column is wrong for 338 tales. 20 divisions hold three or more types: 1,359 tales, 159 types.
method: Five folds by tale type; the other types build each key. A key is 15 yes/no characters ('is unit X present?') chosen greedily; a tale joins the division whose build tales share most answers. Unit names are Transluce's public descriptions, checked blind on tales. Null: division labels permuted across types within length bands. Repeated with character and animal nouns masked.
rivals: A 15-word key; a key of 15 questions written and answered by an LLM; a key on Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features; e5 nearest neighbours, TF-IDF and a hidden-state probe as unconstrained references; tale length; random non-meme units. The LLM key should win on accuracy at many times the cost. Units earn a place only by beating the word key.
premise: P1. If named units make a better key than words of equal length, the unit carves stories at joints that experts recognise. If the word key ties, the atlas's names add nothing a word list lacks.
bio: Linnaeus's identification keys; diagnostic characters
cost: S. One extraction over 1,518 tales (about 20 minutes per model), an hour of local LLM answering for the rival key, key fitting on a laptop; under two days.
payoff: A readable taxonomy: the 15 units that sort folktales, each with a name, checked against a century of expert classification. It shows whether the atlas can be used the way a field guide is.
risk: The search picks from 900,000 units but about 20,000 words, so the unit key overfits more easily; held-out types guard against it. Divisions are partly defined by who is in the tale (animals, clergy), which favours words. The tales sit on the open web with their type numbers, so both models have probably read them.
review: Changed: divisions are recoded from type numbers, since the file leaves them blank for 20 types and mislabels the chapter of 338 tales; one underpowered 60-type split became five folds; names come from public descriptions. Remaining: divisions are topical, so a tie with words is the likely result.
sources: Hagedorn, trilogy dataset, Zenodo 6575263; Arčon, Robnik-Šikonja and Tratnik 2025, arXiv:2510.18561; Eklund, Hagedorn and Darányi 2023, doi:10.1515/fabula-2023-0005; Peng et al. 2025, arXiv:2506.23845

title: Field test: do admitted entries read real folktales?
question: Does an entry admitted on passages written to order also find its motif in real folktales whose tale type lists that motif, and does passing admission predict how well it does there?
hypothesis: Of entries admitted in AT-21, at least half reach AUC 0.70 (0.5 is chance) on real tales, against at most 20% of entries that failed admission. The mean AUC of admitted entries is at least 0.10 above that of rejected ones.
falsifier: Admitted and rejected entries differ by under 0.03 in mean AUC (bootstrap over motifs, 95% interval includes zero), or under a quarter of admitted entries reach 0.70. With about 25 admitted and 75 rejected motifs and a spread of 0.12 in AUC between motifs, a 0.10 gap is detected with about 95% power.
data: Hagedorn's trilogy data (Zenodo 6575263, CC BY-SA 4.0): 1,518 English folktale texts of 182 tale types, and a table tying each type to its Thompson motifs. 307 motifs are tied to ten or more of the tales (counted 8 November 2026); AT-21 draws 100 of them. A tale counts as containing a motif if its type lists it.
method: Frozen AT-21 entries and thresholds; nothing is tuned on tales. Per motif, AUC for tales whose type lists the motif against tales of other types in the same index division, so topic cannot carry it. Compare admitted with rejected entries. One person reads 200 tale-motif pairs to measure label error. Null: motif labels permuted across types within a division.
rivals: Each built from AT-21 passages or the definition alone, never from tales: a keyword list, an e5 prototype (the average embedding of motif-present passages), a hidden-state probe, a zero-shot LLM reader, tale length, random units. The keyword list is the danger: real tales mostly use the usual words, so keywords may match units here although they fail AT-21 by construction.
premise: P1. Admission on machine-written text is worth having only if it predicts behaviour on real text. A pass makes AT-21's rule a usable gate and its entries citable for folklore. A fail means the catalogue describes one writer model's passages, not stories.
bio: Mock community first, then field samples
cost: S. One extraction over 1,518 tales (about 20 minutes), a few thousand reader calls (under 20 US dollars), three hours of reading by one person; under two days once AT-21 exists.
payoff: An error rate for each catalogue entry on real, expert-indexed stories, and a check that the admission rule means something outside the laboratory. It also gives the first table of which Thompson motifs a model unit can find in the tales themselves.
risk: Labels sit at the level of the tale type: a given telling may lack a listed motif, and only 37 motifs are shared by two or more of the collection's types, so a unit that recognises 'a Cinderella tale' passes as the slipper motif. Same-division negatives reduce this; they do not remove it.
review: Added by the reviewer, because AT-21 admits entries on machine-written text only. Weakness: labels are per tale type, noisy and mostly tied to one type, and both models have probably read these tales online. Alyami and Finlayson's sentence-level corpus would be better; its public release was not confirmed.
sources: Hagedorn and Darányi 2022, doi:10.5334/johd.78; Hagedorn, trilogy dataset, Zenodo 6575263; Alyami and Finlayson 2026, arXiv:2603.19283; Callahan, McMurdie and Holmes 2017, doi:10.1038/ismej.2017.119

title: Eka-meme: does a table predict an unseen unit?
question: When motifs are laid out in a grid of who acts by what they do, do an empty cell's row and column predict the direction, and the neuron, that reads that cell's motif before any passage for it has been seen?
hypothesis: Directions predicted from a cell's row and column reach a mean AUC of 0.70 (0.5 is chance) on held-out cells and do at least as well as the same arithmetic on e5 sentence embeddings. The neuron nearest the predicted direction beats a matched random neuron in at least 24 of 36 cells.
falsifier: Mean AUC of predicted directions under 0.60, or 0.05 below the embedding arithmetic (bootstrap over rows and columns, 95% interval excludes zero), or the predicted neuron beats a random one in fewer than 22 of 36 cells. 24 of 36 has a sign-test p of 0.03; 36 cells put the mean AUC within about 0.03.
data: A grid of 36 motifs: six family roles (father, mother, stepmother, brother, sister, wife) by six acts (rescues, abandons, murders, sells, betrays, curses). Definitions follow Thompson's index in Hagedorn's trilogy data (CC BY-SA 4.0), where a crude keyword match finds 29 cells. Per cell, 96 new passages avoiding the motif's usual words, with twins; 3,456 in all, CC BY.
method: Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. A cell's direction: mean hidden state of motif passages minus twins. Hold out each cell in turn; predict its direction as row mean plus column mean minus grand mean. Score AUC for the held-out cell's test passages against those of its row and column neighbours. The predicted neuron is the one whose output weights lie nearest that direction.
rivals: The same row-plus-column arithmetic on e5 embeddings and on TF-IDF vectors; the neuron whose Transluce description best fits the cell's definition; a random direction; passage length; an LLM reader given the definition, which will win and sets the ceiling. Embedding arithmetic is the danger: analogies are what embeddings are known for. The neuron must also beat the description lookup.
premise: P1. A table that predicts where an unseen meme's neuron sits would give the atlas real periodic structure and a way to find units without examples. If only dense directions compose, the structure belongs to the model's geometry, not its neurons; if embeddings do as well, it belongs to language.
bio: Mendeleev's eka-silicon: properties predicted from the gap
cost: S. About 3,500 short passages by API (under 30 US dollars), one extraction pass of under an hour, arithmetic on a laptop; under two days.
payoff: A direct test of whether meme space has rows and columns: a property of a missing entry is predicted, then checked. If it works, the catalogue can be extended to motifs nobody has written passages for, including the cells the folktale index itself leaves empty.
risk: Row and column words can leak: stepmother passages share vocabulary even when the usual words are avoided, so the predicted direction may be a role detector plus an act detector. Scoring against row and column neighbours limits this. Family roles and violent acts are also an easy grid; a pass may not carry to subtler motifs.
review: Promoted from a seed and made concrete by the reviewer, to take the Mendeleev slot from AT-S1, which US26 already covers. Weakness: embedding arithmetic will probably tie the direction test, so the informative part is whether a single neuron sits where the table says; the grid is an easy one.
sources: Li et al. 2024, arXiv:2410.19750; Hagedorn, trilogy dataset, Zenodo 6575263; Choi et al. 2024, Scaling automatic neuron description (Transluce); Gurnee et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.01610

title: Mendeleev gaps with catalogue entries
question: Do combinations of admitted catalogue motifs that older films never used turn up more often in films released after the model was published than matched unused combinations?
note: Was design AT-S1; demoted because US26 already tests unit gaps against later films. At the study's 3% presence bar (study/paper/paper.md, section 2.3) almost no pair is unseen in 57,000 plots and chance 'realises' over half of pairs: use larger combinations and a blind reader as judge. Rival: a keyword table.

title: Two-generation cross: does a diluted meme breed true?
question: When LLM writers cross two parent stories that differ on planted memes and then cross the offspring, do the parental forms come back at full strength, or does the spread of readings halve each generation as blending predicts?
note: Added by the reviewer. The test Mendel actually ran: AT-23 sees one generation, where partial dominance and blending look alike. Statistic: variance of readings across generations. Machine culture only. Rival: an LLM reader's 0 to 4 ratings; the planted truth.

title: Independent assortment and linkage
question: Do memes from one source enter an adaptation together as linked blocks, or independently of one another?
note: Mendel's second law, on the AT-23 trios. Needs sentence positions, so a re-extraction. Rival: co-occurrence blocks of words; null by shuffling sentences within a work. Neighbour: CJ24.

title: Storage: teach a model an invented meme
question: When a small model is lightly fine-tuned on stories carrying an invented meme, does the weight change sit in a few neurons or a low-rank direction, and does a detector unit appear?
note: The storage half of the Watson and Crick question; AT-22 covers copying. Rival: three in-context examples with an embedding centroid. Cloud et al. 2025 show traits pass between models through training data. Likely needs a GPU.

title: Cistron, recon, muton for memes
question: Are the neurons that detect a meme, the neurons that carry it into a retelling and the neurons that write it when pushed the same neurons?
note: Benzer split the gene three ways with three tests. Joins AT-21 and AT-22 (which now separates reading from writing) with a steering arm. Rival: one difference-of-means direction doing all three jobs. Neighbour: EN-23.

title: Cross-walk between TV Tropes and Thompson's index
question: Does a unit that detects a TV Tropes trope in film synopses also detect the matching Thompson motif in folktales?
note: The TV Tropes half of the taxonomy check. TiMoS has 5,623 synopses tagged with 95 tropes; TV Tropes text is CC BY-NC-SA, so commit labels only. Rival: embedding similarity between the two index descriptions; an LLM matching them by reading.

title: Type passages as name anchors
question: Does publishing five type passages with each name let a lab re-find the unit in a newer checkpoint better than a twin table does?
note: The type-specimen idea from taxonomy; extends AT-24 to later model releases. Rival: the written definition read by an LLM.

title: Evidence codes that predict durability
question: Do entries that also pass a steering check keep their accuracy in new genres better than entries admitted on text tests alone?
note: Gene Ontology's evidence codes applied to AT-21 entries. Rival: the admission AUC itself as the predictor. AxBench found prompting out-steers internal units, so expect few passes.

title: Strong-regime field for every entry
question: On the texts where an admitted unit is called present, is it firing at 30% or more of its maximum over a large general corpus?
note: Cammarata's legibility claim covers strong activations only; the study's bar is relative to 69 films. IN23 tests the rule; this is the per-entry record, with a blind reader's confirmation rate on random film plots. Rival: the unit's best single word. Needs about 100 million tokens of extraction.

title: Scientific memes along citations, with shared words controlled
question: Does a paper carry the neuron units of a paper it cites more than those of an uncited paper whose wording is just as close?
hypothesis: On held-out pairs where an uncited same-year decoy is matched to the cited paper on TF-IDF similarity (word overlap weighted by rarity; within 0.02), units pick the cited paper at least 60% of the time (chance 50%), and at least 2 points more often than random units with the same firing rate.
falsifier: Unit accuracy under 55%, or within 1 point of random units, on 20,000 held-out pairs from at least 4,000 citing papers (standard error roughly 0.5 points when resampled by citing paper). A second failure after Batman would settle that neurons add nothing to words for descent.
data: SNAP cit-HepTh: 27,770 physics papers with abstracts and all 352,807 citation links among them, 1993 to 2003 (checked 2026-11-08; no licence stated, so commit only IDs). Second field: about 30,000 biomedical abstracts with links from OpenAlex (CC0 per its documentation; needs a free key, anonymous access was refused on 2026-11-08).
method: Unit: a feed-forward neuron (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B), present when it fires strongly. Re-derive Kuhn's propagation score for units and n-grams. Pick the 2,000 best-propagating units on early links. On later links between papers unseen in tuning, sharing no author, count units shared with the cited paper and with the decoy. Repeat without word-detector units. Null: time-preserving link shuffle.
rivals: TF-IDF and BM25 (near 50% by design), Kuhn's n-gram score, a general sentence embedding, a citation-trained embedding (SPECTER2) as ceiling, an LLM reading 2,000 pairs, length, random units, the model's averaged internal state, open sparse-autoencoder features if available. The general embedding is most dangerous: popular ones were trained on citation pairs. If it wins, heredity past words stands, without units.
premise: P1. A pass is the first evidence on natural text at scale that units follow inherited ideas past the wording. A fail, added to Batman, leaves P1 without practical content for descent. Agreement between the two models bears weakly on P2.
bio: Parent-offspring resemblance against relatedness-matched controls
cost: M. About 400,000 sentences, a few hours per model on a laptop; most of the two weeks goes on assembling links and matching decoys.
payoff: Whether Kuhn's finding survives word matching when it is measured in units, and a reusable heredity benchmark with tens of thousands of documented links, the scale Batman lacked.
risk: A citation is weak evidence that an idea was inherited; most references are background. Matching on TF-IDF leaves shared subtopic; a second decoy set, co-cited with the source by a third paper, tests that. Close decoys exist mainly for loosely related citations, so the test pairs may not be typical.
review: Added a closed, key-free corpus (cit-HepTh) so Kuhn's score can be re-derived; split by paper, dropped shared-author pairs, added random-unit and co-cited-decoy checks. Remaining: a citation is weak evidence of inheritance, and embeddings trained on citation pairs will probably beat units.
ranking: 2 of 3 judges thought the area reviewer rated this too high.
sources: Kuhn, Perc and Helbing 2014 (arXiv:1404.3757); SNAP cit-HepTh; OpenAlex; Edmonds 2002, Three challenges for the survival of memetics

title: Sperber's test: are retold ideas copied or rebuilt
question: When a story is retold down a chain, is its new content a copying error passed on to later retellings, or something each chain adds independently because every teller rebuilds the story the same way?
hypothesis: The memetic prediction: of the units a story gains by step 8, those inherited from the chain's own step 4 and absent from sibling chains outnumber those that also arose in sibling chains by at least 2 to 1. A step-8 retelling is matched to its own step-4 ancestor among six siblings at least 50% of the time (chance 17%).
falsifier: A copied-to-rebuilt ratio of 1 or less, with a bootstrap interval lying below 2, in both reader models, over 360 test chains from 60 stories (resampled by story; E3 had 15 works) and at least 2,000 gains; or matching under 30%. That is Sperber's outcome: new content is convergent, so shared units cannot be read as descent.
data: Built for the test and released with its lineage. 80 new 300-word stories without proper names, written from randomly drawn plot elements (20 for tuning, 60 for scoring). Each starts 6 chains that share only the seed. A chain is 8 retellings of about 150 words by two small open models taking turns, not the reader models: 3,840 texts.
method: Readers: Qwen3 8B, Llama 3.1 8B; presence rule set on tuning stories. A gain is a unit absent from the seed and from the story's first retellings, present at step 8, and rare elsewhere (not house style). Copied: also in the chain's own step 4, in no sibling. Rebuilt: in a sibling's step 8. Null: chain labels shuffled within story.
rivals: The same count on content words and on LLM-listed plot points; sentence embeddings, text length, random units and the mean-pooled residual stream for the matching test only. The LLM plot-point list is most dangerous. The ratio is a result about transmission whichever tool gives it; units earn a place only if a human check of 200 gains favours them.
premise: P1. Also bears on how E2 is read. A ratio above 2 answers Sperber for these tellers. A ratio below 1 means resemblance in retold culture is largely convergence, so a neuron-defined meme would measure a shared attractor and not a lineage.
bio: Parallel evolution in replicate lines, against inherited mutations
cost: M. About 3,900 short texts from local 4-bit models, one to two days of laptop time, plus two reading passes and one LLM plot-point pass.
payoff: A number for how much of what a retold story gains is inherited and how much is rebuilt, plus a list of convergent units to exclude from later lineage tests.
risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and the retelling prompt sets how faithfully they copy, so the ratio is a fact about these tellers. Small models may add little, leaving too few gains. Dropped details are not counted, because selection and attraction predict the same losses.
review: The original ratio depended on how profiles were centred and counted house style as attraction. Replaced with six replicate chains per story and a count of inherited gains against gains that recur in sibling chains. Remaining: model tellers, a prompt that sets fidelity, and no human chains yet.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as CE-22, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Sperber 2000; Claidière, Scott-Phillips and Sperber 2014; Perez et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04503); Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023

title: Silent and loud mutations in copied news quotes
question: When a news quote changes by one word as it is copied, can neuron units tell meaning-keeping changes from meaning-changing ones, and are the meaning-changing versions reused less often?
hypothesis: On 600 hand-labelled natural swaps, the change in pre-chosen units separates silent swaps (meaning kept) from loud ones (meaning changed) with an AUC of at least 0.75 (0.5 is chance), within 0.05 of sentence-embedding similarity. Loud versions are then reused by another site at most 80% as often as silent ones.
falsifier: AUC under 0.65, or more than 0.05 below embeddings (standard error about 0.02). For spread: with at least 3,000 swaps, 500 of them loud, a loud-to-silent reuse ratio above 0.95 whose 95% interval excludes 0.8. With fewer swaps the spread test is declared uninformative, not passed.
data: MemeTracker phrase clusters (SNAP; one 220 MB file, reachable 2026-11-08; August 2008 to April 2009; no licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived numbers). One-word swaps mined with Lerique and Roth's method (code GPLv3); the number of swaps is unknown until mined. 800 swaps labelled by hand, 150 of them twice. Tuning pairs built from WordNet synonyms and antonyms.
method: Pairs share every word but one, so word overlap cannot separate them. Drop tense, number and spelling changes. Choose units on built pairs (synonym swap silent, antonym swap loud) and 200 labelled swaps; score on 600. The best tool labels all swaps; compare reuse by a later, different site within parent quote and week. Null: labels shuffled within parent.
rivals: Edit distance (constant by design), WordNet synonymy and word-vector similarity of the two swapped words, sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM judging both versions, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM judge is most likely to win. The silent-to-loud split and the spread test then run on its labels and still give memetics a fidelity figure.
premise: P1. A pass shows units respond to meaning in natural minimal pairs, where the study had 31 hand-made rewordings. A fail says units are too coarse for short texts. The spread result says whether meaning is protected in copying; Atran and the memeticists both expect that, so it does not separate them.
bio: Synonymous against non-synonymous mutation (dN/dS)
cost: M. Model time is under a day because quotes are short; mining the swaps and hand-labelling 800 pairs take about three days for one person.
payoff: A first copying-fidelity figure for ideas as opposed to strings: what share of copying errors is silent, and whether meaning-changing errors are weeded out.
risk: Most MemeTracker variants are truncations, so clean one-word swaps may number only a few thousand. Which version is the parent is inferred from timing, not documented. A loud change may be the correction of a misquote, which would spread more and hide selection.
review: Replaced PAWS (word-order pairs, the wrong kind) with built synonym and antonym swaps; changed the spread outcome to reuse by another site and said when it is uninformative. Remaining: an LLM judge will win the labelling, swap counts are unknown, and parent direction is inferred.
sources: Leskovec, Backstrom and Kleinberg 2009 (MemeTracker); Lerique and Roth 2018; Simmons, Adamic and Adar 2011; Atran 2001

title: Heylighen's selection criteria on randomised headline tests
question: Do the criteria that Heylighen (1998) says help a meme get noticed and accepted, scored by neuron units chosen in advance, predict which headline wins a randomised test?
hypothesis: On confirmatory tests, at least 4 of 6 criteria (distinctiveness, novelty, simplicity, authority, formality, utility) raise click rate with 95% intervals excluding zero, and together they add at least 2 points of winner accuracy over headline length and punctuation.
falsifier: Fewer than 3 of 6 criteria significant in the predicted direction, or under 1 added point, on at least 5,000 confirmatory tests where only the headline differs (standard error about 0.7 points). Separately, units fail if LLM ratings of the same criteria beat them by more than 1 point.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (OSF jd64p, CC BY 4.0): 32,487 randomised tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015. Drop tests the archive's own column flags for unreliable randomisation (about 22%); keep tests where only the headline differs (count not yet checked). Tune on its exploratory part, score once on its confirmatory part. Archived data; nothing is optimised on a live audience.
method: Use only criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation (being noticed, understood, accepted), which a click measures. For each, write 80 contrast pairs (same content, criterion high or low); pick units on 60, check on 20, freeze. No click data chooses units. Within each test, criterion differences predict the winner (conditional logistic regression), controlling length and punctuation. Null: arms shuffled within test.
rivals: An LLM rating each headline 1 to 7 on each criterion, readability and word-rarity formulas, an embedding probe trained on the contrast pairs, word n-grams, sparse-autoencoder features (Movva et al. 2025), random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM rater is most dangerous, because the criteria are defined in words. If it wins, the criteria still get a signed test.
premise: P1. If unit-scored criteria predict as well as LLM ratings, units measure abstract properties of a meme and not only words. If only the ratings work, the theory survives without the unit. If neither works, the criteria fail at the attention stage.
bio: Selection gradients on named traits
cost: M. 150,000 headlines take an hour or two per model; rating six criteria with a local LLM takes about a day.
payoff: The first test of Heylighen's assimilation criteria as a signed set on randomised data, and a check of whether units chosen in advance can stand in for a reader's rating.
risk: Simplicity is already known to win on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024), so one criterion is a replication. Heylighen himself hedges on formality. Contrast pairs written by an LLM may differ in style as well as in the criterion. Click-bait habits may swamp the rest.
review: Cut to the six criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation; expressivity and proselytism belong to later stages. Removed an unsourced count of flagged tests. Simplicity is already published on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024). Remaining: LLM ratings will probably tie the units.
sources: Heylighen 1998; Matias et al. 2021 (Upworthy Research Archive); Shulman, Markowitz and Rogers 2024; Movva et al. 2025 (arXiv:2502.04382)

title: Do reposted ideas wear out beyond their words
question: When an image is reposted to Reddit under a new title, does repeating the idea of an earlier title cost votes even when no words are shared?
hypothesis: Among reposts sharing no content word with earlier titles of the image, similarity in units to earlier titles lowers vote rank by at least 1.5 percentile points more (most against least similar third) than similarity to later titles, which cannot cause fatigue. The penalty is larger when the earlier post was in the same subreddit.
falsifier: An earlier-minus-later gap under 0.5 points, or of the wrong sign, on at least 20,000 reposts that have both earlier and later titles (standard error about 0.6 points, resampled by image). Units also fail if the gap disappears once sentence-embedding similarity is added to the model.
data: SNAP Reddit submissions (Lakkaraju et al. 2013): 132,308 posts of 16,736 images, July 2008 to January 2013, one 7.6 MB CSV. Counted on the file on 2026-11-08: 53,515 reposts share no content word with any earlier title, and 46,201 of those also have a later title. No licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived features.
method: First re-derive the published word-based title effect; units must reproduce it on reposts that share words. Outcome: vote rank within subreddit and month, adjusted for hour, repost number and days since the last post (a content-free baseline, after Weng). Predictor: similarity to earlier titles, and to later titles as placebo, in units, words and embeddings. Tune on 30% of images.
rivals: Word overlap (zero by design), sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM asked whether two titles make the same point, title length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. Embeddings are most dangerous. If they win, idea fatigue is still shown beyond words, which is Coscia's claim under control, and the unit is not needed for it.
premise: P1. A penalty that units detect where words cannot would show units following a short idea through rewording in wild data. A null or an embedding tie leaves P1 where Batman left it.
bio: Negative frequency-dependent selection
cost: S. 132,000 short titles, under an hour per model, and a day of analysis.
payoff: Whether competition for attention acts on ideas or on strings, and an answer to whether similar memes help or hurt each other with the content held fixed.
risk: Titles are short (median 5 words, counted on the file) and describe an image the model never sees, so unit profiles may be mostly noise. A title close to earlier ones may only be a plain description; the later-title placebo removes that only if plain titles are as common early as late.
review: Made the later-title placebo the test statistic and added a same-subreddit contrast, because closeness to earlier titles may only mark a plain description. Confirmed 53,515 eligible reposts on the file. Remaining: titles have a median of 5 words, so unit profiles may be noise.
sources: Lakkaraju, McAuley and Leskovec 2013; Coscia 2014; Weng et al. 2012

title: Do memes survive retelling better in bundles
question: Does a story element survive a chain of retellings more often when its usual partner element (say, a vow of revenge beside an orphaned hero) is in the story than when an unrelated element takes the partner's place?
hypothesis: After four retellings an element survives at least 10 percentage points more often in a whole bundle than in a broken one, the gap is positive in at least 17 of 24 bundles, and a neutral filler element shows less than half that gap.
falsifier: A gap under 3 points, or a 95% interval (resampled by bundle) that includes zero, over 1,440 chains from 480 seed stories (standard error about 3.5 points). That would mean elements are lost one by one, and the memeplex adds nothing to its parts in transmission.
data: Built for the test. 24 two-element bundles fixed in advance, from the trope pairs that co-occur most in the TV Tropes tables of Gala et al. 2020 (pair list only; the site's licence is non-commercial). Each gets 10 outlines, written whole and broken: 480 name-free 300-word stories, 3 chains of 4 retellings, 5,760 texts. Released with its lineage.
method: A memeplex is a set of memes said to help each other spread. A coin flip decides whether the partner is present, so topic cannot explain the gap. Survival at the last step is read by units chosen on separate planted-element stories and checked against 400 human-labelled retellings. Statistic: survival in whole minus broken stories, paired by outline.
rivals: A keyword list for each element, an embedding probe, an LLM reader asked whether the element is present, text length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM reader is most dangerous, and the keyword list will win for elements with an obvious word. If either wins, the bundle effect is still the first randomised test of co-adapted memes.
premise: P1. The bundle effect itself does not depend on the unit. Units earn a place only if units chosen on planted stories track an element through four rewordings as accurately as the LLM reader, judged against the human labels.
bio: Fitness epistasis; co-adapted gene complexes
cost: M. About 6,500 short texts from local 4-bit models, two to three days of laptop time, plus half a day labelling 400 retellings.
payoff: A causal number for whether memes in a complex protect each other in transmission, and a list of bundles that behave as larger units.
risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and four short retellings may keep everything (chain length is set on tuning stories). Memory research already shows that causally linked events are recalled better (Trabasso and van den Broek 1985), so a pass may be old news under a new name.
review: The citation version could not fail: units that co-fire inside the model, and words in set phrases, stay linked whatever culture does. Rewritten as a randomised test of whether a partner element protects an element in retelling. Remaining: model tellers; memory research partly predicts the result.
sources: Dawkins 1976; Blackmore 1999; Trabasso and van den Broek 1985; Gala et al. 2020 (TV Tropes dataset)

title: Know Your Meme family tree
question: Does a meme entry carry the units of its documented parent meme more than those of unrelated memes?
note: IMKG (Tommasini et al. 2023) and the Zannettou et al. 2018 Zenodo set hold the links. Hosting, licence and scraping terms are unchecked. Captions follow templates, so word overlap will probably win; the images need vision neurons.

title: Dennett's grain size
question: At what unit size (single neuron, merged family, sentence, document) does heredity along citations peak, and does the curve differ from the one for unigram, bigram and phrase?
note: Reuses ME21's data. A flat curve, or one that tracks the n-gram curve, means there is no natural meme size.

title: Edmonds' Challenge 1, items 4 and 5
question: Do unit frequencies across generations of papers show a non-zero selection term in a Price-equation split, against a content-free limited-attention simulation?
note: Weng et al. 2012 supplies the null; the rival is the same split on n-grams. Analysis only once ME21 exists.

title: The 1997 learned unit, side by side
question: Do Pocklington and Best's latent-semantic term clusters match neuron units on ME21's word-matched citation test?
note: A learned unit was tried 29 years ago and changed nothing. If it ties neurons here, the instrument was not what memetics lacked.

title: Memorable against forgotten movie lines
question: Do Heylighen's criteria, scored by the units frozen in ME24, pick the memorable quote over a matched line by the same speaker in the same scene?
note: Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. 2012. The Cornell data page failed with a certificate error again on 2026-11-08, so hosting is unconfirmed. The rival is their word-rarity model. It would cover the retention stage, which ME24 cannot.

title: Lynch's pass-it-on unit
question: Is there a unit for 'urge the reader to pass this on', and does it predict copy number in chain letters or copy-pasted posts?
note: No public cascade data found: Adamic et al.'s Facebook data is closed and the chain-letter archive was unreachable. A keyword list is the rival and will be hard to beat.

title: Sperber's test on human chains
question: Does ME22's copied-to-rebuilt ratio hold when people do the retelling, and how much of what survives is explained by the receiver and not the source (Gabora)?
note: Breithaupt et al. 2018 ran 285 human chains of three retellings, but on only three base stories, and whether the retelling texts are public is unconfirmed (one supplementary file). Needed before ME22 says anything about people.

title: Copy the product or the instructions
question: Do chains that regenerate a story from an outline keep more units than chains that paraphrase the finished text, as Blackmore claims?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: CE-S6.
note: Blackmore's distinction is confirmed; which mode she ranks as more faithful is from memory. Rival: content-word retention. A cheap extra arm for ME22.

title: Linkage along citations
question: Are pairs of units passed from a cited paper to a citing paper together more often than their separate rates predict?
note: Demoted. Units that co-fire inside the model and words in set phrases would stay linked across periods whatever culture does, and a shared subtopic gives the same pattern. It needs pairs with no background association before it can fail.

title: A mutation rate per retelling
question: What share of units is lost or gained at each step of a retelling chain, and is the rate lower for units than for content words?
note: Free once ME22's chains exist. Dawkins's copying fidelity as a number. The rival is the same rate on words and on LLM-listed plot points; a figure for people needs the human chains named in the Sperber seed.

title: Citations the paper leans on
question: Does ME21's unit advantage grow for references that the citing paper mentions several times in its full text?
note: Answers ME21's weak ground truth with a dose measure that does not come from the abstracts. Needs open full text with in-text citation counts (the PubMed Central open-access subset that Kuhn used); parsing and coverage are unchecked.

title: Prior-art search still owed
question: Has anyone already used neuron or sparse-autoencoder features as the unit in a citation, headline or retelling-chain test?
note: Web search was unavailable during this review (the shared budget was used up), so checks were limited to dataset pages, Crossref and the arXiv API. Run a proper search before any design here is expanded.

title: Retelling traditions with a known tree and dosed rewording
question: When a story is passed down a tree drawn in advance, with rewording fixed at one of four levels from verbatim copy to retelling through another language, do neuron memes (story units read from which neurons fire) recover each text's true parent better than word and embedding methods?
hypothesis: On the six sealed tales, at the two heaviest rewording levels, neuron memes name the true parent first at least 10 percentage points more often than the best cheap rival, and that lead is larger than at the lighter levels. On verbatim copies every method scores above 95% and the difference is within 3 points.
falsifier: On the 276 sealed parent-child steps at the two heaviest levels, the neuron-minus-best-rival gap has a 95% interval, from resampling tales and then steps within them, that includes zero, or the gap does not widen from copy to heaviest level. That sample gives about 80% power for a 10 to 12-point gap at 30% disagreement; confirm by simulation.
data: Built, then released under CC BY-SA 4.0 like its seed corpus: 8 little-known tales from Folktexts (Zenodo 6575263, pre-1930 editions), each grown at four rewording levels (copy, paraphrase, retold from notes, retold through another language) into a 24-text tree: 768 texts. Two tales for development, six sealed. Two open writer models unrelated to the readers, drawn at random per step.
method: Each step plants plot changes, never swapped names or objects; a second reader confirms they survive. Each method ranks earlier texts as candidate parents, settings frozen on development tales. Statistic: share of true parents ranked first; also a triplet score (which two of three texts are closer). Null: relabel within tradition and generation. A 24-text human-retold tradition checks writer habits.
rivals: Word-overlap scores (TF-IDF, BM25), compression distance, two sentence-embedding models (vectors that summarise a passage), a local LLM ranking candidate parents, text length, random non-meme units, the model's averaged internal state, and learned sparse-autoencoder features (Llama Scope). Most dangerous: sentence embeddings, trained on paraphrase. If they win, the benchmark still shows where each method breaks.
premise: both. P1: a neuron advantage that grows as wording is destroyed would be the first evidence that neurons carry descent that words miss; a tie or loss at heavy rewording leaves P1 without a use in lineage work. P2: it shows whether Qwen and Llama make the same parent errors beyond what a word-based ranking predicts.
bio: Lab-evolved lineages with a recorded tree; simulated sequence evolution.
cost: M: about a week on one laptop. About 740 local retellings with survival checks over two or three nights, extraction in minutes, a few hours of LLM parent ranking, and about 6 volunteer hours for the human-retold tradition.
payoff: The first public known-tree benchmark where wording does not carry descent, and a curve showing the rewording level at which each method stops finding parents.
risk: A child differs from its parent by only a few plot changes, so at heavy rewording every method may sit near the floor; or writer-model habits are read as descent; or sentence embeddings win at every level and neurons add nothing.
review: Changed: eight tales with smaller trees so tales can be resampled (was two sealed tales); planted changes are plot events, not nouns that survive paraphrase; random writer per step; licence CC BY-SA. Remains: model-written text; six sealed tales is few; prior work not searched (search budget spent).
sources: Roos and Heikkilä 2009; Spencer et al. 2004; Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023; Hagedorn and Darányi 2022 (Folktexts, Zenodo 6575263)

title: Cross-language source finding for film adaptations
question: When a film's plot summary is in German, French, Spanish or Chinese and its documented source's summary is in English, so that no words are shared, do neuron memes (story units read from a language model's neurons) find the source better than translating and counting words?
hypothesis: On 400 held-out pairs with names masked, neuron memes read in the film's own language rank the documented source first among 20 matched candidates at least 7 percentage points more often than machine translation followed by word matching, and no more than 5 points below the best embedding model.
falsifier: Neuron first-place accuracy is not above translate-then-word-matching (paired one-sided p at or above 0.05), or is more than 5 points below the best embedding model. 400 pairs give about 80% power for a 7-point gap when two methods disagree on 30% of pairs.
data: Wikidata 'based on' links (CC0). Films whose source has an English Wikipedia article: 6,690 with a French article, 5,220 German, 4,357 Spanish, 2,559 Chinese (Qwen only). Plots are CC BY-SA; the Tell Me Again dataset holds name-free summaries in five languages. 600 pairs, 15 plot sentences a side, one film per source: 200 development, 400 test. Coverage is counted first.
method: Each non-English plot is ranked against 20 English source plots: the true one and 19 decoys matched on medium, decade and genre, excluding same-author and same-series works. Score: share of the source's distinctive units found in the film; thresholds set per language. Settings frozen on development pairs. Null: shuffle source labels within groups. Pairs sharing translated eight-word runs are dropped.
rivals: Machine translation then word matching (BM25); neuron memes on the translated plot; multilingual embeddings (multilingual-e5, LaBSE); story-emb, an embedding trained on name-free summaries of one story; a local LLM reading both plots; plot length; random non-meme units; the averaged internal state. Most dangerous: the embeddings, built for this task. Losing to translate-then-match means the units are tied to language.
premise: both. P1: a pass shows units carry story content when wording cannot; a fail, after the Batman tie, makes two corpora where neurons add nothing to words for descent. P2: units and settings chosen on English must work in other languages, and Qwen and Llama should rank the same sources.
bio: Recognising the same gene across species despite silent spelling changes.
cost: M: one to two weeks on one laptop, no paid services. Roughly 1,800 plots; extraction under an hour per model; translating 600 plots and 8,000 LLM pair readings take most of the time, plus name masking in each language where Tell Me Again does not cover a pair.
payoff: A verdict on heredity outside Batman with over 40 times as many adaptations, where shared wording is ruled out by construction. It supersedes the deferred translation protocol by using summaries that people wrote in each language.
risk: Multilingual embeddings win easily and neurons trail even translate-then-match; French and Spanish plots may be too short, leaving a German-only test; the models have memorised which famous film came from which book, so results are read on the obscure half; and story-emb was trained on these same Wikipedia summaries.
review: German and French counts confirmed. Added story-emb and neurons-on-translation as rivals, per-language thresholds, a same-author decoy ban, one film per source and a reuse audit. Remains: plot coverage unknown (a tiny sample found long German and short French plots); translation is itself a neural reader; famous pairs are memorised.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 6). A family tree across a language border on 400 real adaptations is the strongest possible form of the Batman heredity result, although neurons beating translate-then-match is perhaps a one-in-four chance.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as PO-21, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Wikidata query service counts, 2026-11-08; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again; Story Embeddings); Chaturvedi et al. 2018; preregistration/translation_protocol.md

title: Rebuilding a hidden source from its sibling adaptations
question: Using neuron memes (story units read from a language model's neurons), can the content of a common source be inferred from three or more of its film adaptations alone, and does the result match the surviving source better than a word-based reconstruction and the genre's typical story?
hypothesis: With names masked, the set of units shared by most sibling films picks the true source first among all other sources in the test pool at least 12 percentage points more often than the same consensus built from words, and at least 10 points more often than one sibling used alone.
falsifier: On at least 120 held-out sources, the neuron consensus is not above the word consensus (paired one-sided p at or above 0.05), or it beats a single sibling by under 5 points. 120 sources give about 80% power for a 12-point paired gap when methods disagree on 30% of sources. Not run with fewer.
data: Wikidata 'based on' links (CC0): 482 sources have three or more film adaptations with English Wikipedia articles throughout (recounted 2026-11-08). Many are characters or series with no single plot (Scooby-Doo, James Bond) and are excluded; early films often lack plot sections. Plots are CC BY-SA. Target: 40 development and at least 120 test sources with 15-sentence plots, counted before registration.
method: Treat the source as lost. Ancestral units are those in most siblings; derived units appear in one. Rank the true source among all other pooled sources, themselves much-adapted works. Test whether ancestral units occur in the real source more often than derived units and than units shared by unrelated same-genre films. Report separately where siblings are remakes of each other.
rivals: Word consensus (rarity-weighted words in most siblings), the average of sibling embedding vectors (a general model and story-emb), a local LLM writing the source's plot from the siblings, plot length, random non-meme units, the model's averaged internal state and sparse-autoencoder features. Most dangerous: the LLM, which knows these classics; results are split by fame. The unit-level test stands either way.
premise: P1. If neuron units are heritable traits, those shared by siblings should be the source's own, beyond what the genre supplies. A pass supports the unit as a character for reconstruction; a fail says shared units reflect genre convention, not descent. P2 gets a side check: Qwen and Llama should reconstruct overlapping ancestors.
bio: Ancestral sequence reconstruction checked against a preserved ancestor.
cost: S to M: under 2 days of model time on one laptop, but fetching and name-masking about 1,000 plots is the real work. Extraction under an hour per model; 160 LLM reconstructions.
payoff: A tested way to describe a lost or unknown source from its descendants, and a direct check of whether shared units mark common descent or only a shared genre.
risk: Wikipedia editors reuse wording between a source's summary and its adaptations' summaries, so the word consensus wins (passages with copied eight-word runs are dropped); and later films copy earlier films, so the consensus may rebuild the film tradition, not the book.
review: Recount confirmed 482 sources, but the list includes characters and series, so the sample is cut to 120 with a not-run rule and a 12-point claim. Decoys are now other much-adapted sources. Remains: memorised classics, sibling films that copy each other, shared Wikipedia wording.
sources: Wikidata query service counts, 2026-11-08; da Silva and Tehrani 2016; Fritz and Purvis 2010; Claidière, Scott-Phillips and Sperber 2014

title: Detecting a second parent in blended retellings
question: When a retelling is known by construction to merge two earlier versions, can neuron memes (story units read from a language model's neurons) show that a second parent exists and name it better than word overlap can, against the simpler view that every text has one parent?
hypothesis: Given one parent, neuron memes name the other first among the remaining earlier texts at least 12 percentage points more often than word overlap does, and their second-parent score separates blended from single-parent texts with AUC (ranking accuracy; 0.5 is chance) of at least 0.70.
falsifier: On 120 sealed blended texts, second-parent accuracy is not above the word-overlap version (paired one-sided p at or above 0.05), or the AUC is below 0.60. 120 blended and 276 single-parent texts give about 80% power for a 12-point gap at 30% disagreement and an AUC standard error near 0.03.
data: Built on the LI21 traditions (CC BY-SA 4.0): in each tale at the two heaviest rewording levels, 10 extra texts merge two versions at least four steps apart, keeping a planted change from each: 40 development, 120 sealed. Natural check, descriptive only: of 341 Wikidata films with two or more sources (reviewer's query, 2026-11-08), at most 39 blend unrelated stories.
method: Each method receives the blended text and one true parent, the same for all methods, and ranks every other earlier text as the second parent after discarding units shared with the given parent. Existence test: the best remaining score, for blended against single-parent texts of the same generation. Settings frozen on development tales. Null: shuffle second-parent labels within a tradition.
rivals: The same procedure with rarity-weighted words (TF-IDF), with embeddings after subtracting the given parent's vector, a local LLM asked which other text was used, text length, random non-meme units, the model's averaged internal state and sparse-autoencoder features. Most dangerous: words, because leftover distinctive words point at the second parent. If words tie, sparseness matters, not neurons.
premise: P1. Separate units can be split between two parents in a way one blended vector cannot, so this is where a discrete unit should earn its keep. A pass gives a detector of mixed descent validated on known blends and supports networks over trees; a fail leaves the study's failed tree result without a remedy.
bio: Hybrid detection and gene-flow tests, validated on known hybrids.
cost: S once LI21 exists: about 2 days on one laptop. 160 extra blended retellings with survival checks, extraction in minutes, about 3,000 LLM readings. The natural check adds about 120 plots to fetch and mask.
payoff: A tested rule for saying 'this text has a second parent, and it is this one', which the Batman films need, and evidence on whether discrete units handle mixed descent better than a single vector.
risk: Blends built inside one tale may be too easy or too hard for every method and say little about franchises, and the natural set of at most 39 films is too small to confirm anything.
review: Rebuilt. The Wikidata sample cannot work: of 341 two-source films, 131 have one source based on the other, 76 share a series and at most 39 are real blends. Now uses built two-parent texts in LI21, with the films as a descriptive check. Remains: depends on LI21; blends are artificial.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as RX-27, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Roos and Heikkilä 2009; Wikidata query service counts, 2026-11-08; Greenhill, Currie and Gray 2009; Temkin and Eldredge 2007

title: Shakespeare as a second lineage with original-text parents
question: Does source finding repeat in a second well-documented lineage when the parent is the 400-year-old play text and the child a modern film summary, and do neuron memes (story units read from a language model's neurons) beat words and embeddings there, having tied with words on Batman's Wikipedia summaries?
hypothesis: Across 80 documented films, at most 8 per play, neuron memes rank the true play first among 37 at least 15 percentage points more often than the best of word overlap and sentence embeddings when the parent is the original play text. With the play's Wikipedia synopsis as parent, neurons and words are expected to tie.
falsifier: With original-text parents, the neuron-minus-best-rival gap has a 95% interval, from resampling plays, that includes zero. 80 films from 20 plays, 8 of them with one film, give about 80% power only for a gap near 18 to 20 points; a smaller true gap will read as undetermined, and that limit is accepted in advance.
data: Committed list `preregistration/works_shakespeare.json`: 40 plays, 177 eligible films, 107 primary films documented by a lead sentence or Wikidata link across 20 plays; 80 after capping each play at 8. Parents: the public-domain Moby text (37 plays, shakespeare.mit.edu), Wikipedia synopses (CC BY-SA), and the Lambs' 1807 prose retellings (20 plays, covering 72 of the 80 films; digital copy to be located).
method: With character names masked, each film's summary is scored against every play using the frozen Batman heredity score. Three parent forms are compared (original verse in equal-length samples, 1807 prose retelling, Wikipedia synopsis) and two film tiers (same-title, renamed). Null: shuffle play labels within comedies, histories and tragedies. A 'name the play' question to the model flags films it recognises.
rivals: Rarity-weighted word overlap (TF-IDF, BM25), a general sentence-embedding model and the story-trained story-emb, a local LLM reading film and play, text length, random non-meme units, the model's averaged internal state and sparse-autoencoder features. Most dangerous: the LLM reader, which knows Shakespeare by heart; it is reported apart. The claim is decided against the best of BM25 and the embeddings.
premise: P1. It asks whether the Batman tie between neurons and words came from shared Wikipedia wording. A neuron lead with original-text or 1807 parents but not with synopses would support units as carriers of content across medium and four centuries of language. A second tie means neurons add nothing to words for descent.
bio: A second model organism, as the mouse followed the fruit fly.
cost: M: about a week on one laptop. The 37 play texts extract in under an hour per model; masking names in plays, retellings and film summaries is the main labour.
payoff: Heredity tested in a second lineage with 37 candidate parents in their primary text, showing whether the Batman result was about stories or about Wikipedia summaries. It supersedes the deferred Shakespeare protocol.
risk: Only 80 usable films from 20 plays, so only a large gap can be confirmed; small models may read verse so differently from prose summaries that every method sits near chance; and every model knows these plays by heart.
review: Counts confirmed in the committed list. Changed: the claim is decided against the best of words and embeddings, not BM25 alone; the Lambs' 1807 prose retellings added as a third parent form; an untestable 5-point tie claim dropped; power corrected. Remains: 80 films, memorised plays.
ranking: 2 of 3 judges thought the area reviewer rated this too high.
sources: preregistration/works_shakespeare.json; MIT Complete Works of Shakespeare (Moby text), shakespeare.mit.edu; Lamb and Lamb 1807, Tales from Shakespeare; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Story Embeddings)

title: Open-pool search for documented loose influence
question: Can a search with no candidate list, using neuron memes (story units read from a language model's neurons) and calibrated on credited adaptations, find documented inspirations that were never formal adaptations among thousands of earlier works, better than word search, embeddings or fame alone?
hypothesis: With a shortlist of 30 from roughly 3,000 earlier works (a 1% false-alarm threshold set on development data), neuron memes recover at least 30% of documented inspirations, at least 9 percentage points more than the best of word search, sentence embeddings and a fame-only ranking.
falsifier: Recall in that shortlist is not above the best cheap rival (paired one-sided p at or above 0.05), or is under 10%. 150 test pairs give about 80% power for a 9-point gap when methods disagree on 20% of pairs. Not run with fewer than 150 test pairs having adequate plots on both sides.
data: Targets: Wikidata 'inspired by' links (CC0) with no 'based on' link for the pair. Reviewer's query, 2026-11-08: 3,713 pairs have English articles on both sides; 528 are dated, plot-bearing works, many of them video games, parodies and television formats; 213 targets are film or television. Pool: the 996 random films in `preregistration/culture_pool.json` plus about 2,000 documented source works, names masked.
method: Each target is scored against every earlier work. The threshold is fixed on development 'based on' pairs so that 1% of unlinked earlier works pass: about 30 false alarms per target, a shortlist and not a verdict. Report recall in the top 30 and top 5, parodies apart. One person, blind to method, checks 50 undocumented top hits.
rivals: Word search (BM25), sentence embeddings (a general model and story-emb), BM25 shortlisting 20 works for a local LLM to read, a fame-only ranking (how often a work is a documented source), plot length, random non-meme units and the averaged internal state. Most dangerous: fame alone and shortlist-then-read, since inspirations are famous works; results are split by fame.
premise: P1. Finding influence nobody credited is the use memetics most needs and the study never tested. A pass shows a detector tuned on declared descent transfers to looser influence at a stated error rate. A fail, or a tie with embeddings or fame, means similarity search already does this and neurons unlock nothing here.
bio: Paternity testing, validated on recorded pedigrees.
cost: M: one to two weeks on one laptop. About 3,500 plots to fetch and name-mask, extraction about 30 minutes per model, and about 3 hours for one human reader.
payoff: A shortlist tool for candidate influences with a measured hit rate and false-alarm rate, and a first list of candidate uncredited influences to check, including among Batman's documented relatives.
