risk: Wikidata's 'inspired by' links are sparse, favour famous works and often record a mood or image that no plot summary shows, so recall is low for every method and the comparison is uninformative.
review: Changed: fame-only rival added; decoys are random films and documented sources, since over half the committed culture pool is Batman-like genres; the 1% threshold is restated as a 30-work shortlist; minimum cut to 150 pairs. Remains: 'inspired by' links are declared and sparse, so undeclared influence stays unvalidated.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as RX-22, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Wikidata query service counts, 2026-11-08; preregistration/culture_pool.json; Chang et al. 2024; Kelly et al. 2021

title: Scribe-copy floor on the stemmatology challenge sets
question: On hand-copied traditions with a known tree (Parzival, Notre Besoin, Heinrichi), do neuron memes at least tie string methods at recovering it?
note: Calibration only; verbatim copying means a tie is the best case. Published rivals on Parzival: n-gram clustering 79.3%, compression distance 81.5%. Data is restricted to challenge use; ask permission.

title: Per-unit heritability on a known tree
question: Taken one unit at a time, are neuron units more clumped on the true tree than frequency-matched words?
note: Fritz and Purvis's D on the LI21 traditions, as da Silva and Tehrani did for tales. Rivals: single words and embedding dimensions split at the median.

title: Tree-likeness audit of the Batman distance matrices
question: Is the Batman meme distance matrix tree-like at all, and more or less so than the word-count matrix?
note: Delta scores and NeighborNet on the meme matrices in `study/results/phylo.json.gz`; the rival TF-IDF matrix must be rebuilt from the committed texts, since the file keeps only its tree. An afternoon, no model runs. A good score proves little (Nunn et al. 2010); a bad one ends the tree framing.

title: Human telephone-game chains as real descent
question: From the last retellings in human retelling chains, can a method pick the seed story they came from?
note: Breithaupt et al. 2018 ran 285 three-step chains from 21 seeds (three base stories in seven variants each). The article page has no data statement; whether its supplement holds the retold texts is unchecked. Rivals: sentence embeddings, an LLM reader.

title: Telling parent from child without dates
question: Given two works known to be related, with dates hidden, can a method say which one descends from the other?
note: Similarity is symmetric, so this needs a directed measure. Use documented Wikidata pairs within one medium (remakes). Rivals: text length alone, directed word overlap, an LLM reader. Chance is 50%.

title: Sherlock Holmes canon as a third organism
question: With the 60 public-domain Holmes stories as candidate parents, can adaptations be matched to the story they came from?
note: Holmes and Watson are in every candidate, so names cannot give the source away. Bottleneck: Wikidata lists 41 films over 18 stories, and Wikipedia's Granada episode summaries are one or two sentences. Rival: BM25 on the story texts.

title: A fiction wiki as a primary-text organism
question: Can descent be traced in the SCP wiki, where every text is primary, openly licensed, dated, tagged, rated and linked?
note: Links and translation branches record descent, tags name memes, ratings measure success; CC BY-SA 3.0. No ready dataset joins them, so it needs a crawl. Rivals: TF-IDF and an LLM reader.

title: Do two models' trees agree because both are right?
question: On a known tree, is the agreement between Qwen and Llama trees explained by truth or only by shared vocabulary?
note: On the LI21 traditions, correlate the two models' distance matrices after removing the word-count matrix and true path lengths. Floor: random-unit trees agree at 0.90 to 0.93 on Batman (`study/results/robustness/nulls.json`).

title: Twin films as a convergence control
question: Can any method tell documented descent (remakes, adaptations) from twin films, which have similar plots and no documented link?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: CJ-22.
note: Added in review. Wikipedia's 'Twin films' article lists roughly 200 pairs, 1912 to 2026 (CC BY-SA); some share a pitched script, so 'independent' is soft. This is biology's convergence problem: similarity without descent. Rivals: BM25, story-emb, an LLM reader. Every method at chance would be a useful limit.

title: Post-cutoff adaptations as a memory-free subset
question: Do source-finding results hold for films released after the reader models' training cut-offs, where no model can have memorised which film came from which book?
note: Added in review. Filter the LI22 and LI23 pairs by release date against each model's stated cut-off; count first. It controls recognition, the confound shared by LI22, LI23, LI25 and LI26. Rivals as in LI22. The source itself may still be memorised; only the link is new.

title: Hidden ancestors in built traditions
question: In the LI21 traditions, can the units of a withheld inner text be inferred from its descendants and checked against the real text better than words allow?
note: Added in review. The known-tree version of LI23, as in ancestral sequence reconstruction: withhold each inner text that has two or more children. Rivals: word consensus, averaged child embeddings, an LLM rewriting the parent. Analysis only once LI21 exists.

title: Is everything a remix? A ledger with a floor
question: Once measurement noise is removed, what share of a film plot's meme units and unit pairs had never appeared in any earlier plot, and is that more than chance once release dates are shuffled?
hypothesis: Remix nearly holds. Under 1% of a late film's repeatable units are first appearances. Yet new memes exist: recurring units born after 2000 number at least twice the count found when release years are shuffled. New pairings of old units exceed their shuffled count by at least 1.5 times.
falsifier: Unit birth excess under 1.2 with a bootstrap interval including 1: no detectable invention, or a blind instrument. First-appearance share over 5%: remix fails. Stop early if two-summary agreement (kappa) is under 0.4 or within 0.1 of mismatched films. Check on 1985 to 1999 births that at least 200 born units exist.
data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 plot summaries of 29,505 stories from five Wikipedia language editions, machine-translated to English, with Wikidata year and genre. Sample 8,000 films with two or more summaries. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA; the dataset's own licence is unconfirmed. About 13% of summary pairs are direct translations; drop near-duplicates.
method: Set each unit's presence bar on 1,500 unscored films. A unit is in a film only if present in two differently worded summaries. Count units and pairs seen in two or more films whose first appearance falls after 2000. Null: release years permuted within genre and length band. Statistic: observed-to-shuffled ratio (birth excess), bootstrapped over films.
rivals: The same ledger with word stems and stem pairs, Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features, random non-meme units and embedding clusters; a reconstruction score (Lu 2025); an LLM listing what is new (500 films); length. Most dangerous: word stems, since new things bring new words. If stems give the same excess, the finding stands without neurons.
premise: P1. If presence does not repeat across two wordings better than word stems do, neuron novelty scores are uninterpretable and the unit adds nothing here. Running Qwen and Llama shows whether two models call the same units new, a first P2 check for novelty.
bio: De novo genes versus duplication and recombination.
cost: M: about a week. Roughly 20,000 summaries, a few hours of forward passes per model; the permuted ledger over unit pairs is the heavy computation.
payoff: A version of 'everything is a remix' that can fail, with numbers for inherited, new and newly combined; and the first test-retest reliability figure for meme presence, which every novelty measure depends on.
risk: Summaries in different language editions may share a source, inflating repeatability. A unit seen once cannot be told from noise, so only recurring units count. With 8,000 films, 'new' can still mean 'not sampled'. Birth excess shows time structure, which fashion cycles also produce.
review: The earlier-to-later ratio was 1 by identity (every unit has one first and one last appearance); replaced by a date-shuffle null on recurring units. Tell Me Again now supplies every film. Remaining: dataset licence unconfirmed; the two summaries are not fully independent.
sources: Youn et al. 2015; Lu et al. 2025; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again); Sreenivasan 2013

title: Undeclared influence, checked against the written record
question: Can a method tuned on declared 'based on' and 'inspired by' links find influence between works that Wikidata does not declare but the written record confirms?
hypothesis: On held-out loose links ('inspired by', 'references work'), neurons rank the true source in the top 5% of matched decoys at least 5 points more often than the best cheap rival. At least 10% of their top 1,000 undeclared pairs are confirmed by the record, against under 2% for random matched pairs.
falsifier: Loose-link advantage under 2 points, or its 95% interval includes zero (1,000 pairs give a standard error near 2 points; do not run with under 500). Or the confirmed share of the top 1,000 is no higher than the best rival's. After E2, a second failure would settle that neurons add nothing to words for tracing influence.
data: Wikidata links with English Wikipedia articles at both ends, counted 2026-11-08, CC0: based on (P144) 30,685; inspired by (P941) 3,713; references work (P8371) 1,239. Plot sections, CC BY-SA, names masked. Sample 6,000 pairs with plots at both ends, loose links oversampled: 2,000 for development, 4,000 held out. Non-plot article text is the documentary record.
method: Score pairs by hub-adjusted share of the source's rare units (the E2 statistic). Test 1: rank held-out true sources among decoys matched on decade, medium and genre, per link type. Test 2: for each method's top 1,000 unlinked pairs with different creators and series, an LLM auditor must quote the article sentence naming the source (200 hand-checked). Null: within-decade permutation.
rivals: TF-IDF and BM25 on the same masked plots; e5 sentence embeddings and story-emb, which was built to survive name replacement; an LLM reading both plots (shortlists only); text length; random non-meme units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: story-emb and the LLM. If they win, undeclared-influence search still works, just without neurons.
premise: P1. A pass is the first evidence that neuron units trace influence where plots are not simply retold. A fail leaves P1 with no practical content for descent. For P2, report how many of the top 1,000 pairs Qwen and Llama share, against the random-unit floor.
bio: Detecting horizontal gene transfer, validated on known transfers.
cost: M: about two weeks. Roughly 20,000 plots, a few hours of forward passes per model; the LLM reader on shortlists, the auditor on about 5,000 pairs and a 200-pair hand check are the main cost.
payoff: A search tool for unacknowledged sources with a known hit rate, tested on thousands of works beyond one franchise; or a clear finding that embeddings already do the job.
risk: Similarity is not influence: top pairs may be genre twins, and critics note resemblance, so only statements that the makers drew on the source count. The record misses unwritten influence. Models may recognise famous plots despite masked names. Outputs are candidates, never accusations of copying.
review: Dropped the 'lowest quarter of word overlap' stratum: selecting on a rival's score makes that rival lose by construction. Strata are now link types. Audit made checkable and enlarged; same-franchise and same-creator pairs excluded. Remaining: the number of loose links with plots at both ends is unconfirmed.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 4). It is the closest thing to the tool Mike wants: a search for unacknowledged sources across thousands of works with a hit rate checked against the written record, and it produces a usable list whichever reader wins.
sources: Wikidata query service counts 2026-11-08; Chang et al. 2024; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (story-emb); Claidière et al. 2014

title: Atypical meme pairings and clicks, topic held fixed
question: Within one randomised headline test, does the headline whose meme units are paired in ways rarely seen in earlier headlines win more clicks?
hypothesis: Yes, modestly. With test and image held fixed, one standard deviation more rare-pair atypicality raises click odds by at least 1%, after controls for length, words, word pairs and single neuron units. A squared term for an inverted U adds nothing detectable.
falsifier: The 95% interval for the rare-pair odds ratio lies wholly below 1.005, or includes 1 while word-pair atypicality passes. Robertson et al. 2023 resolved a 2.3% effect per negative word on these tests, so 1% should be detectable; confirm the standard error on the exploratory set before scoring.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 randomised headline tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015, CC BY 4.0, OSF node jd64p. Fit on the exploratory set (4,873 tests); score once on the confirmatory set (22,743). Drop the faulty-randomisation window (about 22%) and compare only arms sharing an image: roughly 9,000 usable confirmatory tests, to confirm.
method: Fix the 2,000 most frequent units on exploratory headlines. Score each unit pair in a headline by how often it co-occurred in earlier headlines against a shuffle keeping unit frequencies and month (Uzzi's z-score). Model clicks per impression with a fixed effect per test, adding feature sets in nested steps. Null: arms permuted within test.
rivals: Word-pair atypicality; single neuron units without pairs; TF-IDF difference; embedding distance from earlier headlines; an LLM asked which headline wins and which is more surprising; length and punctuation; random units; sparse-autoencoder features (Movva 2025). Most dangerous: word pairs, because headlines are short. If they win, recombination is tested anyway and neurons are surplus.
premise: Assumes both. A pass shows that pairs of neuron units carry combination structure that word pairs and a bag of single units miss. A fail while word pairs pass says recombination matters but this unit does not. Repeat in Llama to see if the pair scores agree.
bio: Epistasis: the fitness of gene combinations beyond single genes.
cost: S: under 2 days. 150,817 headlines is about 40 minutes of forward passes per model on the pre-registration's timing, which is optimistic; the LLM rival on a subsample is the dearest part.
payoff: A topic-controlled test of 'familiar base plus one surprise' (Uzzi; Berlyne's inverted U), and a pair-novelty score that could be used when drafting.
risk: A headline holds too few units for pair statistics to mean much. Novelty is not randomised, only the audience is, so atypical headlines may differ in other ways. Sparse-autoencoder features have already been applied to this archive, so the ground is not new.
review: Arms also vary the image, so compared arms must share it; usable tests fall from 17,700 to about 9,000. Switched from winner-picking accuracy to within-test click odds for power. Added single units as a baseline that pairs must beat. Remaining: the effect is probably tiny.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as CJ-21, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Matias et al. 2021 (Upworthy Research Archive); Uzzi et al. 2013; Robertson et al. 2023; Movva et al. 2025

title: A writer's imprint across a language border
question: Do an author's distinctive units reappear in documented followers who wrote in another language, where shared words and function-word style cannot carry the signal?
hypothesis: Neurons place the documented influencer in the top 3 of 21 candidate authors for at least 30% of pairs (chance is 14%), at least 5 points more often than the best multilingual embedding and than always guessing the most famous candidate.
falsifier: Top-3 rate under 20%, or no higher than multilingual embeddings, translate-then-TF-IDF or the fame-only guess. 300 pairs give a standard error near 2.7 points: ample against chance, but only about 50% power for a 5-point gap over a rival, so a gap between 0 and 5 is undetermined. Do not run with under 250 pairs.
data: Wikidata 'influenced by' (P737): 32,322 statements, counted 2026-11-08, CC0. Pairs where both authors died before 1955, share no writing language and have Wikisource pages: 798 pairs, 364 followers. Only 166 such followers have Project Gutenberg author pages, so take texts from Wikisource dumps (public domain or CC BY-SA). Target 300 pairs, 20,000 words of prose per author, original language.
method: Choose each influencer's distinctive units on half of that author's text, against same-language authors of the same era. For each follower, rank the documented influencer among 20 decoys matched on language, era and fame (number of Wikipedia language editions) by how many of those units the follower's text carries. Statistic: top-3 rate, clustered by follower. Null: decoys permuted within era.
rivals: Multilingual sentence embeddings; machine translation to English, then TF-IDF and Burrows Delta (function-word stylometry); an LLM given both texts and the 21 names; always picking the most famous candidate; length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: the LLM, which may simply know that Baudelaire read Poe. Report obscure pairs separately to blunt that.
premise: Both. P1: a unit that survives a change of language is not a word detector. P2: Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 should rank the same influencers; report their agreement against the random-unit floor. A fail bounds 'a person's influence' to style and translation.
bio: Introgression: tracing one parent's alleles in a hybrid lineage.
cost: M: up to two weeks. About 600 authors at 20,000 words is a few hours of forward passes per model; assembling clean public-domain prose in several languages from Wikisource is the labour.
payoff: A per-person influence score that works across languages and is checked against documented influence; or a bound showing neurons add nothing to embeddings for it.
risk: Too few pairs survive the prose and length filters. P737 records fame as much as influence, and followers often read the influencer in translation. The models have probably memorised these classics, so units may recognise the texts instead of their content; the LLM reader shares that flaw.
review: Gutenberg yields only 166 qualifying followers, below the design's own floor, so texts now come from Wikisource (364 followers). Added fame-matched decoys and a fame-only rival, because P737 favours famous influencers. Remaining: Wikisource prose coverage per author is unchecked and the expected signal is weak.
sources: Wikidata P737 counts 2026-11-08; Burrows 2002; Hughes et al. 2012; Wegmann et al. 2022

title: Novelty and resonance over time, across two models
question: Do novelty, transience and resonance scores built from neuron units predict later citations beyond word-based versions, and do two models give the same scores?
hypothesis: Neuron resonance adds at least 0.01 AUC (ranking accuracy; 0.5 is chance) over TF-IDF, topic-model and embedding resonance together with venue and team size, and adds more with a 10-year forward window than with 3. After removing TF-IDF resonance, Qwen and Llama scores rank-correlate at least 0.1 above scores from random units.
falsifier: Added AUC under 0.005 with an interval including zero (15,000 test abstracts; paired standard error about 0.004, to confirm by bootstrap): no use beyond words. Or residual cross-model correlation no higher than for random non-meme units, which agree almost freely: the score carries nothing specific to memes.
data: OpenAlex (CC0; the API now needs a free key with a daily budget): about 45,000 abstracts from one field, 2000 to 2025, with reference lists, venue and citations counted to 2025. Abstracts average about 8 sentences. Years 2000 to 2007 fix units and settings; 2008 to 2015 are scored once; later years serve only as the future pool.
method: Novelty is an abstract's mean distance from abstracts of the previous 3 years; transience is its distance from the next 3 (or 10); resonance is novelty minus transience (Barron 2018). Predict top-10% citations within field and year with nested logistic models. Null: abstracts shuffled within year. Fields rename ideas, so word scores should fade with the longer window.
rivals: TF-IDF backward and forward similarity (Kelly 2021); topic-model resonance (Barron 2018); sentence-embedding resonance; an LLM rating novelty from the abstract (subsample); abstract length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: TF-IDF, which already tracks patent quality. If it wins, resonance works and neurons are surplus; the cross-model figure still tests P2.
premise: Both. P1 gains only if the neuron score adds prediction where vocabulary has turned over. P2 gains if two models' scores agree beyond what shared words and random units explain; the study's one beyond-words result held in Llama and failed in Qwen.
bio: Fate of a new mutation: lost, transient or fixed in descendants.
cost: M: about 4 days. API pull of 45,000 abstracts, under two hours of forward passes per model, then regressions.
payoff: A model-independent influence score for any dated body of text, or a finding that the TF-IDF ratio is all one needs.
risk: Citations reward fame and venue, so every text measure adds little. Later papers cite what they resemble, so resonance partly restates citation. Resonance in a 3-year window rewards joining a trend as much as starting one.
review: The sample ended in 2015, leaving scored years without later abstracts; the pool now runs to 2025. The cross-model bar was an absolute 0.3, which random units would pass; it is now a margin over random units. Venue and team size added. Remaining: 'TF-IDF suffices' is the likely result.
sources: Barron et al. 2018; Kelly et al. 2021; Vicinanza et al. 2022; OpenAlex

title: Who or what: a Girard and Dawkins split
question: When a researcher is exposed to an idea new to them, is adoption explained more by which idea it is (Dawkins) or by who displayed it (Girard)?
hypothesis: Dawkins: an idea's adoption lift repeats across separate halves of exposers (r of 0.5 or more) and predicts held-out adoption better than the exposer's lift does. Girard: with the idea held fixed, one standard deviation more exposer prestige raises adoption odds by 20%. Our bet: Dawkins on both counts.
falsifier: Prestige odds ratio of 1.2 or more with an interval excluding 1, or exposer lift predicting held-out adoption as well as idea lift: a content-only account fails here. Idea split-half r under 0.2: ideas show no stable merit. Needs 5,000 exposers and 2,000 ideas with 20 or more offers each; confirm on development years.
data: OpenAlex (CC0; free API key): the RX25 field sample widened to about 60,000 abstracts, 2000 to 2020, with citation links and author identifiers. Prestige is an author's citations received inside the sample before the exposure year. A citation is the exposure record. Early years fix a dictionary of 3,000 repeatable units; later years are scored.
method: Event: B's authors cite A in year t; a unit in A, absent from their earlier abstracts and from B, is 'offered'. Outcome: it appears in their abstracts within 3 years. Lift is adoption over the unit's field-year base rate. Logistic model: fixed effect per unit, prestige and prior citer-to-cited similarity. Null: cited authors permuted within field and year.
rivals: The same analysis with keywords and noun phrases, embedding clusters and LLM-extracted claims (subsample) as the idea; exposure count alone; random units. Most dangerous: keywords, since in abstracts a new term is the idea. If keywords give the same answer, it stands without neurons. Wording does not confound the who-or-what split itself.
premise: Assumes both. Neuron memes measure only the 'what'. If who-effects dominate, a content-only science of memes misses most of the story however good the unit. If the answer changes with the unit type, the unit matters (P1).
bio: Strain fitness versus super-spreader hosts.
cost: M: one to two weeks. Pulling author histories is the labour; about 2 hours of forward passes per model; the models fit on a laptop with subsampling.
payoff: A head-to-head of the mimetic and memetic accounts on one dataset, which the literature search did not find, and a ceiling on what any content measure can explain.
risk: Citing is not random exposure: authors cite those they already resemble, and famous papers draw ceremonial citations that lower adoption, which biases against Girard. A citation does not prove reading. Girard's distinctive claims, rivalry and scapegoating, are not tested; this is prestige bias.
review: The outcome sat in the citing paper itself, so 'adoption' restated why it cited; it is now measured in later papers. The variance ratio reflected unit base rates and group sizes; replaced by split-half and held-out comparisons. Remaining: exposure is self-selected, so identification stays weak.
sources: Henrich and Gil-White 2001; Salganik, Dodds, Watts 2006; Youngblood 2019; Claidière et al. 2014

title: Planted influence with look-alike decoys
question: When a writer is shown a source and told to copy, transform or combine it, can neurons name that source once the wording no longer resembles it?
hypothesis: In the deep-transform condition (new setting, names and wording; content-word overlap with the source no higher than with look-alikes), neurons rank the true source first among 20 candidates for at least 40% of stories (chance is 5%), at least 10 points above the best embedding. For close copies every method is near ceiling.
falsifier: Deep-transform accuracy under 15%, or no higher than the best of story-emb, e5 and the LLM judge. 200 held-out stories per condition give a standard error near 3.5 points, enough to see a 10-point paired gap. Stories written with no source must put any candidate first at the 5% chance rate.
data: Built. 250 source plots of little-known films from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia plots, CC BY-SA). Each gets 19 look-alike decoys of the same genre, decade and length, never shown to the writer. Two LLM writers from families other than the readers produce 1,250 stories: copy, transform, deep transform, combine two sources, or no source.
method: Fix units and settings on 50 development sources; score 200 held out. Rank each story's candidates by the hub-adjusted share of the source's rare units (the E2 statistic). Statistic: top-1 accuracy by condition, plus second-source recall for combined stories. A script checks that word overlap falls across conditions. Null: source labels permuted within genre.
rivals: TF-IDF and BM25; e5 embeddings and story-emb; an LLM judge reading the story and its candidates; length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: story-emb and the LLM judge, both made to ignore surface wording. If they win, influence search works without neurons, and the depth of rewording at which each method fails is still new.
premise: P1. Truth is known by construction and wording is removed by design, so a pass is direct evidence that units carry inherited content beyond words. A fail leaves no setting where neurons trace influence better than cheap tools. For P2, compare Qwen and Llama rankings against random units.
bio: Experimental crosses with known parentage.
cost: S to M: about 3 days. 1,250 generated stories of about 400 words, minutes of forward passes per model; the LLM judge over 1,250 stories with 20 candidates each is the main cost.
payoff: The first test where influence is certain and wording cannot explain it; a curve of accuracy against depth of rewording for every method; and a calibration set for RX21 and RX22.
risk: Reader neurons may detect LLM writing habits instead of content; a small human-written arm would settle that and is not costed here. Instructed transformation may be easier to trace than real influence. Overlaps with the paused planted-story plan, which plants memes, not sources.
review: Added by the reviewer, promoted from the planted-influence seed: the area had no design where influence is known by construction. Weakness: writers and readers are both language models, so a human-written arm is needed before a pass is trusted.
ranking: In the top twelve of 3 of 3 judges (what decides the premises fastest: rank 11; speed and cost: rank 12; upside: rank 5). Three days buy the first source-tracing test where the true source is known by construction and the wording is removed on purpose, so a loss to story embeddings or the LLM judge closes the influence use and a win opens it.
sources: Wang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2026 (FakeWiki); Chang et al. 2024; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (story-emb)

title: Remix ledger calibrated on built remixes
question: If stories are assembled from known sources plus planted new elements and then reworded, does the measured inherited share track the true share?
note: The instrument check for RX21; RX27's combined stories can supply the material. Falsified if the neuron ledger's correlation with the planted proportions is no higher than a word n-gram ledger's. From l8 S3.

title: Naming the second parent
question: After removing a work's best single source, can a method name the second source of works documented to draw on two?
note: Blending, not branching, is the honest model for franchises. RX27 covers the built case; this is the real one, on documented multi-source films. Rivals: TF-IDF residuals and an LLM asked directly. From l6 seed 5.

title: Do rivals become doubles?
question: Do documented rivals (competing franchises, feuding authors) grow more alike in their units over time than matched non-rival pairs, as Girard predicts?
note: The part of Girard that RX26 leaves untested. Needs a defensible list of rivalries with dates; the rival measure is embedding convergence.

title: An author's imprint by construction
question: When an LLM writer is steeped in one public-domain author and writes on unrelated subjects, do neurons identify that author against decoys?
note: Expected to lose to function-word stylometry; worth running because it bounds what 'influence of a person' can mean for content units. Cheaper and cleaner than RX24. From l8 S6.

title: Descent or attractor
question: Can incidental 'hitchhiker' units separate pairs with documented descent from pairs documented as independent invention?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: CJ-22.
note: Answers Sperber's objection that shared traits need no line of descent. The lexical rival is rare shared words and named details. The labelled pairs are the work.

title: Declared remix trees
question: On a platform with declared parent links (Scratch, Thingiverse), how much of a remix is inherited from its parent, and does the parent's popularity or its content predict what is kept?
note: Declared links give exposure for free and would sharpen RX26. Data access and licences were not checked; Scratch projects are code, so text is thin.

title: Citations the author did not declare
question: Do neuron units link a patent to prior art that the examiner added but the applicant did not cite?
note: A possible real ground truth for undeclared influence. Alcacer and Gittelman 2006 (doi:10.1162/rest.88.4.774) is now confirmed; examiners add about 40% of citations. Patent text data and licence still to check; TF-IDF is the rival (Kelly 2021).

title: A chamber as shared exposure
question: When every member hears every speech, is the later uptake of a new unit predicted by who introduced it (leader, senior member) or by which unit it is?
note: Added in review. Fixes RX26's self-selected exposure. ParlSpeech V2: 6.3 million speeches, nine parliaments, date, speaker and party, CC0 (Harvard Dataverse, checked 2026-11-08). Confounds: party talking points and the agenda. Speaker rank must be joined from elsewhere. Rival unit: keywords.

title: Same idea, different author
question: When two teams publish the same discovery at the same time, does the more prominent team's wording spread further in later papers?
note: Added in review. Holds the 'what' fixed so only the 'who' varies, the cleanest Girard test found. Bikard 2020 lists simultaneous discoveries; Huber et al. 2022 randomised author prominence in peer review. Dataset access and size not checked. Rival: word and phrase adoption.

title: Meme heritability across languages, against a retelling ceiling
question: When a film adapts a documented source and the two plot summaries come from different-language Wikipedias, are neuron units inherited nearly as reliably as they are re-measured in a second summary of the same story, and more reliably than translated words?
hypothesis: On 500 or more held-out sources, among units repeatable across languages (ceiling at least 0.2 above floor on development sources), concept units reach a median heritability index of at least 0.30 (0 = unrelated works, 1 = the same story summarised in another Wikipedia), at least 0.10 above translated words screened the same way.
falsifier: Median index at or below 0.10, or a lead over translated words whose 95% bootstrap interval (resampling sources) includes zero. Void, and reported as an unreliable reader, if fewer than 200 concept units pass the repeatability screen. At 500 sources one unit's correlation has a standard error of 0.045.
data: Tell me again! (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 plot summaries of 29,505 stories from five Wikipedias, with English machine translations, name-masked versions and Wikidata IDs; CC BY-SA 4.0; 1.7 GB. Joined to Wikidata 'based on' links (CC0): 1,363 film-source pairs over 958 sources have both ends in it (reviewer's join, 2026-11-08), before length filters.
method: A unit is one sign of one neuron, word-like if one word predicts its presence, else concept; classes and bars fixed on 20% of sources. Non-English summaries are machine-translated. Correlate presence across: one story in two Wikipedias, close translations dropped (ceiling); source and adaptation (transmission); source and genre-matched unrelated film (floor). Index = (transmission - floor)/(ceiling - floor).
rivals: Per feature, with the same screen: machine-translated word presence; an LLM answering 50 motif questions per text (most dangerous: repeatable by design); Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features; random active units; length. Whole profile: multilingual-e5 and the dataset's published retrieval baselines. If the LLM reader wins, we still learn each unit's repeatability, the reader's first error rate.
premise: both. P1: a concept-unit lead means units are wording-independent hereditary markers; a tie leaves P1 where words left it; too few repeatable units means the reader is unreliable. P2: heritability rankings of matched units should agree between Qwen and Llama (rank correlation at least 0.5).
bio: Parent-offspring regression; repeatability as the ceiling on heritability; synonymous-site baseline.
cost: M. About a week: the dataset is ready-made and name-masked; roughly an hour of extraction per model on one laptop, then the Wikidata join and analysis.
payoff: A per-unit table of repeatability, silent-change rate and heritability; a list of units fit to be hereditary markers; and a working definition of synonymous change, which dN/dS-style tools need.
risk: Genre-typical content that recurs without descent counts as inherited unless the floor is matched tightly. Machine translation may flatten wording differences. Few units may pass the repeatability screen.
review: The index rewarded unreliable features (small denominator): every class now passes a repeatability screen first. Swapped self-scouted Wikipedias for a ready, name-masked five-language dataset; pair count checked (1,363). Remaining: how tightly the floor is genre-matched decides how much 'heritability' is convergence.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (what decides the premises fastest: rank 12). Reruns the one robust Batman result, heredity, across languages on ready-made name-masked data with a same-story ceiling, so a tie with translated words would finally be informative instead of ambiguous.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as LI-22, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Hatzel and Biemann 2024; Visscher et al. 2008; da Silva and Tehrani 2016; Nei and Gojobori 1986

title: ABBA-BABA test for borrowing in crossover works
question: Can an excess-sharing statistic on name-free unit presence tell which outside franchise a crossover work borrowed from, more often than plain similarity or the same statistic on words?
hypothesis: Calibration: when donor sentences are spliced into host plots, D rises with the spliced share (rank correlation at least 0.8). Test: on 40 crossovers between separate franchises, D is higher for the true donor than for a wrong donor of the same genre and decade in at least 80%, and more often than word D.
falsifier: Tool claim fails at 65% or fewer correct (40 crossovers give about 0.8 power to tell 80% from 60%). Unit claim fails if word D or plain similarity is correct as often (paired interval, clustered by franchise pair, includes zero). Void if calibration fails, or ordinary franchise entries in the crossover slot give mean D outside plus or minus 0.05.
data: Code check only: committed matrix (`study/results/qwen3-8b/memes.json.gz`, 114 works, names present). Test: 40 crossovers between two separate franchises, over 15 or more franchise pairs, plus parent works. The cached pool (`preregistration/sources/t3_candidates.jsonl.gz`) has 143 crossover-category plots, but most are same-universe team-ups; about 20 qualify by the reviewer's reading of titles. Fetch the rest from Wikipedia's crossover categories (CC BY-SA 4.0).
method: Mask names; keep every unit (the committed matrix keeps only families in six or more Batman works, missing donor material). Equal sentence counts. For crossover X, host work A, donor work B: ABBA = units in X and B, not A; BABA = units in A and B, not X. D = (ABBA - BABA)/(ABBA + BABA), averaged over choices.
rivals: The same D on word presence (most dangerous: donor vocabulary survives name masking); plain similarity of crossover to donor with no host correction; embedding similarity gain; an LLM asked to name the donor from masked text (probably near ceiling); random non-meme units. A tie with words still validates D as a tool for unit matrices.
premise: both. P1: if unit D only matches word D, borrowing detection needs no neurons; a unit lead on name-free text would be the first population statistic where units see more than words. P2: Qwen and Llama should rank donors alike (rank correlation at least 0.6).
bio: Introgression test between non-sister lineages (Green 2010; Durand 2011).
cost: S. A day to list crossovers, donors and wrong donors from Wikipedia leads; about 600 works, minutes of extraction per model; splicing needs no new text.
payoff: A tested, tree-free statistic for borrowing between franchises with a known smallest detectable share, and a plain answer on whether name-free unit matrices carry donor signal beyond words.
risk: An easy win for every method: crossovers contain the donor's characters and world, so words and the LLM reader will probably tie or lead. It must skip the 39 held-out Batman works (`preregistration/works_batman_extended.json`), several of which are crossovers.
review: The free pilot was biased: the committed matrix drops donor units, so it is now a code check. Added spliced-dose calibration, a plain-similarity rival, a harder wrong donor, separate-franchise crossovers only. Remaining: documented crossovers are easy for words, so the unit claim will probably tie.
sources: Durand et al. 2011; Green et al. 2010; Patterson et al. 2012; preregistration/sources/t3_candidates.jsonl.gz

title: Random-copying null and frequency-increment test on film plots
question: Across eighty years of film plots, does any unit's frequency change more than random copying with innovation predicts, and does that verdict differ from the one its own words receive?
hypothesis: At 5% false discovery, in at least two of three time binnings, at least 1% of a 5,000-unit panel reject drift, and for at least 30% of those the unit's word shadow does not reject in the same direction. Before freezing, simulated power must reach 0.8 for a doubling of odds over 40 years.
falsifier: Under 0.25% reject (drift suffices at this power), or over 90% of rejecting units are mirrored by their word shadows. Void if the control with release years shuffled within genre, or simulated drift with threshold noise, rejects more than 1% of units.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus: 42,306 English Wikipedia plot summaries (November 2012 dump) with release date, genre and country from Freebase; 46 MB; CC BY-SA. Median length is 9 sentences; 20,933 have ten or more, leaving 410 to 3,937 films per 5-year bin from 1930 (reviewer count, 2026-11-08). One dump, so the editors' era is constant.
method: Mask names; keep plots of ten or more sentences, cut to ten. On 2,000 development films, merge co-firing units and set each unit's bar at its top fifth. Frequencies in 5-year bins, resampled to equal size and a constant genre-by-country mix. Fit drift; apply the frequency-increment test, a t-test on variance-scaled frequency changes. Word shadow: presence predicted from words alone.
rivals: The identical test on each unit's word shadow, on frequency-matched word types, LDA topics and embedding clusters; an LLM tagging 50 motifs on 2,000 films; random non-meme units. Most dangerous: words, because most strong units are word detectors. If words flag the same items we still gain the first drift baseline for plots.
premise: assumes both. A pass licenses later selection claims and shows units move differently from words; mirrored verdicts mean P1 adds nothing here. P2 gets a functional test: Qwen and Llama twins should receive the same verdict (kappa at least 0.4).
bio: Kimura's neutral theory; frequency-increment test on allele time series (Feder 2014).
cost: M. One pass over about 21,000 summaries, roughly an hour per model, stored at one bit per unit per film (about 2.5 GB); a week of analysis and power simulation.
payoff: A fitted drift baseline for film plots and a short, binning-stable list of units whose rise or fall drift cannot explain: the entry ticket for any selection claim.
risk: Equifinality and survivorship: Wikipedia covers the old films that stayed famous, which mimics selection; binning changes verdicts (Karjus 2020); 16 bins give little power per unit, so a low count may mean weak power, not drift.
review: 'First 15 sentences' left most plots shorter (median 9): now exactly ten. The 3% bar gave about 12 present films in early bins: now top fifth. Added equal bin sizes, a multi-word shadow rival, a 1% void threshold. Remaining: Wikipedia survivorship looks like selection.
sources: Bentley, Hahn and Shennan 2004; Feder et al. 2014; Karjus et al. 2020; CMU Movie Summary Corpus (Bamman, O'Connor and Smith 2013)

title: Are linked memes inherited together, beyond chance co-occurrence?
question: Do pairs of units that co-occur across a population of films also pass together from a source to its adaptation more often than their separate transmission rates and ordinary co-occurrence predict?
hypothesis: For linked pairs (top 1% of co-occurrence after controls) that peak in different scenes, the odds ratio of joint retention in true source-adaptation pairs is at least 1.3 times that in matched unrelated pairs, after dividing out the same figure for unlinked pairs, and larger than for frequency-matched linked word pairs. Up to 760 held-out sources before length filters.
falsifier: Ratio at or below 1.1 with the 95% interval's upper end under 1.3 (bundles are co-occurrence, not co-inheritance), or linked word pairs show an equal or larger ratio (interval of the difference includes zero). Intervals by bootstrap over sources.
data: Tell me again! (Hatzel and Biemann 2024; 96,831 name-masked summaries of 29,505 stories; CC BY-SA 4.0). Population panel: 5,000 English film summaries outside any documented pair. Transmission panel: the 1,363 film-source pairs (958 sources) that Wikidata 'based on' links (CC0) join inside it (reviewer's join, 2026-11-08); 20% of sources for development.
method: Merge units that co-fire within sentences. On the population panel, correlate presence pairwise after removing genre, decade, length and 20 principal components; keep linked pairs from different layers with different best-matched words whose top sentences in the source lie three or more apart, plus frequency-matched unlinked pairs. Where a held-out source carries both units, compare odds ratios of joint retention.
rivals: Word pairs linked by pointwise mutual information; LDA topic pairs; embedding-cluster pairs; an LLM's motif answers paired the same way; random non-meme unit pairs. All under the same different-scene rule. Most dangerous: word pairs, because topic vocabulary travels together. A tie means memeplexes are a text statistic.
premise: P1. Co-inheritance beyond word bundles would show units capture inherited structure that vocabulary misses; a tie or a null says the memeplex is co-occurrence. The test only has meaning if single units are heritable (PO21).
bio: Linkage disequilibrium, co-segregation and hitch-hiking.
cost: M. Shares PO21's dataset and extraction (about 9,000 summaries, an hour per model) plus sentence positions for a 5,000-unit panel; one to two weeks.
payoff: A list of meme bundles that travel together down documented lineages, each with a chance baseline: the first empirical test of the memeplex idea.
risk: Leftover sub-genre structure makes any linked pair travel together when an adaptation keeps its source's genre, for words as much as for units, so a tie is the likely result.
review: A probability excess grows mechanically with retention rates: replaced by an odds-ratio contrast against unlinked pairs. Added a different-scene rule (same-sentence pairs co-transmit trivially), principal components and merging. Remaining: residual genre structure; word pairs will probably tie; depends on PO21.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as CJ-24, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Maynard Smith and Haigh 1974; da Silva and Tehrani 2016; Hatzel and Biemann 2024; Wikidata P144 links (query service, 2026-11-08)

title: Meme-wide association with success, corrected for lineage
question: Which units go with a film's box-office rank once genre, era, length, budget and documented lineage are controlled, and do the hits hold in held-out franchises and between instalments of one series?
hypothesis: At least 20 units pass 5% false discovery; at least 60% replicate in sign at p < 0.05 in held-out franchises; their combined score picks the better-earning of two consecutive instalments in at least 55% of within-series pairs, ahead of word and embedding scores. About 450 usable pairs (of 624) give roughly 0.5 power at 55%, 0.85 at 58%.
falsifier: Fewer than 5 hits replicate, or within-series accuracy's 95% interval includes 50%, or a word or embedding score does as well (difference interval includes zero). Void if hits survive shuffling outcomes between franchises (inflation factor, observed over expected median test statistic, above 1.1).
data: Discovery: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (CC BY-SA): 7,531 plots carry Freebase revenue, 5,693 of them with ten or more sentences (reviewer count, 2026-11-08). Within-family test: Wikidata (CC0; query service, same day) lists 179 film series with two or more films that have box office and an English article (803 films); 3,236 films have both box office and budget.
method: Mask names; cut plots to ten sentences. Fix a 5,000-unit panel on development films. Per unit, a mixed model of within-year revenue rank on presence; covariates: genre, country, decade, budget where known, full summary length (a proxy for editor attention) and ten principal components; random effect: franchise. Split discovery and replication by franchise. Then score consecutive instalments within series.
rivals: The same pipeline on TF-IDF terms; ridge regression on sentence embeddings; an LLM rating 20 named story features; random non-meme units; length and metadata alone. Most dangerous: metadata (budget, sequel number, genre) overall and embeddings for prediction, since content explains little of success. A null still measures how far lineage inflates naive hits.
premise: P1. Replicated, within-series unit hits beyond words would give neuron memes practical content; none, or a tie, leaves the case for neurons resting on readability. Each hit is re-tested on reworded sentences to see whether it is a word or an idea.
bio: Genome-wide association with a kinship mixed model; within-family design against confounding.
cost: M. About 7,000 plots, under an hour of extraction per model; one to two weeks for joins, models and the within-series test.
payoff: A replicated list of success-linked memes with the shrinkage from between-family to within-family effects measured, or a documented null with its cause.
risk: Summaries are written after release, and hits attract longer, more polished ones, so units may detect editor attention, not story content. Budget, stars and marketing dominate revenue; a null is the likely result.
review: The sibling test was unpowered: only 111 sources have two box-office adaptations, so it now compares instalments within 179 series. Added budget and summary-length covariates; revenue count confirmed. Unrepaired: summaries are written after success, so hits may read editor attention.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as FI-26, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Klein et al. 2005; Eliashberg, Hui and Zhang 2007; Martin et al. 2016; CMU Movie Summary Corpus (Bamman, O'Connor and Smith 2013)

title: Open or closed: pan-memomes of retellings and series
question: Does the rate at which each added work brings new units recover a documented ordering (retellings of one source below sequel series below matched random film sets), and does it do so better than vocabulary growth?
hypothesis: Name-free, the share of a set's sixth work that is new separates 25 retelling sets from 25 sequel series with AUC at least 0.80 (chance 0.5), and at least 45 of the 50 real sets are more closed than all 50 of their matched random sets. Twenty-five against 25 gives a standard error near 0.06 on the AUC.
falsifier: AUC at or below 0.65, or 10 or more of the 50 real sets fall inside their random-set range (no more closed than chance). Units add nothing if word-type growth separates the classes as well (paired bootstrap interval of the AUC difference includes zero).
data: Sets of six or more works with English Wikipedia plot sections (CC BY-SA 4.0). Wikidata (CC0; reviewer recount, 2026-11-08) lists 118 sources with six or more film adaptations (22 single stories with twelve or more, such as Dracula) and 119 film series with six or more films. No Shakespeare sets: that list is a paused test. Plus 1,000 random films.
method: Mask names; cut to equal length. Keep every unit: the committed matrix drops families found in under six Batman works (`study/discover.py`), hiding rare memes. Per set, average over orderings the share of the sixth work's units absent from the first five; with twelve works, also fit the power-law decline. Compare with 50 random sets matched on decade, genre and length.
rivals: Heaps'-law growth of word types and TF-IDF terms; spread of sentence embeddings; distinct motifs an LLM tags on a subsample; random non-meme units. Most dangerous: word types, which will probably give the same ordering. Then the pangenome view is confirmed as a tool but needs no neurons.
premise: both. P1: a pass shows the presence matrix carries population structure beyond threshold noise; equal performance from words says canon tiers describe vocabulary. P2: Qwen and Llama should rank the 50 sets alike (rank correlation at least 0.7).
bio: Pangenome: core and accessory genes, open or closed (Tettelin 2005).
cost: M. About 1,500 plots, minutes of extraction per model; three days to assemble and check the sets; a week in all.
payoff: A noise-corrected openness measure with core, shell and cloud tiers for 50 story traditions: a way to say whether a franchise's meme pool is still growing.
risk: The ordering is close to guaranteed for any text representation, so the test may only show that unit matrices behave like vocabulary. Threshold noise (about 3% false presence per unit) may swamp the rare tier.
review: Ten against ten could not tell units from words (an AUC gap of 0.05 is noise): now 25 against 25 sets of six or more, scored at a fixed depth. Dropped the paused Shakespeare list. Remaining: words will give the same ordering; the value is the tool.
sources: Tettelin et al. 2005; Snel, Bork and Huynen 1999; study/results/canon.json; study/results/robustness/nulls.json (f1_chance)

title: One film population, two Wikipedias: an Fst check
question: When the same films are summarised in two Wikipedias, is the differentiation between the two sets of summaries (which should be zero) small beside the differentiation between national film industries, and smaller for units than for translated words?
hypothesis: Per-unit Fst (the share of a unit's frequency variance that lies between groups) between US and German productions agrees across English and German summaries (rank correlation at least 0.5), and for concept units the median ratio of industry Fst to summariser Fst is at least 2 and above that of translated words.
falsifier: Rank correlation below 0.3, or median ratio at or below 1 (the reader measures the summariser, not the film), or translated words reach as high a ratio (bootstrap over films, interval of the difference includes zero). With 1,000 films a side, sampling alone gives Fst near 0.0005.
data: Tell me again! (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 summaries of 29,505 stories (25,860 films) from five Wikipedias, with English machine translations and name-masked versions; CC BY-SA 4.0. German covers 98% of stories and English 89%. Country of origin from Wikidata (CC0). Needs 1,000 US and 1,000 German-language productions with both summaries of ten or more sentences; count to confirm.
method: Read English summaries and machine-translated German ones, names masked, cut to ten sentences. Units, classes and bars fixed on 500 development films. Summariser Fst: the same films, English against German summary. Industry Fst: US against German productions within one Wikipedia. Sampling noise is subtracted; nulls shuffle group labels within decade and genre.
rivals: The same two Fst values for machine-translated word presence (translation wording should inflate its summariser Fst; if units do no better, P1 loses an easy case); an LLM's answers to 50 motif questions (most dangerous: probably the cleanest reader); multilingual-e5 dimensions; sparse-autoencoder features; random active units; length.
premise: P1. Units that differ between industries but not between summarisers read content and are fit for population comparisons; if summariser Fst matches industry Fst, cross-population claims from summaries are unsafe. P2: per-unit ratios should agree between Qwen and Llama twins (rank correlation at least 0.5).
bio: Fst between populations, with a technical-replicate control (the same individuals genotyped twice).
cost: S to M. Shares PO21's dataset; about 4,000 summaries, minutes of extraction per model; three days of analysis.
payoff: A list of units safe for comparing populations of works, the size of the summariser artefact, and the first Fst-style statistic for memes with a built-in zero point.
risk: German Wikipedia summaries tend to be longer, so some summariser Fst is real difference in what gets told; machine translation adds its own style. Too few German productions may have long English summaries.
review: Added by the reviewer: the area names Fst but had only a low-power seed. The same films in two Wikipedias give a true zero for differentiation. Weakness: summariser Fst mixes wording with real differences in detail; film counts per industry are unconfirmed.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as IN-25, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Hatzel and Biemann 2024; Lewontin and Krakauer 1973; Ross, Greenhill and Atkinson 2013; Wikidata query service (2026-11-08)

title: McDonald-Kreitman test for two franchises
question: Are wording-robust units over-represented among differences fixed between Batman and Superman works, compared with differences that vary inside each franchise?
note: Needs PO21's synonymous class and 20 or more works per franchise. Rival: the same two-by-two table with LLM-coded tropes against word types.

title: dN/dS by canon tier
question: Is change along documented descent, scaled by the retelling (synonymous) rate from PO21, lowest for core memes and highest for optional ones?
note: Purifying selection on the canon. Rival: embedding distance over lexical distance. Falsified if core and optional ratios are equal or the embedding ratio gives the same ordering.

title: Is the meme frequency spectrum just threshold noise?
question: Does the count of units present in exactly k of n contemporaneous works differ from what the presence rule's roughly 3% false-positive rate (`study/paper/paper.md`, section 2.3) produces alone?
note: A Tajima's-D-style check that needs a re-extraction keeping rare units. Rival: the word-type spectrum. Without it, singleton counts and any spectrum statistic are uninterpretable.

title: Fst against documented remake flow
question: Is per-unit differentiation (Fst) between national film industries lower where Wikidata records more cross-industry remakes, beyond what word-based Fst shows?
note: CMU corpus has country labels. Partial Mantel test controlling word Fst. About a dozen industries, so power is low. Run after PO27, on summariser-safe units only. A better-powered cousin: labelled hybrid genres (horror comedy) should test as mixtures of their parent genres, and unrelated genres should not.

title: Sweeps and hitch-hikers after a hit
question: After a hit such as The Dark Knight (2008), do its optional memes rise in other superhero films and drag linked passenger memes with them?
note: Needs PO23's drift baseline and PO24's linked pairs. Rival: phrase-frequency series and embedding-cluster frequencies over the same years.

title: Price equation split per unit
question: Is change in a unit's frequency along documented descent carried more by selection among parent works or by transformation during adaptation?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: CE-24.
note: Wikidata P144, with number of adaptations as fitness; PO21's 1,363 checked pairs are a starting sample. Sperber against Dawkins in one number. Rival: the same split on word presence and on LLM-coded tropes.

title: Admixture fractions for two-source works
question: Can a mixture model on unit presence recover how much of The Dark Knight comes from The Long Halloween and how much from The Killing Joke (both documented in `study/results/experiments.json`)?
note: Validate first on stories built from two known sources at set proportions, as in PO22's spliced calibration. Rival: a topic model on words, the same model family as genetic admixture tools.

title: Forecast the next work's new memes
question: Does an accumulation curve fitted on the 32 studied Batman works predict how many new units each of the 39 held-out works in `preregistration/works_batman_extended.json` adds?
note: Tettelin-style out-of-sample forecast; follows PO26. Rival: the same forecast from word types. Uses up the held-out Batman works, so register it before anything else touches them.

title: Does lineage correction recover randomised truth?
question: On archived headline tests, do unit associations with click rate estimated across tests, after standard corrections, match the randomised associations measured within each test?
note: Added by the reviewer. Upworthy Research Archive (32,487 tests, CC BY 4.0; drop the 22% flagged for failed randomisation). Within-test effects are causal, so this measures how much topic confounding principal components and mixed models remove, before PO25-style film results are trusted. Rival: the same comparison on words and embeddings.

title: Silent-change rate from fourteen years of rewrites
question: Between a film's 2012 plot summary (CMU corpus) and today's Wikipedia one, how fast do units change per unit of wording change, and which units stay put under heavy rewriting?
note: Added by the reviewer. Same film, same language, a natural dose: in a 37-film spot check (2026-11-08) 11 kept under half of their 2012 content words. Gives a per-unit synonymous rate without machine translation, complementing PO21's ceiling. Rival: each unit's word shadow, embeddings, an LLM's motif answers.

title: Do neuron units track what survives retelling?
question: When people retell a story in their own words, do fixed neuron units predict which statements survive, and recover the published content and prestige effects, better than cheap readers?
hypothesis: On 87,421 human-coded cells from 163 people's spoken recall, unit persistence predicts present-or-absent with AUC (ranking accuracy; 0.5 is chance) at least 0.05 above the better of content-word overlap and BM25 word matching, and at least 0.65 where under half a statement's words appear. Unit-coded recall reproduces Berl et al.'s five significant effects: social, survival, negative, biologically counterintuitive, prestige.
falsifier: AUC gain over word overlap below 0.03, or AUC under 0.60 on the low-overlap cells, or fewer than 4 of the 5 published effects with the right sign. Sample: 87,421 cells, 538 statements, 163 people, two stories. Bootstrap by person and by statement; the standard error should be near 0.01, to confirm by simulation.
data: Berl et al., OSF 72v3f (CC BY 4.0): 326 transcripts of spoken recall, 538 statements coded present or absent, speaker prestige randomised. Acerbi and Stubbersfield, OSF 6v2ps: ChatGPT chains on the same two stories and three older materials, two coders, about 9,000 cells. Breithaupt et al., OSF jr2py: 348 human retellings. The last two state no licence: commit scores only.
method: Units chosen for rewording robustness on Breithaupt's human retellings, frozen. A statement's signature is the units firing on its words in the source story; its score, the share still firing in the recall. Cut-offs set on one story, tested on the other. Mixed logistic model on content type and prestige. Nulls: random firing-rate-matched units; recalls shuffled across people; length covariate.
rivals: Content-word overlap, BM25, best-match sentence-embedding cosine, an 8B model asked whether each statement is present (20,000-cell sample), recall length, random matched units, mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: the LLM reader, since judging paraphrase is its home ground. If it wins, recall can be coded automatically and neurons are not needed for this work.
premise: P1. A pass shows units follow ideas through human rewording against human coders, the regime the paper says it needs. A fail on the cleanest public paraphrase data with human coding leaves P1 little as a measurement claim.
bio: One passage, many replicate lines
cost: S. No generation needed. Two extraction passes over about 900 short texts and 20,000 short reader calls on one laptop.
payoff: An error rate for unit readout under human paraphrase against human coders (their own agreement, kappa 0.74 on a re-coded tenth, sets the ceiling), and a check that unit-coded recall gives the same content and prestige effects as hand coding.
risk: Only two stories, so statements share names and setting. Statements are finer than sentences, so neighbours may share one signature. The LLM reader probably wins outright.
review: Moved the main test to Berl et al.'s human recall (87,421 coded cells), because the ChatGPT chains keep most words: a rough parse put word overlap near AUC 0.85 there, 0.78 on human recall. Dropped the fresh-chain test, which had no independent coder. Weakness: two stories.
ranking: In the top twelve of 3 of 3 judges (what decides the premises fastest: rank 3; speed and cost: rank 4; upside: rank 12). The only cheap test against human coders of human rewording (87,421 coded cells, nothing to generate), so a failure cannot be blamed on machine-written items; judge it against the best embedding and the LLM reader, because the registered pass bar only asks units to beat word overlap.
sources: Berl et al. 2021; Acerbi & Stubbersfield 2023; Breithaupt et al. 2024; Mesoudi, Whiten & Dunbar 2006

title: Do retelling chains converge whatever the starting story?
question: Do chains started from different texts drift toward the same forms, and can units separate content copied from the seed from content that appears whatever the seed?
hypothesis: With retellings held to about 150 words, the starting seed's share of unit-profile variation falls at least 30% by generation 8 under an open-ended retelling prompt, more than under a plain rephrase prompt. After subtracting the rephrase arm's drift (house style), a drift direction fitted on 20 seeds predicts drift on 20 held-out seeds with cosine at least 0.3.
falsifier: Seed share falls less than 10%, or held-out drift cosine beats random matched units by under 0.05, or sentence-embedding centroids show the same drift consistency (within 0.05). 40 seeds, 3 chains, 8 generations, 2 writers, 2 prompts: 3,840 texts. Inference is by seed: 20 held-out seeds give a standard error near 0.03 if seeds spread 0.15; confirm by simulation.
data: Seeds: the 20 initial texts in Perez et al.'s public code (GitHub jeremyperez2/TelephoneGameLLM; no licence file, so commit hashes only) plus 20 tale openings from Hagedorn and Darányi's Folktexts (1,518 tales; Zenodo 6575263; CC BY-SA 4.0 per its README). Chains generated locally. Human check: Breithaupt et al., OSF jr2py, 116 stories with 3 human retellings each; no licence stated.
method: Unit profile per text from a reader model that wrote no chain. Statistics: seed share of variance by generation; per-unit rate of persisting where seeded against appearing where not seeded; held-out drift cosine. Nulls: texts re-paired across chains within generation; random firing-rate-matched units. Drift sign checked on human chains within length bands. Repeat with Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features.
rivals: TF-IDF vectors (words weighted by rarity), sentence-embedding centroids, mean-pooled residual stream, text length, random units, and the published property scorers (toxicity, positivity, difficulty). Most dangerous: embedding centroids, which see convergence of style and tone cheaply. If they win, attraction is confirmed in open models and units add only names for what converges.
premise: P1, with a side reading on P2. If widely shared units are attractors, similarity without descent is expected and unit trees are exposed to false kinship, which would explain the failed identity test. Two writer models agreeing on the attractor is mild behavioural support for P2.
bio: Convergent evolution; homoplasy
cost: S. About 11 hours of local generation and one hour of extraction.
payoff: A list of attractor units to exclude from lineage work, and a measured split of stability into copying and convergence.
risk: Once house style is subtracted nothing may be left to converge; or writer models differ so much that no common attractor exists.
review: Perez et al. already showed attractors on four scalar properties; the news here is the unit-level list. Fixed text length and switched to seed share of variance, since shrinking texts lower any count's variance; subtracted rephrase drift as house style; inference by seed. Weakness: reader and writers share LLM style.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as ME-22, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Perez et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04503); Acerbi et al. 2021; Claidière, Scott-Phillips & Sperber 2014; Breithaupt et al. 2024

title: Are meme units particles or thresholded continua?
question: When a story is passed on blended with a second parent, do unit values in the child behave like particles, as replicator memetics needs, or like a graded quantity that blends, as Henrich and Boyd's continuous model allows?
hypothesis: Memetics predicts that in free blends rewording-robust units fit segregation (child takes one parent's value) better than blending at least 20 percentage points more often than random directions in the residual stream, and at least 20% of units have two-peaked activations against under 5% of random directions. The slot arm must show segregation for at least 80% of slot units.
falsifier: The segregation share of units is within 10 points of random directions or of embedding components, or under 20% of units favour segregation on held-out blends. Then discreteness comes from the text and the pooling, not the unit, and no replicator is needed. 150 parent pairs, 8 children per arm; proportions over 500 units have error under 0.03.
data: Parents: 300 tales of 300 to 3,000 words from the 1,518 in Hagedorn and Darányi's Folktexts, labelled with ATU tale types (Zenodo 6575263, 10.8 MB; CC BY-SA 4.0 per its README), paired across types. Children written by two open models in three arms: free blend, slot copy, merged summary. Background: 20,000 sentences from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (CC BY-SA).
method: Units chosen for rewording robustness on 50 development pairs, frozen. Per trait, compare held-out likelihood of segregation (mixture of parental values) and blending (weighted parental mean pulled toward the population mean); Hartigan dip test for two peaks. Slot and merged-summary arms calibrate both patterns. Null: children re-paired with wrong parents of similar length. Repeat with sparse-autoencoder features and at 8-bit.
rivals: The same comparison on TF-IDF term weights, principal components of sentence embeddings, random residual-stream directions pooled like units, Llama Scope features, random units and length; an LLM reader only codes which parent each event came from. Most dangerous: random directions, because a maximum over tokens can make anything look all-or-nothing. If they match units, Henrich and Boyd's case holds.
premise: P1. Segregation and two peaks beyond what random directions show support 'a meme is a neuron firing' as more than a threshold. Blending supports treating neurons as a continuous trait measure and dropping replicator language; the paper's presence rule becomes a convenience.
bio: Mendel's crosses against blending inheritance
cost: S. 3,600 generated children and two extraction passes; about two days. The two-peak test can be tried first on the study's saved activations if they are still on disk.
payoff: Decides which mathematics to use: particulate population genetics or quantitative genetics on continuous traits.
risk: The verdict may describe how LLM writers blend, not how human authors do (see the seed on two-source works), and 4-bit activations may blur real peaks; the slot arm and the 8-bit check bound both.
review: Text is made of discrete events and unit values are maxima over tokens, so any detector looks particulate. Made the claim relative to random directions, added a merged-summary arm as the blending anchor, and replaced binary word presence (which cannot blend) with term weights. The LLM-writer weakness remains.
sources: Henrich & Boyd 2002; Claidière, Scott-Phillips & Sperber 2014; Hagedorn & Darányi 2022; He et al. 2024 (Llama Scope)

title: Price split: selection against transformation in adaptations
question: Along documented book-to-film links, is change in how common a unit is carried by which books get adapted (selection) or by what adaptation does to them (transmission), and are units inherited more faithfully than words?
hypothesis: Memetics predicts selection carries at least half the change: once the change seen under randomly re-paired children (the shift of medium) is subtracted, the selection term exceeds the transmission term for at least 50% of units, and noise-corrected parent-to-child fidelity (regression slope) of units beats frequency-matched words by at least 0.05.
falsifier: Transmission exceeds selection for more than 80% of units after that subtraction, or the fidelity gap over words is below 0.02. At least 3,000 book-to-film pairs and 3,000 never-adapted novels, split by source work; with 1,500 held-out pairs a slope difference of 0.05 has standard error about 0.015.
data: Wikidata 'based on' links (CC0): 6,110 film-from-written-work links with English Wikipedia articles at both ends, 4,312 distinct sources (query of 2026-11-08). In a sample of 10, 8 had plot sections at both ends; confirm the count before registration. Plots are CC BY-SA 4.0, names masked with the pre-registration's deterministic masker. Plus novels with plots and no recorded adaptation.
method: The Price equation splits change in a trait's mean into selection (its covariance with number of adaptations) and transmission (mean parent-to-child change). Both per unit, standardised within medium. Fidelity: parent-child slope, noise-corrected using each film's 2012 (CMU corpus) and current plots. Units chosen on half the sources. Null: children reassigned within decade, genre and length; pairs sharing 8-word runs dropped.
rivals: The identical decomposition on word presence, TF-IDF terms, sentence-embedding dimensions and LLM-coded tropes on a 300-pair sample; random units; length. The equation holds for any trait, so only these comparisons are informative. Most dangerous: word presence, because Wikipedia editors reuse phrasing between a book's page and its film's. If words tie, the split still answers Sperber against Dawkins for plots.
premise: P1. Higher fidelity than words under a change of medium is the heritability evidence P1 lacks. A dominant transmission term says units are reconstructed, which favours attraction theory over replicator memetics whatever the unit.
bio: Price equation; parent-offspring heritability
cost: M. Wikidata and Wikipedia pulls, name masking, about 9,000 plots through two models; one to two weeks.
payoff: Edmonds's fifth challenge answered with numbers: selection and transmission shares per unit, and a fidelity figure to set beside words.
risk: Plot summaries are written by Wikipedia editors, not the adapters, so the transmission term mixes adaptation with summarising. Wikidata misses adaptations, so 'never adapted' is noisy.
review: Counted the links on Wikidata. Added subtraction of the medium shift, within-medium scaling and a noise correction, because book and film plot pages differ in length and style. Run CE27 first. Weakness: editors, not adapters, wrote both texts, and the selection term will be small and noisy.
sources: El Mouden et al. 2014; Nettle 2020; Mesoudi 2021; Wikidata P144

title: Content, prestige or conformity along citations?
question: Along documented citation links, do some ideas pass from sources to citing papers more readily than others, even without their words, and does passing depend on how eminent the carrier is?
hypothesis: Content: a unit's propagation score (how much more often papers citing a carrier show it than papers citing none) is stable between 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, rank correlation at least 0.5. Adoptions sharing none of its trigger words occur at 1.5 times the swapped-reference rate. Prestige: within a paper, adoption odds rise 10% per standard deviation of the carrier's earlier citations.
falsifier: Stability under 0.3, or word-free adoptions no more common than under swapped references, or neuron units predicting held-out adoption no better than n-gram units (log-loss gain under 1%). 5,000 citing papers with at least 10 abstract-bearing references each give several hundred thousand paper-by-unit exposures, ample for odds ratios of 1.1; papers split by year.
data: 5,000 papers from one arXiv category, 2015 to 2024 (arXiv metadata, CC0 1.0), plus every reference that has an abstract, with yearly citation counts, from OpenAlex (CC0). OpenAlex's keyless quota was exhausted when checked, so a free key is needed. How fully it lists references for arXiv preprints is unconfirmed: check before registration.
method: 500 units chosen on 2015 to 2018, fixed. Propagation score per unit after Kuhn, Perc and Helbing. Logistic model of unit presence in the citing abstract on carrier share, the carrier's citation rank within the list, and unit effects. Control: each reference swapped for its nearest uncited same-year paper by embedding. Conformity reported, not tested: authors choose what they cite.
rivals: The same model with n-gram units (the Kuhn, Perc and Helbing meme score), embedding-cluster units, LLM-tagged concepts on 500 papers, random units, abstract length. Most dangerous: n-grams, since a field reuses its terms. If they tie, the estimates stand as cultural-evolution results and neurons are shown unnecessary here.
premise: Assumes both. It re-runs a published propagation analysis with the new unit. Neuron units earn credit only if word-free adoptions exceed the swapped-reference rate and add prediction; otherwise P1 gains nothing. Conformity needs assigned exposure, which a citation list is not.
bio: Transmissibility of variants; hitch-hiking with fit carriers
cost: M. Data assembly dominates; several hundred thousand sentences per model is a few hours of extraction.
payoff: A count of ideas that pass along citations without their words, a stability figure for per-idea transmissibility, and a within-paper prestige estimate.
risk: Topic similarity between a paper and what it cites mimics transmission; the swapped-reference control is matched by embedding, so it may remove real transmission too.
review: Rebuilt around the published propagation score. Dropped the content-share test (unit base rates make it a tautology) and the conformity test (authors choose their sources, and a presence cut-off alone bends the curve). Exposure now covers all references with abstracts. Still observational: association only.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as ME-21, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Kuhn, Perc & Helbing 2014; Henrich & Boyd 1998; Acerbi et al. 2016; Henrich & Gil-White 2001

title: Do meme sets grow and ratchet in chains?
question: In chains where each writer learns a hidden rule set from the previous guide plus a few new examples, does the set of units in the guide grow and keep what it gained, in step with measured skill?
hypothesis: Given pilot chains where skill rises 15 points over 10 generations, length-adjusted unit repertoire tracks the number of rules a guide supports (rank correlation at least 0.5, and 0.1 above word-type count) on chains using a renamed game. Units are lost at most half as often from intact guides as from guides missing 40% of sentences.
