falsifier: Repertoire correlation below 0.3, or within 0.05 of word-type count or length, or equal loss rates in the two arms. 60 chains by 10 generations by 2 arms: 1,200 guides; a chain-level bootstrap on 40 held-out chains should detect a 0.1 correlation gap at about 0.8 power, to confirm by simulation.
data: Built, nothing downloaded: an invented card game with 12 coded rules in two skins (same rules, different names for suits and actions), examples generated by program, guides written by two open models to a fixed word budget. Skill is a frozen solver's accuracy on 144 held-out judgments, twelve per rule, given only the guide. Texts released CC BY 4.0.
method: Units chosen on 20 development chains in the first skin, frozen; scored on 40 in the second. Per guide: repertoire size after regressing out length. Per unit: gains and losses. Truth: a rule is supported when the solver gets 10 of 12 judgments right. Nulls: guides shuffled across chains within generation; random firing-rate-matched units. Reader differs from writers and solver.
rivals: Word-type count, guide length, embedding-cluster count, an LLM asked to list the rules a guide states, random units, mean-pooled residual norm. Most dangerous: the rule-listing LLM, which reads rules directly; then length, because a maximum over tokens rises with length. If length wins, repertoire counts in the study need the same correction.
premise: P1. Shows whether a unit count measures accumulated ideas or only text size. A pass licenses growth and ratchet claims for franchises; a fail says the canon tiers partly count length.
bio: Gene gain and loss along a lineage; open pangenome
cost: M. Game code, 1,200 generated guides and about 173,000 short solver calls; one to two weeks.
payoff: A validated way to count accumulation, with loss rates under high and low fidelity, the quantity the ratchet argument turns on.
risk: Invented rules may have no dedicated units, so the eligible set is generic and the rule-listing LLM wins.
review: Replaced the one-sentence arm, where loss is forced by length, with sentence deletion at a fixed word budget; raised solver judgments from 4 to 12 per rule; test chains use a renamed game so word lists cannot transfer. Weakness: invented rules may have no dedicated units.
sources: Tennie, Call & Tomasello 2009; Mesoudi & Thornton 2018; Zhuang 2025 (arXiv:2507.21166); Perez et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.08882)

title: Price split on chains with imposed selection
question: When selection of known strength is imposed on retelling chains, does a unit-based Price split report it, and report none when parents are picked at random?
hypothesis: With parents picked at random, no more than 7% of units are flagged as selected at the 5% level. With parents picked by a hidden score, units chosen on development texts as tracking that score are flagged in at least 80% of populations at the strong setting, and their selection term rises with imposed strength (rank correlation at least 0.6).
falsifier: More than 10% of units flagged under random parents, or detection under 50% at the strong setting. 3 strengths by 30 populations by 8 texts by 10 generations: 7,200 retellings. Rates over 30 populations have standard error about 0.09, enough to tell 80% from 50%; confirm by simulation.
data: Built: 30 starting sets of 8 short tales from Hagedorn and Darányi's Folktexts (Zenodo 6575263; CC BY-SA 4.0 per its README). Each generation, 8 children each retell one parent in about 120 words. Parents are drawn at random, or with odds rising in a hidden judge's score of how badly the story ends. Texts to be released CC BY-SA 4.0.
method: The Price equation splits change in a trait's mean into selection (covariance of the trait with number of children) and transmission (mean parent-to-child change). Compute both per unit per generation; flag selection by shuffling parent choices. Units chosen on separate development populations. Reader, writers and judge are different models. Nulls: the random-parent arm; random units matched on firing rate.
rivals: The same split on word presence, TF-IDF terms, sentence-embedding components, an LLM reader re-scoring the hidden property, random units and length. Most dangerous: the LLM reader, which nearly is the judge; then word presence, since bad endings have their own words. If they detect as often, units add nothing, but the sample-size curve still stands.
premise: P1. A calibration, not proof of memes: it shows whether unit readouts can carry a selection analysis and at what sample size. A fail puts selection claims made with units, such as the study's underpowered E3, out of reach.
bio: Artificial selection lines beside drift lines
cost: M. 7,200 retellings and as many judge calls, two extraction passes; about three days on one laptop.
payoff: A false-alarm rate and a sample-size curve for detecting selection with units, and a worked case where transmission (writers softening endings) can oppose selection.
risk: The hidden property may be carried by a few obvious words, so every rival detects it; or writers' drift may swamp selection at every strength tried.
review: Added by the reviewer. The Price equation is an identity for any trait, so CE24 cannot show the unit readout is right; this gives a known answer first. Weakness: LLM writers under an artificial rule; the selected property may be lexical. Area-wide, novelty was checked on arXiv only.
sources: El Mouden et al. 2014; Nettle 2020; MacCallum et al. 2012; Perez et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04503)

title: Minimal counterintuitiveness in Grimm tales
question: Can units count violations of intuitive expectations per tale and reproduce the inverted U, where successful tales carry a few such elements?
note: Grimm tales are public domain; Norenzayan et al. 2006 supply the success measure. Rivals: an LLM counting violations, a magic-word list, tale length. Small n and a contested theory (Purzycki and Willard 2015). Berl et al.'s coded recall (OSF 72v3f, used in CE21) tests counterintuitive content with far more data.

title: Does the idea survive the word swap?
question: When one word of a quotation is replaced during copying, do concept units stay on, and do meaning-preserving swaps spread further than meaning-changing ones?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: ME-23.
note: MemeTracker quotation families with Lerique and Roth's substitution pairs (SNAP, no licence stated). The attractor there is lexical, so WordNet synonymy and embedding cosine are strong rivals.

title: Same attractor across writer families and humans
question: Do chains run by three unrelated model families and by people converge on the same attractor units?
note: A behavioural test of P2 needing no neuron mapping; extends CE22. Perez et al. report model and size dependence, so a null is likely and still informative.

title: Knock out the attractor
question: If the units that chains drift toward are ablated in the retelling model, does the drift stop while the rest of the story is kept?
note: The causal check for CE22. Rivals: a prompt instruction to avoid the theme, a keyword ban, ablating random units. Needs a hooked local model; about a day.

title: Source or receiver?
question: How much of the variance in which units survive a retelling is explained by the story and how much by who retells it?
note: Gabora's objection in testable form. Berl et al.'s 163 people each recalled the same two stories (OSF 72v3f, CC BY 4.0), which gives the receiver share directly in human data; add 4 writer models and the retellers in OSF jr2py. Compare with the same split on words and embeddings.

title: Copy the product or the recipe
question: Are more units retained when a retelling is made from an outline of the story than from the story itself?
note: Blackmore's distinction between copying the product and copying the instructions, run as two chain arms; that she ranks instructions as the higher-fidelity mode was not confirmed in the notes. Rival: an LLM coding retained statements.

title: Recency against Lindy in borrowed material
question: Is the age of the sources a work borrows from better described by a preference for recent works or by a 30-year return?
note: Karsdorp and van den Bosch 2016 found retellings prefer young sources. Dated Wikidata adaptation links against an availability-weighted null; unit ages must add to documented-source ages to count.

title: Two-source works in the wild
question: Do real works with two documented sources show the same segregating or blending pattern as the generated blends in CE23?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: AT-23.
note: Wikidata lists 1,277 works with exactly two 'based on' sources and English Wikipedia articles for all three, 302 of them films (query of 2026-11-08). Plot-section coverage is unchecked, and one source may itself be an adaptation of the other. Answers the objection that LLM writers blend unlike human authors.

title: Does the neutral verdict survive the merge threshold?
question: When unit frequencies over time are fitted with random-copying and biased-copying models, does the verdict stay the same across unit-merging thresholds and match the verdict from keywords?
note: Added by the reviewer: the area had no neutral-model test. Dated film plots (CMU Movie Summary Corpus, 42,306 plots, CC BY-SA). Frequency tests of neutrality are weak (Leroi et al. 2020) and the unit count moves with the threshold, so stability of the verdict is the result. Rivals: keyword and trope-tag counts.

title: Assigned exposure sets
question: When a writer model is handed a randomly assigned set of sources, does its uptake of an idea depend on how many sources carry it and on who is said to have written them?
note: Added by the reviewer. Conformity and prestige can be identified only where exposure is assigned, which CE25's citation lists are not. Uptake hand-coded on a sample; rivals: an LLM reader and keywords. It measures writer models, not people; human counterparts: Muthukrishna et al. 2016, Berl et al. 2021.

title: Do neuron profiles pick winning headlines beyond embeddings?
question: Within a randomised headline test, does the difference between two headlines' neuron-unit profiles predict which got more clicks, beyond length, word counts, sentence embeddings, the model's own averaged internal state and an LLM's guess?
hypothesis: Adding neuron-unit differences to a model that already holds every cheap rival raises held-out pairwise accuracy (which of two headlines with the same image and teaser text won) by at least 1.0 percentage point, in Qwen3-8B and in Llama 3.1 8B. Our honest expectation is a tie: a gain under 0.5 points.
falsifier: The gain is under 1.0 point, or its 95% interval (resampling whole tests) includes zero. The holdout should hold about 1,900 usable tests and 15,800 headline pairs (counted on the equal-sized exploratory file), so the gain's standard error is 0.3 to 0.6 points. If simulation shows more than 0.35, register the cross-fitted score over confirmatory plus holdout instead.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (OSF jd64p, CC BY 4.0): 32,487 randomised tests, 150,817 headline-and-image packages, 2013 to 2015, in exploratory (4,873 tests), confirmatory (22,743) and holdout files. Drop tests from 25 June 2013 to 10 January 2014 (faulty randomisation, 22%). Keep arm pairs that share image, excerpt and lede, so only the headline differs.
method: Units: both signs of every feed-forward (MLP) channel, maximum over tokens. Choose 2,000 units and settings on exploratory, fit on confirmatory, score once on holdout. Statistic: accuracy gain over the rival stack, beside the ceiling click noise allows. Nulls: arm labels swapped within test; random units matched on firing rate and layer. Repeat using only firing that words cannot predict.
rivals: Headline length and punctuation; rarity-weighted word and character counts (TF-IDF); sentence embedding plus linear model (46.3% at naming a test's winner in LOLA, chance 33%); sparse-autoencoder features on embeddings (HypotheSAEs) and inside Llama (Llama Scope); a local LLM asked which wins. Most dangerous: a probe on the same model's averaged internal state, which units only re-express.
premise: P1. A pass means units carry success-relevant content that words and embeddings miss, and justifies the costlier fitness designs. A fail, which we expect, means neuron profiles re-describe what embeddings already hold: useful for naming causes of success, not for forecasting it. Says nothing about P2.
bio: Competition assay; named genes against anonymous markers
cost: S. About 150,000 headlines through two 8B models, under an hour each on the laptop; the rest is CPU. Run the LLM-judge rival on a subsample.
payoff: A click effect for each named unit, estimated from randomised tests, and a plain answer on whether neuron profiles forecast success better than embeddings. The activations are reused by FI-22, FI-27 and several seeds.
risk: A tie with embeddings is the likeliest result. The labels are noisy: only about 28% of headline pairs differ significantly in click rate, so accuracy tops out far below 100%. Headline memes are packaging (curiosity gap, negativity), not story ideas, so even a win may not carry over to stories.
review: Counted the data: about 1,900 clean headline-only tests in the holdout, so the stated 0.3-point error was optimistic. Added a fallback, a noise ceiling, same-teaser matching and a same-model sparse-feature rival. Prior-art check used arXiv only (web search was unavailable). Remaining weakness: a tie is likely.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (speed and cost: rank 8). One 40-minute pass per model over a free archive of randomised headline tests gives a clear win-or-tie against embeddings, and the same activations feed five other designs.
sources: Matias et al. 2021, Upworthy Research Archive (with the 2024 correction); Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng 2025 (LOLA); Movva et al. 2025 (HypotheSAEs); He et al. 2024 (Llama Scope)

title: Forecast forward: do winning headline units spread?
question: Do units that raised clicks in randomised tests before a cut-off date become more common in headlines written afterwards, and do they still pick winners months later?
hypothesis: Using only tests before 1 July 2014: the fitted weights pick 54% or more of winning headlines three to ten months later (chance 50%), and a unit's click effect correlates 0.15 or more (rank correlation) with its later change in share of headlines, after allowing for its starting share and earlier trend.
falsifier: Forward accuracy under 52%; or the correlation's 95% interval (resampling tests in weekly blocks, not units) includes zero; or click effects measured after the cut-off predict share changes before it equally well. Exploratory plus confirmatory files should hold about 4,100 clean headline-only tests on each side (scaled from the exploratory count); simulate before registering.
data: The Upworthy archive of FI-21 (CC BY 4.0), exploratory and confirmatory files only, so FI-21's holdout stays unopened; tests dated by creation time. Click effects use clean-period same-image headline pairs (24 January to 24 June 2013; 11 January 2014 on). Headline frequencies use every tested headline, including the faulty-randomisation months, which spoil clicks but not what was written.
method: Units firing in at least 1% of pre-cut-off headlines, chosen without looking at clicks; settings frozen from FI-21. Click effect from within-test contrasts before the cut-off; if its split-half reliability is under 0.2, call the spread test uninformative. Report word-like units and units no single word reproduces separately. Nulls: test dates shuffled; effects reassigned among units of equal frequency.
rivals: The same two forecasts from word sequences (most dangerous: stock phrases probably show the cleanest rise), from sentence-embedding clusters, from headline length, and from 'last quarter's frequency persists'. An LLM judge is excluded as a forecaster because it was trained after 2015. If phrases win, selection on packaging is still shown with causally measured fitness.
premise: P1. A pass shows measured fitness followed by spread, with fitness set by randomisation, in one newsroom whose editors saw the results: guided selection, not blind selection. P1 gains only if units that no single word reproduces also respond. A fail says editors did not copy what won, or that fitness is too short-lived to forecast.
bio: Response to selection (breeder's equation)
cost: S. Reuses FI-21 activations; two to three days of CPU analysis and date tabulation.
payoff: A direct test of whether fitter memes spread, with fitness measured by experiment and not inferred from fame, plus the shelf life of a fitness estimate. The wear-out seed falls out of the same tables.
risk: One newsroom is one history. Upworthy changed its style on purpose and Facebook changed its feed in 2014, so frequency shifts may reflect policy, not test results. Click effects for single units, estimated from about 4,100 tests, may be too noisy to correlate with anything.
review: Moved the cut-off from 1 April to 1 July 2014: the original left about 2,800 tests to estimate fitness, now about 4,100 each side. Kept FI-21's holdout unopened; added block resampling, a reliability gate and a reverse-time check. Remaining weakness: one newsroom, whose policy also changed.
ranking: 2 of 3 judges thought the area reviewer rated this too low.
sources: Matias et al. 2021, Upworthy Research Archive (with the 2024 correction); Robertson et al. 2023; Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng 2025 (LOLA); Parikh et al. 2026 (TEA-Time)

title: Selection rerun: do sequels keep what sold?
question: Within a film series, does a later film carry more of the distinctive units of those earlier instalments that earned more at the box office?
hypothesis: On name-free plots, the within-series rank correlation between an earlier film's box office and a later film's inheritance from it is 0.10 or more, after allowing for position in the series and years apart, with the same sign in both models.
falsifier: A 95% upper bound below 0.10; or a neuron effect that vanishes once word-overlap inheritance is regressed out. An interval spanning both zero and 0.10 is inconclusive, not a null. With 250 series, 80% power is reached somewhere between 0.10 and 0.15, depending on how alike a series's film pairs are (E3: 27% at 0.30). Stop under 200 series.
data: Wikidata (CC0) lists 317 to 539 film series with three or more films on English Wikipedia, depending on how a series is defined (recounted 8 November 2026). Only 137 have Wikidata box office for three films, so most figures must come from Wikipedia infoboxes, adjusted for inflation. Plots from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), names masked by the pre-registration's rule-based masker.
method: No unit selection; present means beating nearly all of 1,000 reference films. Plots in a series cut to equal length; series capped at 12 films. Inheritance: the share of an earlier instalment's unique units carried by a film at position three or later. Regress on within-series box office rank, position and gap; resample series. Null: box office shuffled within series.
rivals: The same statistic from rarity-weighted word counts (TF-IDF or BM25), sentence-embedding similarity, the model's averaged internal state, random non-meme units, and an LLM reading three name-free plots and saying which earlier film the later one borrows from. Most dangerous: TF-IDF, which matched neurons on heredity. If it wins, selection is still measured; only the neuron claim fails.
premise: P1. A pass shows success-biased copying can be measured across hundreds of lineages; only a signal beyond word overlap raises belief in P1. A well-powered null says the selection claim does not hold at the level of plot summaries. Agreement between two models is replication, not a test of P2.
bio: Selection differential: fitter parents pass on more traits
cost: M. Between 1,600 and 3,000 plots (under an hour per model). One to two weeks, mostly building the series table, parsing box office from infoboxes and masking names.
payoff: A far better powered answer to the question the study's selection test (E3) asked, with success measured at release, and a reusable table of series, order and box office for other lineage tests. Positive control: the immediate predecessor should rank first.
risk: Box office coverage may cut the sample below 200 series. A sequel continues its predecessor's story whatever it earned, which leaves little room for choice. Sequel summaries recap earlier plots, and editors describe sequels in terms of the famous instalment. Word overlap may tie again.
review: Recount: 317 to 539 series by definition, 137 with Wikidata box office, 40% only three films long, so the claimed 80% power at 0.10 was optimistic. Added equal-length plots, a series cap and an inconclusive zone. Remaining weakness: box office needs infobox parsing, and story continuity limits choice.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as FI-28, which the judges would run instead.
sources: study/results/experiments.json (E3: rho 0.25 and 0.00, n = 15, power 0.27); Wikidata query service, series counts, 2026-11-08; Martin et al. 2016; Salganik, Dodds, Watts 2006

title: Which new memes catch on, against random copying?
question: When a unit first appears in a film genre, does its later spread exceed what random copying predicts, and can the spreaders be picked from what was known at its birth?
hypothesis: Units absent from a genre's first 300 films, then present in 5 or more of the next 300 after first appearing, are at least twice as common as under shuffled release order. Features fixed at birth (earlier spread in other genres, number of co-arriving units, host film's box office) predict which spread, with AUC 0.60 or higher (0.50 is chance).
falsifier: No excess over shuffled release order (first appearances are then noise or steady background rates, and the design stops). Or AUC under 0.55, or no higher than the 95th percentile in shuffled-order and simulated random-copying worlds. Or new words through the same pipeline score as well. Thousands of first appearances give a standard error near 0.02.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (CC BY-SA, version not stated): 42,306 Wikipedia plots with release dates and genres. Five genres with 1,169 to 2,279 dated plots of ten or more sentences (horror, science fiction, crime, fantasy, romantic comedy; recounted 8 November 2026). Names masked using the corpus's own entity tags; plots cut to their first 10 sentences.
method: Present: a unit's score beats all 1,000 out-of-genre reference films (0.1% false alarms). Mutation: first presence after a genre's first 300 films; a series counts once. Nulls: release order shuffled within genre (keeps each unit's rate, removes time); simulated random copying with invention (Bentley 2004). Scored on held-out genres. Positive control: ten documented genre innovations, pre-listed; five must register.
rivals: New words and rarity-weighted terms through the same pipeline (most dangerous: new ideas often arrive with new words, such as cyborg or hacker, and word counts carry no hindsight); embedding clusters first populated in a given year; an LLM reading the host plot and naming the element most likely to be imitated; copies in the first three years alone.
premise: P1. One-sided. If neither units nor words beat random copying, drift is enough to explain meme turnover in film genres. If new words do as well as units, P1 gains nothing. A pass by units alone is weak support, because models trained on later culture may detect the ideas that won more easily.
bio: Fate of a new mutation: drift or positive selection
cost: M. About 8,000 plots of 10 sentences (80,000 sentences, under an hour per model), storing only units above the strict bar. About two weeks, mostly simulations and name masking.
payoff: A dated list of mutations per genre with their fate, a calibrated test of selection against drift, and an early-warning score for new memes. A stronger successor to the Batman-only mutation plan.
risk: The models were trained after all these films, so units exist mainly for ideas that later became common: failed mutations are under-detected. With about 900,000 units, chance alone gives roughly 900 false presences per film. Neutral-model tests are sensitive to time bins and population size (Karjus et al. 2020).
review: Added a shuffled-release-order null and a fixed 300-film window, because steady background rates and unequal exposure could fake 'spread'. Dropped firing strength as a predictor (it leaks hindsight); added host box office. Remaining weakness: models trained on later culture detect winners more easily, so only a fail is clean.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as PO-23, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Bentley, Hahn, Shennan 2004; Feder, Kryazhimskiy, Plotkin 2014; Karjus et al. 2020; CMU Movie Summary Corpus (Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013)

title: Plant one meme, measure real reader preference
question: When two versions of one story premise differ only in which meme is planted, do readers reliably prefer one, and which method forecast those preferences beforehand?
hypothesis: Meme appeal is measurable: scores for the 34 memes from one half of the premises and raters correlate 0.6 or more with scores from the other half, and at least 6 story memes beat the neutral-motif average by 8 points of choice share. Unit-based forecasts correlate 0.3 or more with the scores; we expect an LLM reader to do better.
falsifier: Split-half correlation under 0.3: single planted memes have no stable appeal at this dose, and forecasting is moot. Or unit-based forecasts correlate under 0.2 while another forecaster passes 0.4. Thirty-four memes detect a true correlation of 0.5 with about 85% power, but cannot separate two forecasters closer than about 0.4.
data: New, by construction: the 34 memes in preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json (24 story memes, 10 neutral motifs). Ten name-free premises, each written in 34 versions that differ in one planted sentence avoiding the meme's usual words (the file's ban list). About 20,000 paired judgments from a consented, paid adult panel. Texts and anonymised judgments released under CC BY 4.0.
method: Each judgment: two versions of one premise carrying different memes, equal length, 'which would you rather read?'. Scores from a paired-comparison model allowing for premise and rater. Before launch: a second model family and the author confirm each plant blind; record whether the meme's unit fires; freeze forecasts and code. Ethics: fiction only, AI authorship disclosed, debrief, no optimisation loop.
rivals: An LLM reading both versions and predicting the choice share (most dangerous: simulated samples tracked survey experiments at r = 0.85 in Hewitt et al.); human forecasters; sentence-embedding differences; sentiment and negative-word counts; text length. Unit, embedding and word models are trained alike, leaving whole memes out. If the LLM reader wins, the causal dataset still stands.
premise: P1. If unit profiles forecast a causal preference shift for memes they were not trained on, units carry fitness information. If the LLM reader forecasts better, neurons are the wrong tool for prediction, though planted memes with measured effects remain the first fitness data at the level of ideas.
bio: Knock-in mutation followed by a competition assay
cost: L. About 20,000 paid judgments (roughly 2,000 to 4,000 US dollars; a guess, not a quote), 340 planted texts to write and audit, and an ethics review. The one design here that needs more than a laptop.
payoff: The first open dataset that randomises the idea and not the packaging: causal appeal scores for 34 memes, how far they hold across premises, and a scoreboard of forecasters.
risk: One sentence may be too small a dose. How well a meme fits a premise may matter more than the meme itself. Units may not fire on plants that avoid the usual words: only four of 31 study units survived rewording in both models. Stated preference is not real reading.
review: Replaced the neutral-filler comparison (any eventful sentence beats filler) with meme-against-meme choices and added a reliability gate. Corrected the meme list: 34 memes, 10 neutral, not 30 and 6. Remaining weakness: 34 memes cannot rank forecasters, and units may not fire on plants written without the usual words.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 11). Paying real readers to choose between stories that differ in one planted idea gives the first causal appeal scores for ideas and not packaging, valuable even if an LLM forecasts them better than units do.
sources: Hewitt et al. 2024 (published as Ashokkumar et al. 2026); Hackenburg et al. 2025; preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json; study/results/robustness/nulls.json (rewording test)

title: Does a meme's track record forecast a film?
question: After metadata, can a new film's box office be forecast from how earlier films carrying the same units, and the same pairs of units, performed?
hypothesis: For films released from 2005 to 2012, unit and pair track records built only from earlier films add 0.01 or more to out-of-sample R-squared (share of variance explained) over metadata plus the embedding nearest-neighbour rival, and pair novelty shows an inverted U. We expect metadata to dominate and no gain.
falsifier: A gain under 0.01, or an interval that includes zero; or pair terms that add nothing over single units; or a gain confined to films an LLM can name from the masked plot (memorised fame). The 1,784 held-out films detect a correlation of 0.1 after controls with over 95% power; the 607 with a Wikidata budget give about 70%.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (CC BY-SA, version not stated): 7,588 films have a plot and box office; with ten or more sentences, 3,881 before 2005 and 1,784 from 2005 to 2012 (recounted 8 November 2026). Wikidata (CC0) gives a budget for 2,133 of these; parse the rest from Wikipedia infoboxes. Names masked; plots cut to their first 10 sentences.
method: Outcome: log revenue minus what year, genre, runtime, country, sequel flag, summary length and budget (flagged where missing) predict. A unit's record: mean outcome of earlier films carrying it, shrunk toward zero when few; each pair gets a record and a novelty score (observed against expected co-occurrence). Units chosen on pre-2005 films. Null: outcomes shuffled within year and genre.
rivals: Metadata alone; the mean outcome of the 20 most similar earlier films by sentence embedding (most dangerous: a track record that needs no units); the same pipeline on rarity-weighted terms and on the corpus's own genre-tag pairs (363 tags, after Sreenivasan 2013); random units; an LLM guessing from the masked plot, contaminated because it has read which films were hits.
premise: P1. A pass says fitness accumulates at the level of units and their combinations, so a work's promise can be read from its parts. A fail says success lives in metadata and whole-work similarity, and that memes are, for forecasting, no better than nearest neighbours.
bio: Breeding value from marker records; gene interactions
cost: M. About 5,700 plots of 10 sentences (57,000 sentences, under an hour per model); one to two weeks for budget parsing, metadata joins, name masking and the forward-in-time fit.
payoff: A fitness table for units and pairs with honest out-of-sample value, and a test of the marketing rule that work 'just past the familiar' does best.
risk: Metadata and budget take nearly all the variance (content features stayed under 0.05 R-squared for tweets). Units may only stand in for budget or genre. Hits get far longer summaries (median 33 sentences in the top revenue third against 12 in the bottom), and the models have read the future.
review: Recounted the corpus. Hits have summaries nearly three times longer, so plots are cut to 10 sentences and length joins the baseline. Wikidata budgets cover only 2,133 films; added a memorised-fame check and a genre-tag rival. Remaining weakness: metadata will dominate, and the models know which films were hits.
sources: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013); Uzzi et al. 2013; Sreenivasan 2013; Martin et al. 2016

title: Do click weights survive a change of model?
question: Do click weights learned on Qwen3-8B units still pick held-out winning headlines when carried to Llama 3.1 8B through matched units, with no refitting?
hypothesis: Weights carried through matched units keep at least half of the accuracy above chance that Llama's own fitted unit weights reach, in both directions, and beat weights carried through random units by 1.0 point. The same holds for units that no single word reproduces.
falsifier: Carried weights keep under a quarter of the fitted lift, or do no better than random-unit mapping; or the transfer disappears once units that a single word reproduces (correlation 0.5 or more) are removed. About 1,900 holdout tests give a standard error of 0.4 to 1.1 points on accuracy; confirm by simulation.
data: The FI-21 activations and splits of the Upworthy Research Archive (OSF jd64p, CC BY 4.0). Units are matched on text with no usable click data: the roughly 30,000 packages from the faulty-randomisation months that FI-21 discards.
method: Fit click weights on 2,000 Qwen units (confirmatory file). Pair each with the Llama unit whose firing over the matching headlines is most similar. Score holdout pairs in Llama using Qwen's weights on the paired units; repeat in reverse. Statistic: share of the fitted lift retained. Nulls: random Llama units matched on firing rate and layer; pairings shuffled.
rivals: Word-count weights, which move between models for nothing (most dangerous: if units carry only what words carry, transfer proves nothing about P2); a straight-line map between the two models' averaged internal states, fitted on the matching headlines; sentence-embedding weights reused unchanged; refitting in Llama on 10% of the data.
premise: P2, in its functional form. A pass on units that no word reproduces says a meme's measured fitness belongs to the meme, not to one model. A pass only through word-like units says P2 holds for vocabulary. A fail while the straight-line map transfers says models agree as whole spaces, not unit by unit.
bio: Does a gene's measured effect carry to its counterpart in another species?
cost: S. No forward passes beyond FI-21; one to two days of CPU.
payoff: The first test of whether a fitness estimate, not just a firing pattern, carries between models, and a list of unit pairs that agree on what wins.
risk: Units may give little lift over chance in either model, leaving nothing to carry. Or all transfer runs through word detectors, as in the study, where twin units correlated 0.82 on original text and 0.14 once names were removed.
review: Added by the reviewer, promoted from a seed: the only P2 test in this area, and nearly free after FI-21. Remaining weakness: if unit lift is small or runs through word detectors, transfer shows only that vocabulary is shared, which word weights already give for nothing.
sources: study/results/robustness/nulls.json (twin correlations); Matias et al. 2021, Upworthy Research Archive (with the 2024 correction); Gurnee et al. 2024; Huh et al. 2024

title: Do hits leave more descendants than matched flops?
question: After a film's release, do later unrelated films carry more of its distinctive units if it was a hit than if it was a matched flop, compared with films made before it?
hypothesis: Among matched pairs (same broad genre, released within two years, budgets within a factor of 1.5, box office at least three times apart), the hit's units gain more ground from the ten years before release to the ten years after than the flop's in 57% or more of pairs (chance 50%), in both models.
falsifier: A share of 52% or less, which with the roughly 390 pairs countable today puts the 95% upper bound below 57%; or an advantage that vanishes once the same before-and-after gain in rarity-weighted word overlap is regressed out. 390 pairs give about 80% power for a true share of 57%.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (CC BY-SA, version not stated): 42,306 plots; 5,665 have box office and ten or more sentences. Wikidata budgets (CC0) cover 2,133. Target films from 1960 to 2002 yield about 390 budget-matched pairs, about 1,390 if budget is ignored (rough count, 8 November 2026). Names masked with the corpus's entity tags; plots cut to 10 sentences.
method: A film's distinctive units: present in it and in none of 1,000 reference films from other genres. Ground gained: the average share of those units present in same-genre films, over the ten years after release minus the ten years before. Same-series films and remakes excluded. Statistic: hit minus flop within pairs. Null: hit and flop labels swapped within pairs.
rivals: The same before-and-after gain from rarity-weighted word overlap (TF-IDF; most dangerous, it matched neurons on heredity), sentence-embedding similarity, the model's averaged internal state, random units, and an LLM shown a later plot and both films and asked which it resembles (subsample). If words win, success-biased copying is still shown; only the neuron claim fails.
premise: P1. A pass says cultural selection can be measured across the film record: success raises a work's number of descendants, which E3 could not test. P1 gains only if units show it beyond word overlap. A well-powered null says hits are imitated in ways plot summaries do not record, or not at all.
bio: Fitness as number of offspring, measured against ancestry
cost: M. About 20,000 plots of 10 sentences (200,000 sentences, about an hour per model at the measured rate; shared with FI-24 and FI-26). One to two weeks, mostly budgets and pair building.
payoff: A culture-wide answer to whether a popular work gains offspring, from hundreds of matched comparisons in place of 15 works, plus a list of which units each hit passed on.
risk: Budget matching leaves only about 390 pairs unless more budgets are parsed from infoboxes. Imitators of a hit may be summarised in the hit's own terms, which favours words. Ten sentences may be too little plot. Word overlap may tie again.
review: Added by the reviewer: a culture-wide successor to E3. Comparing before with after cancels 'hits were more mainstream anyway' and any difference in how easily units detect a hit. Remaining weakness: only about 390 budget-matched pairs today, and imitators may be described in the hit's own words.
sources: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013); study/results/experiments.json (E3: rho 0.25 and 0.00, n = 15, power 0.27); Salganik, Dodds, Watts 2006; Martin et al. 2016

title: Readable hypotheses: named units against sparse features
question: Do named neuron units yield more headline hypotheses that replicate on held-out randomised tests than sparse-autoencoder features on embeddings or an LLM's own proposals?
note: Reuses FI-21 activations. Rivals: HypotheSAEs, negative-word lists, an LLM shown 200 example pairs. Fails if the units that replicate reduce to single words. This, not accuracy, is where neurons could plausibly win.

title: A second paired domain: Reddit resubmissions
question: When the same image is reposted under a new title, do title units predict its score beyond community, timing and embeddings, and is a unit's advantage specific to one community?
note: SNAP web-Reddit (page checked 8 November 2026): 132,308 submissions of 16,736 images, 7.9 each, July 2008 to January 2013; no licence stated. Rival: Lakkaraju et al.'s community-language model. Observational, so weaker than FI-21. The paired-tweet data (Tan et al. 2014) is unusable: the page returns 404 and held tweet IDs only.

title: A third domain: cartoon caption contests
question: Within one cartoon, do a caption's units predict the crowd's funniness rating beyond sentence embeddings, length and an LLM judge?
note: Added by the reviewer. New Yorker caption ranking data (Hugging Face yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking): 365 contests, over 2.2 million captions, over 250 million ratings; CC BY-NC 4.0, so commit IDs only. Ratings are far less noisy than Upworthy clicks. The cartoon is an image, so text carries only part of the signal. Rival to beat: sentence embedding plus linear model.

title: Reading the model against asking it
question: Do a model's internal activations forecast headline winners better than the same model's stated guess?
note: The neuroforecasting analogue (brain activity 59% against stated choice 53% on 36 projects; Genevsky et al. 2017). In LOLA embeddings scored 46% against 38% for GPT-4 asked directly, so the rival to beat is the plain embedding probe, not the verbal guess.

title: Do common memes wear out?
question: Does a unit's click effect fall as its share of headlines rises?
note: Negative frequency-dependent selection, from the FI-22 tables. Early effects must be estimated on split halves, or regression to the mean fakes the result. Rival: the same curve for stock phrases, which may show it more cleanly.

title: Lindy and the thirty-year return
question: Does a meme's age forecast its survival, and do faded memes come back after about thirty years?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: CJ-23 and CJ-25.
note: Two rules named in the paper's future-work section. Needs meme dates that do not come from the neurons (trope or keyword labels on dated films), or the test is circular. Rivals: survival curves for words; 'last decade's frequency persists'.

title: Unit pairs in randomised tests
question: Do pairs of units predict headline winners beyond the sum of the single units?
note: The randomised version of FI-26's pair term. The prior is unfavourable: in LOLA a non-linear model on larger embeddings (45.2%) did no better than a linear one (46.3%). Rival: that non-linear embedding model.

title: Directed evolution with people as the judge
question: At an equal budget of human judgments, does search over meme combinations reach higher rated appeal than a one-shot 'make this more appealing' rewrite?
note: Needs FI-25's panel and ethics rules. The evaluator is the weak link: LLM judges name headline winners 38 to 47% of the time (chance 33%), so evolving against one optimises its taste. Fails if gains vanish with a fresh panel.

title: Steer the named memes: a causal label test
question: When a labelled meme unit is pushed up while the model writes, do blind judges recover its label, even with the meme's usual words banned?
hypothesis: At one fluent dose per unit, at least 8 of the 31 named Qwen3-8B units pass: judges choose the unit's own label, from 31 plus 'none', on at least half of 20 held-out openings. With the label's words banned from the output, at most 4 still pass, mostly story patterns such as the funeral and the secret identity.
falsifier: Fewer than 4 of 31 units pass, or no more pass than at the 99th percentile when labels are shuffled among the 31 units' texts: then the labels are not causal. More than 4 passes under the ban refutes the word-emitter half. Shuffled labels should give about one pass or fewer, so 31 units are enough.
data: No new corpus. The 31 unit labels fixed in October 2026 (`study/results/labels.json`, MIT). Ban lists fixed before generation: keywords from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, each unit's 20 most-promoted output words, and character names. 30 neutral story openings written for this test (10 to set doses, 20 held out). Qwen3-8B at 4-bit and 8-bit; Llama 3.1 8B twins as a replication.
method: Steering adds a fixed amount to one unit's activation as the model continues an opening. Each unit keeps the largest of five doses that leaves text at most three times as surprising as normal to the unsteered model. Two LLM judges, checked on 200 blind human ratings, choose a label. Secondary: switch the unit off and ask for the meme.
rivals: The unit's 20 most-promoted output words handed to the same judges with no generated text (most dangerous: if it ties, units emit names, confirming labels as words, not ideas). A prompt that asks for the label (ceiling). A direction built from keyword-matched sentences. 62 random units matched on layer and firing rate, showing how often any push draws a label.
premise: P1. Passes under the keyword ban are the first causal evidence that a unit carries an idea. Passes only without the ban mean units are word emitters. A general fail means the paper's labels describe what units read, not what they do.
bio: Gene overexpression: turn one gene up, look for the trait.
cost: S. One to two days on the laptop, a few dollars of judge calls, two hours of human rating.
payoff: The causal check the paper named as missing, for every showcase meme, and a shortlist of units safe to use as edit handles.
risk: In small 4-bit models the gap between no effect and gibberish is narrow, so many units may fail for dose reasons and the result reads as untested, not refuted.
review: Replaced the invented 5% null with a shuffled-label null, fixed one dose per unit on tuning openings, and fixed ban lists in advance. Remaining weakness: the file tags only 13 of the 31 labels as tropes; 8 are characters, which can hardly pass the ban.
ranking: In the top twelve of 3 of 3 judges (what decides the premises fastest: rank 4; speed and cost: rank 2; upside: rank 1). Steering is the test the source essay treats as decisive and the project has never run; in two days it separates units that carry an idea from units that only emit their words, though a blanket fail may be a dose problem in 4-bit models and not a refutation.
update: Set doses as multiples of the unit's own strong-firing level on general text. Add the companion paper's test that needs no steering: a model writes sentences from the label alone with the usual words banned, and the unit must reach its strong range more often than on sentences written from other labels. Score steered text for any consistent effect, not only the labelled one: in the paper's one steering example, raising a unit that fires on self-questioning made the model question itself less.
sources: Kran Research 2026, Evil Qwen replication (blog.kran.ai/evil-qwen); Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean; Liu 2026, arXiv:2606.19831; Arad, Mueller, Belinkov 2025, arXiv:2505.20063; Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: More A, less B: rewriting against prompting
question: Can any internal handle (one neuron, a direction or a sparse-autoencoder feature) move an existing story toward meme A and away from meme B better than simply asking a model to rewrite it?
hypothesis: No. The prompt-only rewrite gets the highest combined score, and the best internal handle reaches under 80% of it. Among handles, the difference-of-means direction (average activation on texts with the meme minus texts without) does best and the single neuron worst.
falsifier: The handle arm that scored best on the tuning stories, alone or added to the prompt, beats prompt-only by 0.05 or more on the 0-to-1 combined score, with a 95% interval above zero, on 160 held-out stories. That gives about 85% power if per-story differences have a spread of 0.2, less if meme pairs differ a lot.
data: 208 film plots from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia summaries, CC BY-SA), skipping the pre-registration's reserved films, cut to 10 sentences, names masked. For each of 16 seeded meme pairs from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`: 13 plots containing B and not A, confirmed by an LLM reader and a human (3 tuning, 10 held out). Llama Scope sparse autoencoders (Apache 2.0).
method: Six arms on Llama 3.1 8B: prompt only; one neuron; 20 neurons; direction; sparse-autoencoder feature (a unit from a separately trained dictionary of activations); prompt plus direction. Handles use EN-23's contrast sentences. A Qwen3-8B judge and blind humans score A up, B down, story kept and fluency, combined so that failing one sinks the score. Repeated with A's keywords banned.
rivals: Prompt-only rewriting, the most dangerous: it beat every activation method on AxBench. Also keyword insertion (paste A's typical words in), a random direction of equal size, and text length. If prompting wins, neurons stay meters and editing tools should be built on prompts scored by the instrument.
premise: P1. A handle that beats prompting shows units are causal levers on meaning, strong support. If prompting wins, P1 survives only as a way to read memes, and meme engineering means prompt and measure.
bio: Gene editing against selective breeding.
cost: M. About a week on the laptop, with PyTorch for the feature arm or a small rented GPU; judge calls; four hours of human rating.
payoff: A straight answer on whether to build a meme editor on activations or on prompts, and a benchmark for narrow story motifs, which AxBench does not cover.
risk: A prompt win is the expected result after AxBench, so the news value is modest. Judges may reward stated keywords, so arms look alike. The public sparse autoencoder was trained on the base model; if it rebuilds under 90% of the 4-bit Instruct model's activation variance, that arm is dropped.
review: The 1,000 random films are the paused pre-registration's held-out set, so the data moved to the CMU corpus. Base stories must now contain B, or 'less B' is empty. One pre-chosen handle contrast replaces five. Remaining weakness: a prompt win is already expected.
sources: Wu et al. 2025, AxBench, arXiv:2501.17148; Chen et al. 2025, Persona vectors, arXiv:2507.21509; He et al. 2024, Llama Scope, arXiv:2410.20526; Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013, CMU Movie Summary Corpus

title: Do reading units write?
question: Is the unit that best detects a meme in text also the unit that best produces it when pushed?
hypothesis: Mostly not. Across 20 memes, the 10 best detector units and the 10 best writer units share under 20% of their members, and detectors steer successfully less than half as often as writers.
falsifier: Detectors steer as well as writers (success rates within 10 points on held-out prompts), or the two top-10 sets overlap by more than 50%. Twenty memes give about 85% power for a 25-point gap if memes differ with a spread of 35 points. Detectors that steer no better than random units are sensors only.
data: 20 of the 34 meme definitions in `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`. For each, 60 LLM-written sentence pairs with and without the meme, its usual words banned, checked by a second model and a 10% human sample: 30 pairs to pick units, 30 held out. The study's own 18 mapped units (`preregistration/dev_units.json`). Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B open weights.
method: Detectors: units ranked by how well activation separates the pairs. Writers: 2,000 shortlisted units, each pushed on tuning prompts and ranked by the rise in probability of meme sentences. Steer the top 10 of each on 20 held-out prompts, keywords banned; a blind judge from the other model, human-checked, scores meme and coherence. Paired permutation test across memes.
rivals: Random same-layer units; a difference-of-means direction from the same pairs; a prompt asking for the meme (ceiling); a keyword list on the detection half. Most dangerous: the direction. If it both reads and writes while single units do one or neither, the meme is a direction, not a neuron.
premise: P1. If detectors do not write, 'which neurons fire' is a sensor reading and editing needs separately found units. If they do, one unit serves both, the strongest form of P1.
bio: Sensory against motor neurons.
cost: S to M. Three to five days on the laptop; the writer screen is forward passes only, a few hours.
payoff: A rule for choosing edit handles, and a verdict on whether the study's detector units can be reused for engineering at all. It also records whether writers detect, and whether a detector fires when the model is simply asked to write its meme.
risk: Writers are picked by the kind of push they are then tested on, so part of their lead over detectors is built in; the informative numbers are the overlap and detectors against random units. In 4-bit models the dose window may be too narrow for either set.
review: Writers were picked by gradient attribution, which Liu 2026 reports mispredicts control; now a direct push screen on tuning prompts. Added the keyword ban, a human check and the study's own 18 units. Remaining weakness: writers' lead is partly built in by how they are chosen.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 7). It settles whether the units that detect a meme are the ones that write it, which decides if the study's units can ever be edit handles or are only gauges.
sources: Arad, Mueller, Belinkov 2025, arXiv:2505.20063; Kran Research 2026, Evil Qwen replication (blog.kran.ai/evil-qwen); HedwigAI 2026, Qwen personality neurons; Liu 2026, arXiv:2606.19831

title: Breeding captions on an archived fitness landscape
question: When a score-and-select loop may only move among captions that real people already rated, does scoring with model-internal units find funnier captions than scoring with embeddings or an LLM judge?
hypothesis: A tie. After 10 generations the unit-scored loop's final 20 captions sit within 3 percentile points of the embedding-scored loop's in real crowd rating, and both beat random selection by at least 5 points.
falsifier: The unit-scored loop ends more than 3 percentile points above or below the embedding-scored loop, with a 95% interval excluding zero across 100 held-out contests; a tie is claimed only if the whole interval sits within 3 points. Or no loop beats random selection by 5 points: caption text alone carries no breedable signal.
data: New Yorker caption contest rankings (Zhang et al. 2024; Hugging Face `yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking`): 365 contests, over 2.2 million captions, over 250 million crowd ratings, plus a text description of each cartoon. CC BY-NC 4.0, research use only: commit only IDs and scores. The earliest 265 contests train the scorers; the latest 100 are held out. Captions with under 25 ratings dropped.
method: Unit scorer: a linear model on Qwen3-8B units chosen on training contests. Every scorer sees the cartoon description. Gate: stop if no scorer picks a top-tenth caption over a bottom-half one 55% of the time in training. Runs start from 20 random captions; each generation offers every survivor's 5 nearest real captions by word overlap; the scorer keeps 20.
rivals: Scorers built on sentence embeddings (most dangerous: they tie fine-tuned models on headline data), TF-IDF, the mean-pooled residual stream, caption length, an LLM asked which caption is funnier, and random selection. Real ratings used as the scorer give the ceiling. A tie still leaves units able to name what selection favoured.
premise: Assumes both; tests P1 as a selection instrument. A win says internal units see appeal that embeddings miss. A tie leaves readable names as their only edge. A loss says breed with embeddings and use units only to describe the result.
bio: Directed evolution on a mapped fitness landscape (deep mutational scanning).
cost: M. About 10 hours of forward passes for every caption, or 3 on a sample; the LLM-judge arm is the slow part. One week.
payoff: The first test of meme breeding in which every candidate has a real human outcome, with no live audience and no persuasion.
risk: Text carries little of the joke. In Zhang et al. 2024, GPT-4 given a cartoon description picked a top-10 caption over one ranked near 1,000 only 65 to 67% of the time. All loops may hover near random and the gate may stop the study.
review: Added a go/no-go gate, the cartoon descriptions as input, a minimum rating count (the contest's bandit gives weak captions few ratings) and a proper rule for claiming a tie. Remaining weakness: nothing is generated, so this tests selection only, where text signal is weak.
sources: Zhang et al. 2024, Humor in AI, arXiv:2406.10522 (caption contest data); Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng 2025, LOLA, arXiv:2406.02611; Bradley et al. 2023, QDAIF, arXiv:2310.13032; Novikov et al. 2025, AlphaEvolve, arXiv:2506.13131

title: What click-optimised breeding drifts toward
question: When a breeding loop selects headlines on a click predictor trained on real randomised tests, does it drift toward negativity and unsupported claims, and which brake holds it: a word list, named internal units or an LLM reviewer?
hypothesis: Against a random-selection loop, five generations of click selection raise negative words per headline by at least 50% and unsupported claims by at least 10 points. The word-list brake is evaded by rewording. The LLM reviewer holds judged negativity within 10% of the start while keeping 70% of the predicted click gain; the unit brake does no better.
falsifier: No drift beyond random selection (negative words up under 10%, unsupported claims up under 3 points); or the word list holds judged negativity as well as the reviewer; or the unit brake beats the reviewer (a safety use for units). 500 paired tests give about 90% power for a 3-point difference if per-test differences have a spread of 20 points.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 randomised headline tests, CC BY 4.0, OSF node jd64p. Drop the 22% of tests flagged for faulty randomisation and arms differing in image. Predictor and unit brake (10 named negativity and exaggeration units) fitted on the exploratory and confirmatory sets; 500 hold-out tests seed the loops. 300 headlines get blind human ratings.
method: Each loop starts from a test's losing headline. A local LLM, told only to rewrite, offers 8 variants per generation; the predictor selects. Unseen by the loop, drift is read by a negative-word count, a human-checked judge from another model family, and whether the test's own headlines and excerpt support each new claim. Arms: unbraked; three brakes; random selection.
rivals: Brakes: a negative-word list; an LLM reviewer asked whether a variant is more negative or less supported than the original (most dangerous, probably the best brake); a limit on embedding distance. Predictors: embeddings plus a linear model against unit profiles. The real gap between archived winners and losers is the yardstick for how much drift readers reward.
premise: Assumes both; tests a use. Because the optimiser rewords its way around word lists, this setting is built for units to beat words. If they still lose to the reviewer, P1 has no safety use here.
bio: Serial passage: selecting a pathogen for spread also selects for virulence.
cost: M. About 100,000 generated headlines and their forward passes, three days on the laptop, plus judge calls and two hours of human rating.
payoff: Measured limits for the programme's ethics rules: which brakes any optimiser must carry, and whether the instrument can enforce them. Nothing generated is shown to an audience.
risk: The click predictor is weak (about 46% at picking the winner among roughly three headlines), so drift may reflect its quirks, not what readers reward. El and Zou 2025 already showed this kind of drift with simulated audiences, so the new part is the comparison of brakes.
review: Drift is now measured against a random-selection loop, because LLM rewriting drifts unaided; the judge differs from the reviewer and is checked by humans; the hypothesis no longer contradicts its falsifier. Remaining weakness: selection is on predicted, not real, clicks.
sources: Matias et al. 2021, Upworthy Research Archive, doi:10.1038/s41597-021-00934-7; Robertson et al. 2023, Negativity drives online news consumption; Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng 2025, LOLA, arXiv:2406.02611; El and Zou 2025, Moloch's Bargain, arXiv:2510.06105

title: Knock one motif out of the weights
question: Can a small edit to a model's weights stop it writing one story motif, including in paraphrase, with less side damage than a system prompt or a word ban?
hypothesis: Removing one direction from under 0.1% of the weights halves the motif's rate in free story writing, but a system prompt forbidding the motif leaves the rate at least 10 points lower still, with no more loss of story quality, averaged over 12 motifs. Switching off the motif's 10 best detector units changes nothing.
falsifier: Averaged over motifs, the weight edit leaves the motif rate at least 10 points below the prompt's at equal or smaller quality loss, with a 95% interval above zero. Or the edit fails outright: a fall of under 20%, no better than random directions. Twelve motifs give about 75% power if motifs differ with a spread of 12 points.
data: Apache 2.0 weights: Qwen3.5-0.8B (the model edited in the MIT post), Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B (the study's models). 12 motifs from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, kept only if the unedited model writes them on at least 40% of tuning prompts. Per motif, 300 LLM-written story prompts that invite it without naming it (100 to find the direction, 200 held out) and 100 unrelated prompts.
method: Direction: mean activation difference between stories with and without the motif, subtracted from the output weights of two layers, as in the MIT post. On 4-bit Qwen3-8B it is applied at run time. A second arm zeroes the motif's 10 best detector units. A blind, human-checked judge from another model family scores the motif as an idea, not a word.
rivals: A system prompt forbidding the motif (most dangerous: prompts and filters matched fine-tuning for forgetting concepts in Thaker et al. 2024). A ban on the motif's keywords, which should leave paraphrases. A fine-tune on motif-free stories. 20 random directions. If the prompt wins, weight edits are a curiosity, but the paraphrase result still shows whether an idea has a location.
premise: P1 in its direction form. A clean knockout shows a motif has a compact causal home in the weights. A fail means motifs are spread out or rebuilt elsewhere, so 'the meme is a unit' holds for reading at most.
bio: Gene knockout.
cost: M. One to two weeks on the laptop, plus judge calls. An agent-found edit, as in the MIT post, would be L.
payoff: Meme-free and meme-dosed model variants to use as control writers for planted-story tests, and a first check of weight-space editing on meaning.
risk: Sub-2B models write weak stories and may ignore a 'do not' instruction, so the prompt could lose for a reason that vanishes at 8B; the 8B run decides. The MIT authors found edits remove obstacles and cannot add abilities.
review: The '6 of 10 motifs' rule could not tell a win from a coin flip; replaced by a mean difference across 12 motifs. Added an 8B run, a base-rate gate and a detector-unit knockout arm. Remaining weakness: the prompt is expected to win, as in work on making models forget.
sources: Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab 2026, Sparks of weight-space programming; Arditi et al. 2024, arXiv:2406.11717; Thaker et al. 2024, Guardrail baselines for unlearning, arXiv:2403.03329; Hase et al. 2023, arXiv:2301.04213

title: Is the unit needed to read the meme?
question: When a meme's detector units are switched off, does the model get worse at saying whether a passage contains that meme, and only that meme?
hypothesis: No. Switching off a meme's 10 best detector units lowers the model's yes-or-no accuracy on that meme by under 3 points, the same as matched random units. Removing the meme's difference-of-means direction (average activation with the meme minus without) lowers it by at least 10 points, and other memes' accuracy by under 3.
falsifier: Switching off the 10 units lowers accuracy on their own meme by 5 points or more beyond both matched random units and other memes' questions, with a 95% interval above zero. Twenty memes detect a 5-point drop with about 75% power if memes differ with a spread of 8 points.
data: EN-23's material: 20 memes from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, each with 60 LLM-written passage pairs with and without the meme, its usual words banned, checked by a second model and a 10% human sample; 30 pairs pick units, 30 are held out. The study's own 18 mapped units (`preregistration/dev_units.json`). Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B open weights.
method: The model reads a held-out passage and answers 'does this contain [definition]?' while the units are held at their average value on neutral text. Outcome: the fall in accuracy, and in confidence in the right answer, against the unharmed model. Own meme against other memes, paired permutation test across memes. Null: random units matched on layer and firing rate.
rivals: Removing the meme's difference-of-means direction (most dangerous: if it blinds the model while units do not, the meme is a direction). Switching off units that detect the meme's keywords. Matched random units. As a ceiling, deleting the meme's sentence from the passage. A null still tells us detector units are gauges beside the computation, not parts of it.
premise: P1. If the model reads the meme just as well without its detector units, they are correlates, and 'the meme is which neurons fire' holds as a measurement only. A specific loss would be the first evidence that the units are part of how the model understands the idea.
bio: Lesion study: remove one brain area, test one skill.
cost: S. One day on the laptop once EN-23's passages exist: forward passes only, no text generation, no paid judges.
payoff: The causal check from the reading side: whether the instrument's units are used by the model or merely move with the meme. It decides whether later work should track units or directions.
risk: Redundancy. Models often have several routes to an answer, so a null may mean back-up routes, not irrelevant units. The 2026 census found that silencing a neuron moves a model about a thousand times less than pushing it. The question may also be too easy or too hard for a 4-bit 8B model.
review: Added by the reviewer: the area steered units but never tested whether detector units are needed for reading. Remaining weakness: a null is ambiguous because of redundancy, and the areas on neurons as units or measurement validity may register a similar lesion test.
update: Add arms of 100 and 500 units ranked by their effect on the answer, since the companion paper traces half of the push toward one name to 155 neurons. Silence units only where they are in their own strong range, and report the paper's damage measure (the change in next-word predictions over the firing token and the next 16) beside accuracy.
sources: Öztürk 2026, LLM Electrodes, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11577020/v1; Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean; Arditi et al. 2024, arXiv:2406.11717; Arad, Mueller, Belinkov 2025, arXiv:2505.20063; Tigges et al. 2026, Neurons as an Interpretable Basis

title: Calibrate the judges first
question: Do the LLM judges used across these designs agree with blind human raters on whether a narrow motif is present when its usual words are banned?
note: Added by the reviewer; a shared prerequisite for every LLM-judged design here. About 600 short passages, from EN-23's material and from steered output, rated by two people and by each judge model. Rivals: a keyword check and an embedding probe. If judges agree with people much less than people agree with each other, enlarge the human samples.

title: Dose-window census of meme units
question: What share of the study's meme units have any dose that changes the text and keeps it fluent, compared with non-meme units matched on how word-like they are?
note: 500 meme and 500 matched units in Qwen3-8B. A 2026 census of Qwen3.5-4B (Öztürk, Research Square rs-11577020) confirmed 130 consistent neurons and reported that at least 6% of random pushes give a nameable, coherent change. Rivals: word-matched units and random directions. About one GPU-day.

title: Does 4-bit quantisation change steering?
question: Do dose windows and steering success differ between 4-bit, 8-bit and full-precision copies of the same model?
note: HedwigAI saw one neuron break the model at full precision but not at 8-bit; the study used 4-bit throughout. Cheap: rerun EN-21's best 10 units at three precisions (8-bit MLX builds of both study models exist). Decides whether laptop results transfer.

title: Write in Qwen, read in Llama
question: Does a meme written into text by steering Qwen with its keywords banned get picked up by Llama's twin unit better than by word-matched units, word overlap or an LLM reader?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: UN-27.
note: Tests P2 through an intervention, not a correlation. Expect a null: the study's twin pairs fall to r = 0.14 on name-free text (`study/README.md`). Also a second way to make planted-meme stories for the paused pre-registration, with ground truth set by the push. About three days; depends on EN-21 finding handles that survive the ban.

title: Carry an edit across models
question: Does a meme direction found in Llama still write the meme after a learned map carries it into Qwen?
note: Oozeer et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.04429) report this for refusal and backdoor-removal steering vectors. Rivals: finding the direction afresh in Qwen, a map fitted on word-matched units, and plain prompting. No verified result yet for narrow story motifs.

title: A dial, not a switch
question: Can a handle set how much of a meme a text carries in graded steps more reliably than prompt wording such as 'slightly more' or 'much more'?
note: Graded control is the one place steering might beat prompting. Outcome: blind judges rank five dose levels; score rank agreement. Rivals: prompt adverbs, and the number of meme sentences requested. Could run on EN-22's stories at little extra cost.

title: Do meme handles add up?
question: When two memes are pushed at once, do both appear in the text, or does one swamp the other?
note: A test of whether meme complexes can be assembled from parts. Rival: a prompt asking for both memes, and keyword insertion. Judge each meme separately and blind. Depends on EN-21 finding at least a few working handles.

title: Does breeding from the loser head toward the winner?
question: When a loop rewrites an Upworthy test's losing headline for several generations, do its outputs come to resemble the real winning headline more than the other real losers?
note: Added by the reviewer: an archived-outcome check on a loop that writes new text, which EN-24 cannot give. Arms differ only in the scorer (units, embeddings, LLM, random); blind judges say which real headline each output is closer to. Weak proxy: arms of one test share most words. Another archived mutation set: Humicroedit (Hossain et al. 2019, arXiv:1906.00274), 15,095 headline edits, mostly one word, rated for funniness.

title: Agent-found motif edit
question: Can an agent given a Python sandbox over a small model's weights find a cleaner motif knockout than the human recipe in EN-26?
note: Cost L: frontier-model agent time, as in the MIT weight-space post. Rivals: EN-26's direction removal, a system prompt, a keyword ban. Run only if EN-26 shows a knockout is possible at all.

title: Add one meme, ask real readers
question: When one meme is added to or removed from matched fiction premises, does reader preference move, and did any method forecast the direction?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: FI-25.
note: Cost L. Needs an ethics note before registration: consented paid panel, fiction only, AI authorship disclosed, no targeting on personal traits, no raw-click outcome. Rivals: LLM-simulated readers, embeddings, human forecasters.

title: Most advanced yet acceptable: the headline novelty optimum
question: Within a randomised headline test, does the arm that is moderately new relative to recently published headlines win more clicks than very familiar or very new arms?
hypothesis: Click rate is an inverted U in novelty (an arm's distance from the site's previous 90 days of headlines). On confirmatory tests both slopes of a two-lines test are significant at 0.05, the peak falls between the 30th and 80th novelty percentiles, and the peak beats both extremes by at least 3% relative.
falsifier: On confirmatory tests no novelty measure shows a sign change at 0.05 (flat or monotonic), or the U is as strong against headlines from six months away (then it is house style, not familiarity). For neurons: adding neuron novelty to embedding and TF-IDF novelty gives no held-out likelihood gain (95% interval includes zero), overall and in the low-word-overlap subset.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015, CC BY 4.0, OSF jd64p. Fit on the exploratory split (4,873); score once on the confirmatory split (22,743). Drop tests flagged for the 2013 randomisation fault and arms differing in image: about 10,000 confirmatory tests should remain. Robertson et al. detected a 2.3% effect in 12,448.
method: Units: Qwen3-8B neuron families (neurons that fire together), chosen on exploratory data. Novelty: mean distance from an arm's unit profile to the prior 90 days' headlines. Arms compared within their own test, length controlled; two-lines test (one slope below a break point, one above). Null: novelty against a window six months away. Pre-set subset: arms sharing few stream words.
rivals: Novelty from TF-IDF backward similarity, sentence embeddings, the mean-pooled hidden state, sparse-autoencoder features on embeddings (a learned feature dictionary; Movva et al. 2025), an LLM rating 'how unusual for this site' against 20 recent headlines, headline length, random units. Embedding novelty is most dangerous: smooth and cheap. If it wins, the hunch is still tested causally; neurons add nothing.
premise: P1. A U found equally with words or embeddings settles the marketing claim and leaves P1 unmoved. A U that survives in the low-word-overlap subset for neuron novelty alone would show units track a familiar frame under new wording. Repeating it in Llama bears on P2.
bio: Optimal outbreeding: mates preferred slightly unlike kin.
cost: S. About 150,000 short headlines: under an hour of forward passes per model on the laptop. The LLM-rating rival runs on a 3,000-test subsample. No live audience; archived data only.
payoff: A causal answer to whether 'just past the familiar' wins, with the size of the effect and where the peak sits. If any measure works, a novelty ruler for planning creative tests.
risk: Arms of one test share a story, so their novelty may differ too little to trace a curve; the U then leans on comparing stories, which were not randomised. Upworthy effects are tiny, and Berger and Packard found a monotonic pattern for lyrics.
review: Replaced the within-month date shuffle, which barely moves a 90-day window, with a misplaced-window null; added headline length, the fault flag, the image rule and an estimated usable sample. Remaining weakness: novelty may vary little within a test. Prior-work check was arXiv only (nothing found); web search was unavailable.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (speed and cost: rank 9). It rides on FI-21's pass and gives a causal answer on whether moderately new headlines win, which stands whichever measure does best.
sources: Hekkert, Snelders and van Wieringen 2003; Matias et al. 2021 (Upworthy Research Archive); Simonsohn 2018 (two-lines test); Sreenivasan 2013

title: Copied or coincidence: remakes against twin films
question: Do incidental 'hitchhiker' details shared by two similar films separate documented descent (remakes) from independent arrival at the same premise (twin films)?
hypothesis: With remake and twin pairs matched on overall likeness (sentence-embedding similarity), genre and length, a hitchhiker-sharing score separates them at AUC 0.70 or more (0.5 is chance) under two-fold cross-fitting (threshold set on one half of the pairs, scored on the other, then swapped), and neuron hitchhikers beat rare-word hitchhikers by at least 0.10 AUC.
falsifier: AUC below 0.60 for every hitchhiker definition: similarity cannot show descent in plot summaries. For neurons: AUC not above rare shared words (bootstrap interval of the difference includes zero). About 90 twin against 270 remake pairs gives a standard error near 0.035: enough to tell 0.70 from chance, and to see a neuron advantage only if it is about 0.10.
data: Wikipedia 'Twin films' list: 149 pairs (2026-11-08; CC BY-SA); about 110 after screening out shared sources and real events, perhaps 90 with usable plots. Remakes from Wikidata film-to-film 'based on' links (932 with both on English Wikipedia; CC0). Where available, the later film's plot comes from another-language Wikipedia, machine-translated (Tell Me Again, CC BY-SA 4.0). Names masked; dates withheld.
method: Hitchhiker: a unit shared by the pair but rare in the genre's other films (rarity set on films outside all pairs). Score: share of the earlier film's rare units found in the later one, discounting units common to many films (the study's heredity statistic). Each twin pair gets up to three likeness-matched remake pairs. Null: mismatched same-genre, same-decade pairs.
rivals: Rare shared words and named details, TF-IDF cosine, mean-pooled hidden state, random units, and an LLM asked 'remake or coincidence?', scored only where it cannot name either film, as it may remember them. Sentence-embedding similarity is neutralised by the matching. Rare shared words are most dangerous: remakes keep odd details as words. If they win, descent is readable without neurons.
premise: P1. A meme must be copied, not merely present. A pass shows units carry lineage information that similarity lacks. If rare words do as well, P1 gains nothing. If every method fails, Wikipedia plots cannot support the study's influence claims at all.
bio: Homology against convergent evolution; neutral markers such as shared pseudogenes.
cost: S to M. About 900 plots, minutes of forward passes. Cleaning the twin list, matching pairs and fetching translated plots is the work: three to four days.
payoff: A way to say 'this was copied' instead of 'this is similar', the gap in every influence claim so far. Also a reusable labelled set of descent and convergence pairs.
risk: Twin films are often not independent: studios race from leaked scripts, so some 'coincidences' are copies. Remakes resemble their originals far more than twins resemble each other, so matching on likeness may leave too few pairs.
review: Counted the list: 149 rows, about 110 after a keyword screen for shared sources, not 150. Added cross-language plots against copied wording, a named matching measure and a memory guard for the LLM judge. Remaining weakness: about 90 twin pairs can resolve only a 0.10 neuron-over-word gap.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 8). Remakes against twin films is the one design that tries to tell 'copied' from 'merely similar', the gap in every influence claim, and it is a few days of work on real films.
sources: Claidière, Scott-Phillips and Sperber 2014; Wikipedia: Twin films (list); Wikidata (based on, P144); Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again)

title: Lindy effect: does a meme's age forecast survival?
question: Among story memes alive in films at a cut-off year, does age predict how well each holds its share over the next 20 years, beyond current frequency and random copying?
hypothesis: Each doubling of a meme's age at the 1992 cut-off raises its 1993 to 2012 retention (later share of films divided by its 1973 to 1992 share) by at least 5%, controlling that earlier share and its trend, and the effect exceeds 95% of 1,000 random-copying simulations.
