falsifier: The age effect's 95% interval lies below 2% per doubling, or inside the random-copying range, for every unit type: Lindy is frequency in disguise. For neurons: the neuron age effect is no larger than the effect for TF-IDF terms or trope tags (difference interval includes zero). About 300 unit clusters give power 0.94 for a partial correlation of 0.2.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus: 42,306 Wikipedia film plots, 39,589 with a release year (counted 2026-11-08), CC BY-SA; 7,951 fall in 1973 to 1992 and 19,791 in 1993 to 2012. About 1,300 predate 1930, so ages are capped near 60 years. Series links from Wikidata (CC0). Trope tags from Gala et al. 2020 (licence unconfirmed; commit IDs only). Names masked.
method: Units: neuron families chosen on a random third of films from all years, scored on the rest. Age: years since a unit first passed 0.5% of films, capped for units already common in the 1930s. Regression across unit clusters, with bootstrap intervals. Null: random copying (each film draws memes from earlier films by frequency), with real yearly counts.
rivals: The same analysis with TF-IDF terms, TV Tropes tags, sentence-embedding clusters, LLM-listed traits and random non-meme units; current frequency alone. Frequency alone is most dangerous: under random copying old memes are simply the common ones. Trope tags may show Lindy with no model, which still settles the conjecture.
premise: Assumes both. Lindy found equally in words and tropes is a fact about culture that needs no neurons. A stronger age effect for neuron units than for words, in both Qwen and Llama, would support P1 (ideas outlive their wording) and P2.
bio: Taxon age against extinction risk; Van Valen's constant-extinction law is the null.
cost: S to M. About 6 hours of forward passes per model at the rate in preregistration/sources/neuron_timing_qwen3-8b.json (optimistic); store presence bits only. Simulations take minutes.
payoff: The first measured test of 'old ideas are the safe ones' against the right null. If it holds, age is a free forecasting feature; if not, Lindy is survivorship bias.
risk: Wikipedia remembers the old films that still matter, so a meme that lived only in forgotten early films is dated too young and looks short-lived: survivorship can fake Lindy. Summaries were all written after 2001 in modern words, so wording drift, the neurons' best case, is absent.
review: Units were chosen on pre-1973 films, which excluded every young meme; now chosen on a random third. Thin pre-1930 coverage caps ages, now stated. Swapped an unreachable trope table for Gala et al. Remaining weakness: Wikipedia's memory of old films can fake the effect.
sources: Eliazar 2017 (Lindy's law); Bentley, Hahn and Shennan 2004; CMU Movie Summary Corpus; Gala et al. 2020 (TV Tropes dataset)

title: Memeplexes: are memes gained and lost together?
question: Along documented adaptation links, are memes of the same bundle kept or dropped together more often than their everyday co-occurrence and the link's overall fidelity predict?
hypothesis: For unit pairs in one bundle (bundles defined on unrelated films), the odds of being kept or dropped together across about 2,000 source-to-adaptation links are at least 1.5 times the odds across matched unlinked film pairs, and the excess holds in at least 10 unrelated source lineages.
falsifier: The ratio's 95% interval lies below 1.2: bundles travel together no more than their everyday co-occurrence predicts. For neurons: neuron bundles show no higher co-change odds than word-topic bundles or TV Tropes co-occurrence bundles (difference interval includes zero). Power depends on how many bundle pairs each of the 2,000 links carries; count that on development films first.
data: Wikidata 'based on' and 'derivative work' links (99,206 and 40,376 statements, CC0; 15,706 'based on' links start from a film) where both works have a Wikipedia plot (CC BY-SA): sample 2,000 links from at least 500 sources, plus 2,000 matched unlinked pairs. Bundles learned on CMU Movie Summary Corpus films outside those lineages. Names masked.
method: Units: neuron families, no two tracking one word. Bundle: units that co-occur in development films, each appearing without the others in at least 20% of cases, and peaking in different sentences (so not one scene). Statistic: joint loss and joint gain along links against unlinked pairs matched on genre, decade and likeness. Second null: shuffle keeping row and column totals.
rivals: Bundles from a topic model on the same masked text, from TV Tropes tag co-occurrence, from LLM-listed traits, and from random frequency-matched unit sets; summary length. The topic model is most dangerous: a scene's vocabulary travels together. Then bundles are real but are scenes, and neurons add nothing.
premise: P1. Memeplex is a core term of memetics that has never been measured. Co-change beyond everyday co-occurrence, repeated across lineages, gives the unit a heredity property a concept detector lacks. If word topics do as well, bundling belongs to text, not neurons.
bio: Linkage disequilibrium and supergenes; Pagel's test for correlated trait change.
cost: M. About 8,000 plots plus development films: a few hours of forward passes. Name masking, matching unlinked pairs and cleaning the links take most of a week.
payoff: The first measured memeplexes: a list of bundles that travel as wholes and the lineages they travelled in. Tells an adapter which elements can be dropped alone and which come as a set.
risk: Co-change may still reflect settings: drop the courtroom and every courtroom unit goes. Wikipedia summaries of adaptations are sometimes written from the source's summary, inflating retention; a plot from another-language Wikipedia for one end (Tell Me Again) is the check.
review: Units that co-occur will also seem to change together between any two films, so the shuffle null was too easy. Added matched unlinked pairs as the comparison and a different-sentence rule against one-scene bundles. Remaining weakness: adaptation summaries may be written from the source's summary.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as PO-24, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Blackmore 1999 (The Meme Machine); Pagel 1994; da Silva and Tehrani 2016; Wikidata (based on P144, derivative work P4969)

title: Thirty-year return: do faded memes come back?
question: After a story meme peaks in films and fades, does its share rebound about 30 years later more than at other lags, and is the rebound carried by directors who were young at the peak?
hypothesis: For memes whose share peaked between 1930 and 1965 and then halved, share 25 to 35 years after the peak is at least 10% higher than the mean of the flanking lags (10 to 20 and 40 to 45 years), in at least three peak decades, and beats 95% of simulations where films copy earlier films' memes by frequency alone.
falsifier: The rebound's 95% interval lies below 3%, or inside the simulated range, for every unit type: no 30-year return in film plots. For neurons: the neuron rebound does not exceed the rebound for TF-IDF terms or trope tags (difference interval includes zero). About 200 unit clusters should put a 10% rebound at three standard errors or more (rough estimate).
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus: 39,589 dated Wikipedia film plots, CC BY-SA; 8,373 fall in 1930 to 1965, about 230 a year, so shares use five-year bins. Director birth dates from Wikidata (CC0): 19,200 of a non-random 20,000-film sample had one (2026-11-08). Remake lags from Wikidata 'based on' links (1,499 film-to-film) as a text-free check.
method: Units chosen on a random third of films; series built on the rest. Fade: a five-year peak at least 1.5 times the unit's median share, then 10 years below it. Return curve: mean share at each lag. Null: random copying with real yearly counts. Secondary: is the rebound larger in films by directors aged 5 to 25 at the peak?
rivals: The same return curve from TF-IDF terms, trope tags and genre labels; the histogram of remake lags, which needs no text, against a null that respects how many films existed each year; random units. TF-IDF is most dangerous: revivals reuse period words. If remake lags alone show the 30-year peak, no unit is needed.
premise: Assumes both. Mostly a test of the conjecture. P1 gains only if neuron units show a rebound among name-masked plots where word units show none; P2 only if Qwen and Llama give the same return curve. A known rival view: retellings prefer young sources (Karsdorp and van den Bosch 2016).
bio: Seed banks releasing dormant variants; sensitive-period imprinting.
cost: S to M. Reuses the corpus pass (about 6 hours per model). Series and simulations take minutes; the Wikidata join for the secondary takes a day.
payoff: A number for when a faded meme comes back, which Mike wanted for timing a revival, or evidence that the 30-year cycle is folklore. If the secondary holds, a forecast rule: watch what peaked when today's 45-year-old creators were 15.
risk: One shared cause can fake a cycle: war memes peak in the 1940s and return with 1970s war films. Hence the three-decades rule, but only about four peak decades exist. Wikipedia's coverage of old films favours those later revived or remade.
review: The draft tested a mechanism (directors' youth) before showing any return exists, and period settings confounded it. Rewrote as a direct return-lag test with the director test as a secondary; the mechanism is kept as a seed. Remaining weakness: few independent peak decades, and Wikipedia favours revived films.
sources: Holbrook and Schindler 1989; Candia et al. 2018 (Nature Human Behaviour); Karsdorp and van den Bosch 2016; CMU Movie Summary Corpus

title: Remix ledger: new memes or new combinations?
question: Over a century of films, does novelty arrive as new units or as first-time pairings of old units, once the measurement is checked on remixes with known recipes?
hypothesis: Check: on 300 synthetic remixes the ledger ranks the true sources above matched decoys and its inherited shares correlate at least 0.6 with the planted shares. Then, in films after 1980, the share of units that were rare before exceeds the date-shuffled baseline by under 2 percentage points, while the new-pair share exceeds it by at least 5.
falsifier: Check correlation below 0.4 for neurons, or not above the best rival by 0.1: the ledger cannot be trusted (300 remixes separate 0.6 from 0.4 by over four standard errors). Conjecture: a post-1980 excess of rare-before units of 5 points or more means real novelty beyond recombination.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (39,589 dated plots, 25,208 after 1980, CC BY-SA), names masked. 300 synthetic remixes written by a small open model from two to four known source plots in set proportions, reworded by a second model; released CC BY-SA. Paired summaries of one story (Tell Me Again: 96,831 summaries, 29,505 stories, CC BY-SA 4.0) set the noise floor.
method: Units chosen on a random third of films from all years. For each other film, in release order: the share of its units that were rare before (in under 0.5% of earlier films) and the share of its unit pairs never seen together. Baseline: the same ledger with release dates shuffled within genre, which removes a fixed list's saturation.
rivals: The same ledger with word n-grams, TV Tropes or keyword pairs (Sreenivasan's method), embedding nearest-neighbour distance, and an LLM asked to list each film's sources. Keyword pairs are most dangerous: human-named and model-free. The check on synthetic remixes says which ledger to believe, so a rival's win still answers the conjecture.
premise: P1. A model's units are a closed list, so the ledger registers only novelty the model has a unit for; training after every film in the corpus helps here. Failing the check exposes that limit. Passing it ahead of keyword pairs would support P1 as a way to measure originality.
bio: Recombination against new mutation; exon shuffling against de novo genes.
cost: M. About 6 hours of forward passes per model for the corpus, a day of local generation for the remixes, a week in all.
payoff: 'Everything is a remix' turned into three measured shares per work (inherited, new, newly combined) with a known error. An originality score that can be audited.
risk: 'New' units may be new things in the world (phones, wars) more than new story ideas, and words catch those equally. Wikipedia covers few early films, so early works look more original than they were. LLM-written remixes may be easier to unpick than human ones.
review: Units chosen on pre-1950 films could never be new, and a fixed list is all seen within a few hundred films, so the hypothesis passed by construction. Units now come from all years and 'new' means rare before. Remix licence corrected to share-alike. Remaining weakness: the closed unit list.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as RX-21, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Ferguson, Everything is a Remix (video series); Youn et al. 2015; Uzzi et al. 2013; Sreenivasan 2013

title: Do acclaimed creators borrow from more sources?
question: Do directors whose films draw on a wider spread of earlier works earn more critical recognition, and within one director's career are the recognised films the broader ones?
hypothesis: Within a director's films, one standard deviation more source breadth (the effective number of distinct genre-and-decade groups among a film's 20 closest earlier sources) raises the odds of an award nomination by at least 10%, with summary length and release year controlled. Between directors, mean breadth predicts nominations in the same direction.
falsifier: The within-director effect's 95% interval lies below 3% per standard deviation, or is negative, for every unit type: the hunch fails. For neurons: neuron breadth adds no held-out likelihood over breadth from trope tags and embeddings (interval includes zero). If the declared-source gate fails, the test is not run.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia plots, CC BY-SA), summaries cut to one length band. Directors, nominations and awards from Wikidata (P57, P1411, P166; CC0): 6,950 films with a Freebase ID carry a nomination (counted 2026-11-08). Expect about 3,000 directors with four or more films, where a 10% effect is roughly three standard errors (an estimate); count before registering.
method: Sources: earlier films ranked by inheritance of a film's rare units (the study's heredity statistic), own films excluded. Gate: where Wikidata declares a source (P144, P941), the ranking must put it in the top 20 at least 20% of the time (chance: about 0.1%). Breadth: effective number of groups in the top 20. Null: breadth shuffled among each director's films.
rivals: Breadth from TF-IDF neighbours, sentence-embedding neighbours, the mean-pooled hidden state, TV Tropes tags, the count of declared Wikidata sources, an LLM asked how many sources a plot draws on, the film's own genre count and summary length. Genre count is most dangerous: breadth may only mean 'a film that mixes genres'.
premise: Assumes both. Resemblance is not influence, so this tests a correlate of the hunch. P1 gains only if neuron breadth predicts acclaim after tag and embedding breadth are in the model and the declared-source gate passes.
bio: Hybrid vigour; gene flow from many source populations.
cost: M. Reuses the corpus pass (about 6 hours per model); a week for the Wikidata join and the declared-source gate.
payoff: Evidence for or against advice given to every creative team: read widely, borrow widely. A per-creator breadth profile that can be checked against declared influences.
risk: Awards track fame, budget and prestige genres, and Wikidata records them unevenly. Famous films have longer, richer summaries, which can fake breadth even after trimming. A 10% effect sits near the detection limit.
review: Sources came from the method itself, and famous films have longer summaries, which fakes breadth. Added a numeric declared-source gate, equal-length summaries and a within-director comparison that holds fame fixed. Remaining weakness: resemblance is not borrowing, and Wikidata awards are patchy and fame-driven.
sources: Uzzi et al. 2013; Barron et al. 2018; Wikipedia: List of Bob Dylan songs based on earlier tunes; Wikidata (nominated for P1411, award received P166)

title: Obscure sources win acclaim, familiar sources win revenue
question: Do films whose closest earlier sources are little known earn critical recognition, while films with well-known sources earn box office?
note: From the originality grid in Mike's earlier notes (obscure or familiar source, conscious or not). CMU plots (7,531 with box office), Wikidata awards; source fame from Wikipedia pageviews, which measure fame today, not at release. Rival: embedding nearest ancestors. Shares CJ27's pipeline and its declared-source gate.

title: Does a bundle protect its members in retelling?
question: In LLM retelling chains, do the remaining parts of a meme bundle decay faster when one part has been removed from the seed story?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: ME-26.
note: The causal half of the memeplex claim ('none would be remembered alone'). Truth by construction, after Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023. Rivals: keyword and LLM-judge detection of the parts. Laptop, small open models; follows CJ24. LLM retellers are not human audiences.

title: Fidelity, fecundity, longevity in folktales
question: Do tale types whose tellings vary least in meme profile occur in more populations and reconstruct as older?
note: Dawkins's three replicator traits. ATU-labelled Folktexts (Zenodo 6575263) against the da Silva and Tehrani 2016 matrix of 275 types by 50 populations. Rival: lexical variance across tellings. The overlap may be under 100 types, so power is the worry.

title: Meme fatigue in headline frames
question: Does the click lift of a winning headline frame shrink with how often that frame ran in the previous 4 to 6 weeks?
note: The ad-fatigue rule of thumb, on Upworthy's dated randomised tests; frames chosen on the exploratory split. Rival: regular expressions and n-gram counts, which should win on literal templates. Biology: negative frequency-dependent selection. Complements CJ21.

title: Concept beats variant
question: Does the distance between two headline arms predict the size of their click gap, so that bigger creative changes give bigger differences?
note: From the concept, theme, variant testing framework the notes credit to Seufert. Upworthy arm pairs; model true-effect variance against distance, net of sampling noise. Rivals: edit distance, TF-IDF, embeddings. Upworthy fixes the story, so only variant-level distance is testable.

title: Do rivals converge?
question: Does the distance between competing firms' descriptions of themselves shrink year on year, as 'memetic convergence' claims?
overlaps: A registered design or another seed asks nearly the same question: US-S8.
note: Candidate dated public text: annual-report business sections on SEC EDGAR (not checked this session). Rivals: TF-IDF cosine and Mike's tag-count distance, likely winners because firms repeat words. Register as an expected loss that marks the method's boundary.

title: Mike's three declared families, words forced apart
question: Are the 15 works in the three story families named in Mike's 2022 talk deck recoverable against matched decoys when shared vocabulary is banned?
note: An author-declared test set that pre-dates the study. Paraphrase under a banned-word list built from TF-IDF top terms. Rivals: embeddings and an LLM asked which works belong together. Fifteen works is small; treat as a pilot.

title: Lindy across space
question: Does a work's success in a second language market forecast spread to many more, beyond its first-market success?
note: From the notes' claim that Lindy 'works across space as well as time'. Needs dated translation records; Wikidata language-edition and translation data are a candidate, not checked. Rival: metadata alone (editions so far). Neurons matter only for which memes travel.

title: Do creators replay their youth?
question: Among films of the same year and genre, does a film resemble the films released when its director was aged 5 to 25 more than other past films?
note: The mechanism moved out of CJ25; run only if CJ25 finds a return. CMU plots; Wikidata birth dates (19,200 of 20,000 films in a non-random sample had one). Exclude the roughly 2,100 plots tagged period, costume or historical, whose setting words fake the effect. Rival: TF-IDF era similarity. After Holbrook and Schindler 1989.

title: Who or what: sharer against content
question: With the content held fixed, how much of a post's success do its words explain, compared with who posted it, where and when?
note: From the notes' point, after Girard, that the sharer often matters more than the meme. Reddit resubmissions (SNAP: 132,308 posts of repeated images; Lakkaraju et al. 2013). Rival: title n-grams. Martin et al. 2016 put content under 0.05 of variance on Twitter. A low ceiling limits any content-only memetics.

title: Are there only so many plots?
question: As films are added, does the count of distinct plot-level clusters level off, as 'seven plots' and 'six arcs' claim?
note: CMU plots, names masked. A species-accumulation curve with a richness estimate. Cluster films, not units: a fixed unit list levels off by construction. Rivals: word-sentiment arcs (Reagan et al. 2016) and embedding clusters. Wikipedia's summary style may impose the sameness.

title: A brand score that pasted trigger words cannot move
question: Can a neuron-based brand score keep ranking genuinely on-brand text in new wording above off-brand text after an optimiser has tried to raise the off-brand score by pasting and rewriting?
hypothesis: After both attacks, a score that counts a unit only when it fires in three or more separate sentences still ranks reworded genuine episodes above attacked off-brand texts: mean AUC (the chance a genuine text outscores an attacked one; 0.50 is a coin flip) of at least 0.75 over 8 series, and within 0.05 of the embedding centroid.
falsifier: After the attacks, the best neuron score chosen on development data has mean AUC below 0.65, or trails the attacked sentence-embedding centroid by more than 0.05, or three pasted sentences alone lift an off-brand text by more than one standard deviation of genuine scores.
data: Plot sections of English Wikipedia episode articles for 8 scripted series, each with about 180 to 800 episode articles by a Wikidata count on 8 Nov 2026 (three are animated sitcoms), capped at 300 per series, names masked, CC BY-SA 4.0. Off-brand: episodes of the other seven series, plus the 1,000 random film plots in preregistration/sources.
method: Choose units and pooling rule per series on 60% of episodes. Reword held-out genuine and off-brand texts alike under a banned-word list (third model family). Attack each scorer twice: paste in 1, 3 or 5 of its top sentences; then 20 scored rewrites per text, at most a fifth of sentences changed, plot kept (blind check). Null: random units.
rivals: TF-IDF centroid (weighted word counts), sentence-embedding centroid, an LLM asked to rate fit, a probe on the model's averaged internal state, sparse-autoencoder features, text length; all attacked the same way. The LLM reader is most dangerous: it should see through pasted clauses. If it wins, we still learn which pooling rule makes an inspectable score hard to game.
premise: P1. A pass shows units can respond to ideas spread through a text and not to pasted wording. A fail says the usable signal is lexical, as the Batman tie with word overlap suggested, and neuron scores should not be handed to an optimising agent as graders.
bio: Batesian mimicry: harmless species wearing warning colours.
cost: M. About 3,400 short texts through two 8B models; the rewriting attack (15 texts per series, 5 scorers) is about 12,000 rewrites by a local model.
payoff: A grader for brand or style fit that an optimising agent cannot satisfy by copying phrases, or a clear statement that no neuron score of that kind exists yet.
risk: Masked, reworded episodes of sibling series may be impossible to tell apart, so every method sits near chance; or summaries are so formulaic that all sit near the ceiling. Either way the result turns on how good the rewording is.
review: Both arms now pass through the same rewriter; sibling series added as hard negatives; a scored rewriting attack with an edit cap is the main test, because a three-sentence rule beats one pasted sentence by construction. Weakness: episode summaries stand in for brand copy; plot sections not yet counted.
ranking: 3 of 3 judges thought the area reviewer rated this too high.
sources: Wikipedia episode articles via Wikidata (count 8 Nov 2026); He et al. 2024 (Llama Scope); Kantamneni et al. 2025; Bradley et al. 2023 (QDAIF)

title: Real dog whistles: routing unseen coded terms
question: On real coded speech, can units chosen on some coded terms name the group targeted by terms never seen during selection, when the term itself is blanked out?
hypothesis: With the term blanked, neuron units name the right one of four target groups for held-out terms with macro-F1 (a 0-to-1 accuracy score averaged over the groups) at least 0.05 above a TF-IDF classifier on the remaining words and within 0.05 of the embedding probe.
falsifier: Term-level macro-F1 is not above the TF-IDF classifier (paired bootstrap over terms, lower 95% bound at or below zero), or is more than 0.05 below the embedding probe, or is no better than a classifier told only the forum or chamber.
data: Silent Signals (Kruk et al. 2024): 16,258 real uses of 298 dog-whistle terms (coded phrases with a hidden meaning for an in-group), Reddit and US Congress, CC BY-SA 4.0. An LLM chose them; the authors judged 85% of 400 truly coded. Primary set: the four target groups with 40 or more terms (237 terms, 11,321 posts). Plus 124 human-labelled uses.
method: Five folds split by term: every term is tested once and never helps choose its own units. Posts are scored with the term blanked, then visible; a term's posts vote. Statistic: macro-F1 over terms, bootstrapped by term. Null: group labels shuffled across terms within source and decade. Secondary: coded against innocent uses of 13 terms in the human-labelled set.
rivals: Keyword list (useless once the term is blanked), TF-IDF classifier on the remaining words, forum or chamber alone, sentence-embedding probe, a local LLM asked which group is targeted, a probe on the model's averaged internal state, random units. The LLM reader is most dangerous, since an LLM chose these examples. A loss still shows whether context alone carries the code.
premise: P1. A blanked term stands in for a newly coined word, so a pass means units read the target from context beyond what word counts give. A fail on real data would undercut the paused plan's invented code-word condition before it is run.
bio: Camouflage against a predator's search image.
cost: S. 16,000 short posts; minutes per model, about an hour for the local LLM rival.
payoff: Evidence for or against using units to route newly coined coded language to the right policy category without retraining a filter.
risk: Context may just be the forum: 47 forums, one supplying 44% of Reddit posts. The four groups overlap in meaning, which caps every method. All posts are coded uses, so false alarms on innocent text are tested on 124 items only. The text is offensive: detection only, nothing is generated.
review: Four of the eight groups had 6 to 15 terms, so the test now uses the four with 40 or more, five folds by term, the blanked term as primary and a forum-only rival. Weakness: an LLM chose the examples, innocent posts are scarce, forum identity may explain a win.
sources: Kruk et al. 2024 (Silent Signals); Mendelsohn et al. 2023; Steen, Yurechko and Klug 2023

title: Which sources did the AI draft borrow from?
question: After an AI draft rewords and re-sets what it borrowed, can units identify which of twenty candidate sources it drew on, and which sentence it took?
hypothesis: On re-set drafts, neuron units recover the two true sources among 20 candidates with recall at 2 (the share of true sources ranked in the top two; chance 0.10) of at least 0.50 and within 0.05 of the best embedding, and find the borrowed sentence inside the true source within 0.05 of the best embedding's hit rate.
falsifier: Recall at 2 on re-set drafts is not above BM25 word matching, or is more than 0.05 below the best embedding (paired bootstrap over 300 drafts), or is below the pairwise LLM reader while costing as much or more.
data: Sources: plot sections of English Wikipedia films first released from 2025 (2,403 articles by a Wikidata count on 8 Nov 2026; about a third of film articles had a usable plot in the paused plan's crawl), after Llama 3.1's December 2023 cut-off, names masked, CC BY-SA 4.0. Drafts: 900 stories by two open models from other families than the readers.
method: Drafts are randomised to three conditions, 300 each: close paraphrase of two random sources; re-set (new setting and names, the sources' top TF-IDF terms banned, one random sentence per source to carry over); no-source control. Methods rank 20 candidates matched on genre and length, then the true source's sentences. Null: random units. The author blind-audits 60 drafts.
rivals: Longest shared word sequence, BM25 (only a floor: the ban handicaps it), sentence and story embeddings, an LLM shown the draft beside each candidate, the model's averaged internal state, text length. Story embeddings and the pairwise LLM reader are most dangerous. If they win on ranking, the remaining case for units is naming which story elements were carried over.
premise: Assumes both. A pass supports heredity beyond words where descent is fixed by random assignment, which the Batman test could not offer. A fail leaves source auditing to embeddings and LLM readers.
bio: Paternity testing with known parents.
cost: M. 900 generated drafts, under 1,000 source plots, 18,000 pairwise LLM reads on one laptop.
payoff: A tested way to show what an AI draft took from supplied material when no wording matches, for provenance and originality checks.
risk: Machine-written drafts may borrow in ways people do not; a writer that ignores an assigned source adds label noise the audit has to catch; and a tie with embeddings at higher cost would leave units with no job here.
review: Beating BM25 was true by construction once source terms are banned, so the embedding margin is now the test. Added a randomly assigned borrowed sentence, writers from other model families and a corrected source count. Weakness: the likely result is a tie with story embeddings.
overlaps: Asks nearly the same question as RX-27, which the judges would run instead.
sources: Gupta and Pruthi 2025; Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (story embeddings); Wikidata film count, 8 Nov 2026

title: Spotting a campaign's claims: accuracy per unit of compute
question: For spotting the named claims of an organised campaign in public text, is any neuron-based reader on the cost and accuracy frontier against an LLM that simply reads each paragraph?
hypothesis: With 10 labelled examples per claim, neuron units reach macro-F1 (a 0-to-1 accuracy score averaged over claims) within 0.05 of a local LLM reader given the written claim definitions, at under one fifth of its measured time per paragraph for 17 claims, and no cheaper rival matches them, in English and on German translations.
falsifier: Any rival that costs no more per paragraph has a 95% lower bound on macro-F1 at or above the neurons' estimate (neurons are dominated), or neuron macro-F1 is more than 0.05 below the LLM reader.
data: CARDS (Coan et al. 2021): paragraphs from climate-contrarian blogs and think tanks, human-coded with one of 17 sub-claims or none; 23,436 train, 2,605 validation, 2,904 cleaned test (files opened 8 Nov 2026; article CC BY 4.0, data licence unstated). Labelled paragraphs carry no outlet or date; the dated 4.6-million-row file has classifier labels and no text.
method: Choose units and fit rivals on 10, 100 or all training examples per claim; test on the cleaned set, in English and after open machine translation into German. Report macro-F1 and measured seconds and storage per 1,000 paragraphs at 1, 5 and 17 claims, including a one-call LLM read and claims added later from stored activations. Null: random units.
rivals: Word-count logistic regression (half of the paper's own ensemble), embedding probe, the paper's released classifier, a local LLM asked once for all claims and once per claim, a probe on averaged internal states. The embedding probe is most dangerous: cheaper to run and store, and probably as accurate. If it dominates, the cost argument for neurons is dead for tracking.
premise: P1. Mostly a usefulness test: a pass shows units carry a named claim across wordings and a language change cheaply. A fail moves the case for neurons from cost to interpretability alone.
bio: Genomic surveillance of a spreading variant.
cost: M. 29,000 labelled paragraphs through two 8B models plus LLM readers; hours of laptop time.
payoff: A measured answer to when, if ever, reading neurons is cheaper than asking an LLM when many claims are monitored over a large public corpus.
risk: Train and test share outlets, so word features may win easily in English and the German arm then carries the test. Spread across outlets and years cannot be checked with these files.
review: The files hold 17 sub-claims, not 27, and no outlet or date on labelled paragraphs, so held-out outlets and yearly shares were replaced by few-shot and translated tests; a one-call LLM read was added to the costs. Weakness: embedding probes will probably dominate, and spread over time is untested.
sources: Coan et al. 2021 (CARDS); preregistration/sources/neuron_timing_qwen3-8b.json; Jiang et al. 2025

title: A drift meter that ignores rewording and catches change
question: Can a neuron-based distance between two bodies of text stay flat when the same kind of stories arrive in other words or another language, and rise when the mix of stories changes?
hypothesis: With the alarm set so that fresh stories of the same genre mix from another language edition trigger it 5% of the time, the neuron meter catches a change in genre mix almost as often as the embedding meter: at the dose where that meter catches half of changes on development stories, its catch rate is at most 0.10 lower.
falsifier: At that dose the neuron meter's catch rate is more than 0.10 below the sentence-embedding meter's, or below 0.25, or the meter reads higher on same-mix stories from another edition than on a true change of that dose.
data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 summaries of 29,505 stories from five Wikipedia language editions, shipped with machine translations and name-masked versions; summaries CC BY-SA 4.0 per the dataset's README. Genre labels from Wikidata (CC0).
method: Reference: 400 English summaries. Comparison sets: different stories from another edition, in its own language, with the same genre mix (null arm) or 1 to 20% swapped for a genre absent from the reference (change arm). Meter: distance between profiles of how often each unit fires; units are picked on other stories for firing alike across editions. 500 resamples.
rivals: Word-frequency divergence on machine translations into English, multilingual sentence-embedding distance, a classifier two-sample test on embeddings, an LLM shown 30 texts from each set, distance between averaged internal states, text length. Embedding distance is most dangerous. If translated word counts match the neurons, drift monitoring needs neither neurons nor a multilingual model.
premise: Both. Flat readings across languages need language-independent units (P1); repeating the result in Llama through mapped units tests P2. A fail says unit profiles track wording and edition, not content.
bio: Allele-frequency change against sampling noise.
cost: S. About 6,000 summaries per model; the resampling is arithmetic.
payoff: A calibrated alarm for content pipelines and localised copy, with a known false-alarm rate under rewording, and the units that moved as a first diagnosis.
risk: Genre mix is a coarse stand-in for themes, and language editions differ in length and detail, which every method may read as drift.
review: Reference and comparison now hold different stories, so no method wins by pairing copies; doses lowered and the test dose fixed where the embedding meter is at half power, to avoid a ceiling; translated word counts added as a rival. Weakness: genre is a crude kind of drift.
sources: Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again); Jiang et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2024

title: Do empty meme combinations predict what gets made next?
question: Are idea briefs built from meme combinations that no earlier film used realised by later films more often than briefs from random pairs, embedding gaps or simply asking an LLM?
hypothesis: Among gaps as of 2012 with no earlier match, neuron-gap briefs are realised by films of 2013 to 2023 at least 1.5 times as often as random-pair briefs matched on unit frequency, and at least as often as embedding-gap briefs. At most 20% of neuron gaps turn out to have an earlier match.
falsifier: The neuron-gap realisation rate is not above the random-pair rate (one-sided two-proportion test, p at or above 0.05, 1,000 briefs each), or is below the embedding-gap rate by a third or more, or over 20% of neuron gaps already existed. If the tuning period's random-pair rate is under 2%, the test is not run.
data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 plots to 2012, CC BY-SA). Wikipedia film plots from 2013 to 2023, still to be crawled, and from 2025 (2,403 film articles by a Wikidata count on 8 Nov 2026), CC BY-SA 4.0. Names masked; sequels, remakes and adaptations removed using Wikidata links.
method: Tune on gaps as of 2000, judged against 2001 to 2012: fix units, ranking rule (two common units that share many partners and never met) and base rates. Test on gaps as of 2012: 1,000 per method, stated by a fixed template; an LLM judge, checked against 100 blind human labels, reads retrieved plots. The LLM-list rival: 2025 films only.
rivals: Random never-met pairs matched on unit frequency, pairs ranked by the product of unit frequencies, gaps between sentence-embedding clusters, word-pair gaps from TF-IDF terms, sparse-autoencoder feature pairs, Llama 3.1 asked for unmade film ideas. The frequency-product baseline and the plain LLM list are most dangerous. If they win, meme maps add nothing to idea generation beyond popularity.
premise: Assumes both. A pass shows unit co-occurrence captures which combinations are viable, which words and embeddings may miss. A fail does not hurt P1 but removes the creativity use.
bio: Vacant niches filled later by adaptive radiation.
cost: M. About 55,000 plots through one model, 6,000 briefs, 120,000 short LLM matching calls, one hour of human checking.
payoff: A test of gap-finding as an idea source that needs no taste judgement: the later record of what was made is the judge.
risk: Common units that never met may exclude each other, not await a first use; unit labels may be too vague to judge; and being realised later rewards obvious combinations more than good ones.
review: The gap rule was undefined and the 8% and 4% rates had no basis. Added a tuning period fixing rule and base rates, a stop gate, name masking, template briefs and a test on 2013 to 2023 films, since few 2025 plots exist. Weakness: a long chain of LLM steps.
ranking: In the top twelve of 1 of 3 judges (upside: rank 10). It is the only registered design that tests spotting promising ideas forward in time, with the films actually made after 2012 as the judge, and gap-finding rules of this kind usually beat random pairs.
sources: Sreenivasan 2013; Uzzi et al. 2013; Krenn et al. 2022; CMU Movie Summary Corpus

title: Prose style with content held fixed
question: Does a unit-based author-style score survive pasted signature phrases when the subject matter is the same?
note: Public-domain authors; the rival is a content-independent style embedding (Wegmann et al. 2022) and an LLM asked who wrote it. Complements US21, which tests content memes, not prose style.

title: AI telephone chains
question: How fast does text drift from its reference when AI models rewrite each other's output, and toward which memes?
note: Transmission-chain design of Perez et al. 2024 with generation number as the known dose. Rivals: embedding distance and an LLM comparing first and last text. Writer and reader must be different model families.

title: One claim, many languages
question: Can units link a social post to the fact-check of the same claim when the two are in different languages?
note: MultiClaim (Pikuliak et al. 2023) has fact-checker links across 27 languages, but access is by research request, so check terms first. A public same-language fallback is the CLEF CheckThat! 2021 and 2022 claim-retrieval sets on GitLab (sizes and licence not yet checked). Multilingual embeddings are the rival and were built for this.

title: Naming what drifted
question: When a theme is planted in a body of text, do the labels of the most-moved units name it?
note: Follows US25. Rivals: an LLM asked to describe the difference between the two sets (Zhong et al. 2024) and sparse-autoencoder embeddings (Jiang et al. 2025), compared on accuracy and cost. Needs a blind judge to match labels to the planted theme.

title: Feedback that helps without being gamed
question: Does telling a rewriting agent which memes are missing raise blind-judged brand fit more than a bare score or an LLM critique?
note: Run only if US21 finds a score that resists stuffing. Outcome is judged by blind readers who never see the score. Rival: an LLM critic's written feedback at equal query budget.

title: Euphemism or literal
question: Do units separate euphemistic from literal uses of the same phrase?
note: The corpus of potentially euphemistic terms (Gavidia et al. 2022) has human labels for both senses of each phrase. Rival: a contextual embedding of the phrase and a local LLM reader. It supplies what US22 lacks: innocent uses of the same words, labelled by people.

title: Human-rated empty spaces
question: Do blind raters find briefs from neuron gaps more novel and more workable than briefs from embedding gaps or a plain LLM list?
note: Cost L: three to five paid raters. Run only if US26 shows neuron gaps are truly empty. Fiction or product ideas only; no persuasion content.

title: Do rival brands converge
question: Does a unit distance separate same-brand from rival-brand copy, and show rivals converging over time, better than word overlap?
note: Expected to be lost to TF-IDF because brands repeat their own words; worth registering as a boundary marker. Needs public dated copy such as archived homepages; ad libraries carry no outcome measure.

title: Does a gamed score fool a second reader?
question: Does off-brand text rewritten to fool one model's unit score also fool another model's, more or less than attacks carry over between two embedding models?
note: Added in review. Reuses US21's attacked texts, so it costs almost nothing. If attacks do not carry over, averaging two reader models is a cheap defence; if they do, shared word detectors are the likely cause, which bears on P2. Rivals: carry-over between two embedding models and between two LLM judges.

title: Claim spread over outlets and years
question: Do unit-based counts reproduce a claim's rise and fall across outlets and years better than word counts or an embedding probe?
note: Added in review. US24's corpus cannot answer this: its labelled paragraphs have no outlet or date, and its dated file has classifier labels without text. Needs about 1,000 dated paragraphs labelled by hand, or another corpus with dates, outlets and human claim labels. Cost L until such data is found.

title: Stuffing pilot on the Batman files
question: Does pasting a few Batman sentences into masked plots of other hero films lift the study's canon score above reworded Batman texts?
note: Added in review. A one-day pilot for US21 using the study's committed texts and units plus fresh rewordings; it sets the paste doses and shows whether the problem is the pooling rule. Rivals: TF-IDF centroid, sentence embedding, an LLM asked whether it is a Batman story. Development data only, so it confirms nothing.

title: A hit's renamed children
question: Can units find a hit's renamed offspring, the 'Die Hard on a ...' films, in a pool of unrelated films?
note: Floated in the working session and never written up. Rivals: TF-IDF, embeddings and an LLM asked directly. Needs a defensible list of documented descendants.

title: Creators as carriers
question: Do the works of one creator carry a signature set of units into each franchise they touch (Miller, Moore, Nolan)?
note: Floated in the working session. Girard's side of the question: people as the route by which memes travel.

title: Who read whom: content plus an exposure graph
question: Where it is known who was exposed to whom, as in an email archive or a follower graph, does a person's later writing take up the units of the people they read?
note: The method sketched in Mike's public post on memetics and mimetics. Girard's theory needs exposure data; text alone cannot test it.

title: Finish labelling the canon
question: What are the 27 core Batman units that still have no confident label?
note: 29 of the 56 core families have a confident label. Left unfinished in the working session.

title: Is Batman the sum of his parts?
question: Can the neurons that fire for a character be predicted from those that fire for its agreed component tropes, better than from random tropes, embedding addition or an LLM's combined tag list?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Semiotics vs Memetics; Billionaire vigilante orphans). Rival to beat: An LLM's list of tags combined by simple set arithmetic; adding sentence embeddings together.

title: Does a buzzword unpack only in its home field?
question: Does a jargon phrase fire the same neurons as its plain-English expansion when the surrounding text sets its home field, and not when the same phrase sits in an unrelated setting?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Buzzwords are compression; The cure for the common meme). Rival to beat: Keyword counts cannot do this at all. The real rivals are a context-aware embedding of the phrase and an LLM reading the passage.

title: Do common memes transfer between models better than rare ones?
question: Does agreement between two models on which neurons mark a meme rise with how often that meme appears in public text, and fall to chance for niche memes?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Memetics as a science; Billionaire vigilante orphans). Rival to beat: The same trend measured with embedding neighbour lists or LLM tag lists instead of neurons.

title: X is Y in Z: setting-swap arithmetic on stories
question: For pairs such as 'The Lion King is Hamlet with lions', does the first story's neuron profile, minus its setting and plus the new one, land nearer the second story than embedding arithmetic does?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Every story ever told; Billionaire vigilante orphans). Rival to beat: The same subtraction and addition done on sentence embeddings, which are known to handle analogies.

title: Do works called original just have obscure sources?
question: Among films equally close to their nearest earlier source, are the ones reviewers call original those whose source is less well known?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Where do you get your ideas?; Meme-Jacking). Rival to beat: Nearest earlier sources found by sentence embedding, with fame taken from page views.

title: Loosened snowclones
question: Does a neuron chosen on literal templates such as 'the cure for the common X' still fire on reworded variants, where a pattern match fails and sentence embeddings are the rival?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (The cure for the common meme; Comparative Phylogenetics). Rival to beat: A regular expression (a text pattern match), which wins on literal templates. Neurons only have a case on reworded variants, against embeddings.

title: Is middling copying fidelity best for survival?
question: Across families of copied quotations or tales, do those with moderate change between copies outlast both the near-verbatim and the heavily altered, as the essays' 'too little, too much mutation' argument predicts?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Universal Darwinism; Modeling viral growth). Rival to beat: The same test using how much the wording varies between retellings.

title: People retelling from memory or from a script
question: In chains of human retellers, do stories passed on by re-reading written notes keep more of their neuron-measured content than stories retold from memory of the last telling?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Mutually beneficial memes). Rival to beat: Drift in wording; an LLM coding which statements survive.

title: Do magic words travel between accounts?
question: Do the neurons that predict winners in one publisher's or community's tests keep predicting winners in another's, and better than the winning word sequences do?
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Finding magic words). Rival to beat: Mike's own n-gram method: word sequences tied to performance.

title: Do faded memes revive by changing medium?
question: When a faded meme's share rebounds, the rebound is carried by works in a medium newer than the one it peaked in, more often than by works in the old medium.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Modeling viral growth). Rival to beat: Franchise names and keywords tracked across media; an LLM reading each synopsis. Words fail when the revived meme is renamed, which is where a unit that reads ideas could add something.

title: Filler or news: what is new in this article?
question: The share of an article's meme units that are new to its running story separates hand-labelled filler from news, and filler share peaks in the hours before scheduled events.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Emerging memes). Rival to beat: New words and new named entities against earlier coverage; embedding distance to earlier articles; an LLM asked what is new. Units must beat these when old content is merely reworded.

title: Does the namer get the credit?
question: Among papers carrying an idea, later papers cite the one that coined its name more than earlier papers that carried the same idea unnamed, after allowing for venue and author fame.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Emerging memes). Rival to beat: Keyword first-use finds the coiner. Finding earlier carriers with no name needs a reader of ideas: sentence embeddings, or an LLM judging whether two abstracts state the same idea.

title: Are a meme's first carriers penalised?
question: Among works carrying a set of meme units that later became common, the earliest carriers did worse against same-year peers than carriers at the middle of adoption.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Emerging memes). Rival to beat: First use of the idea's keywords or tags. Words miss early carriers that lacked the later name, so embeddings and an LLM judging "same idea?" are the rivals to beat.

title: Are ideas turning over faster, or only their words?
question: The time a meme unit spends above half its peak share has shortened decade by decade. The neuron question is whether ideas turn over faster, or only the words for them.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Meme fatigue). Rival to beat: The same lifetime measured on words, phrases and hashtags, where shortening is said to be reported already (from memory; check). Units add something only if their trend differs from the words'.

title: Does a meme's meaning drift as it goes mainstream?
question: For widely quoted lines, the stance of the surrounding text moves away from that of the original passage as the quote spreads, and moves further the further it travels from its first audience.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Meme fatigue). Rival to beat: Word overlap cannot see this, because the quoted words do not change. The rivals are a stance classifier and an LLM reading the surrounding passage.

title: Do units forecast when a conversation turns hostile?
question: Early turns of a conversation contain content that forecasts whether it later turns into personal attack, beyond politeness markers.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Info Hazards). Rival to beat: Politeness and insult word lists; an LLM reading the opening turns; sentence embeddings.

title: One idea per message: do headlines with fewer memes win?
question: Within a randomised headline test, the arm with fewer distinct memes wins more clicks, with length held fixed.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Memetic Confusion). Rival to beat: Word count; an LLM counting the ideas in each headline.

title: Friction without displacement: does a banned meme move or die?
question: After a platform bans a term or community, the idea itself (in any wording) falls nearly as much as the banned words do, in the same accounts. Displacement into new wording would falsify it.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Memetic crime loops). Rival to beat: Keyword counts cannot see reworded substitutes, so they cannot test displacement. The bar is sentence embeddings or an LLM reading posts for the idea.

title: Does a filter breed evaders? Weak against harsh penalties
question: In a loop that breeds text to carry an idea past a detector, a weak penalty yields variants that keep the idea and evade the detector; a harsh penalty makes the idea disappear from the population.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Evolutionary design thinking). Rival to beat: Run the same loop against a keyword filter, an embedding classifier and an LLM reader as the detector. A neuron detector must be evaded less often at equal cost.

title: Levelling, sharpening, assimilation: three rumour distortions in chains
question: Along retelling chains the number of active units falls, the surviving units fire more strongly, and content shifts toward the retelling group's usual units. Versions showing all three are passed on most.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Smoke without fire). Rival to beat: Word counts for levelling, and an LLM listing and grading each retelling's statements for sharpening and assimilation.

title: Life imitating art: a hit's memes in non-fiction
question: After a hit film about a profession, non-fiction about that profession (news, memoirs, trade press) carries more of the film's distinctive neuron units than before release, compared with control professions and matched flops.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Memed into existence). Rival to beat: Counts of the film's catchphrases and props; sentence-embedding similarity to the film's plot summary. Both catch quoted uptake; units must show uptake without the film's words.

title: Is what gets remembered what the model failed to predict?
question: The parts of a story a language model predicts worst are the parts people recall and pass on. Surprise measured in neuron units predicts recall beyond surprise measured word by word.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (All reality is virtual). Rival to beat: Word-by-word surprisal: how unexpected each word is, read from the model's ordinary output with no look inside. Word rarity is a second cheap rival.

title: Do lasting stories overturn a default pairing?
question: Stories that last pair a trait with the opposite of its usual outcome (the weak win, the ugly are good) more often than forgotten stories of the same period and genre.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Non-Obvious Truths). Rival to beat: An LLM asked which common expectation the story overturns; a rare-pairing score built on words, as in RX-23.

title: Fable to advert: same moral, no shared words
question: With names and shared words removed, a campaign's description is closer in neuron units to the fable it is paired with than to decoy fables, where word overlap cannot make the link.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Non-Obvious Truths). Rival to beat: Sentence embeddings; an LLM asked which fable each campaign echoes, which may well win.

title: How fast does a new category shed its parent's memes?
question: Writing about a new technology carries the neuron units of the technology it replaced most strongly at launch, and their share falls steadily as the new category ages.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Making the new feel familiar). Rival to beat: Counts of the old category's words ('horseless carriage') over time; embedding similarity to text about the old category.

title: Does a name make an idea spread?
question: A concept described in papers before it had a name spreads faster after a compact name is coined than its earlier trend predicts. Finding the concept before it had a name is the step keyword counts cannot do.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (A rose by any other name). Rival to beat: Sentence-embedding search, or an LLM reading passages for the concept. Keyword counts work only after the coinage.

title: Jargon and its plain expansion: same units?
question: A jargon passage and its plain-English expansion activate the same neuron units, so the jargon version carries more units per word. The match holds only in a model that knows the field.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Buzzwords are compression). Rival to beat: Sentence embeddings of the two versions; an LLM asked whether they say the same thing. Word overlap should fail, since few words are shared.

title: Same position, different appeal: can units tell what from how?
question: Pairs of ads that take the same position through different appeals share 'position' neuron units and differ on 'appeal' units. Units chosen on some topics separate position from appeal on unseen topics.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Creative Analytica). Rival to beat: An LLM asked to name the position and the appeal of each ad; a probe trained on sentence embeddings; word lists for threat and for sociability.

title: Does blaming the system out-spread blaming yourself?
question: Among versions of one story, the version that blames a system for a personal hardship draws more clicks or votes than the version that puts responsibility on the individual.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Seize the memes of production). Rival to beat: An LLM labelling each text as system-blame or self-blame would probably do. Word lists for blame are the floor.

title: Do movements turn on rival ideas only after they win?
question: In a movement's own dated writings, calls to silence rival views are rare while it is small and rise after it gains power, more than in matched movements that never gained power.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Seize the memes of production). Rival to beat: Keyword lists (traitor, censor, enemy of the people); an LLM reading each passage. Wording differs by era and movement, which is the only opening for neurons.

title: Dehumanising language before a conflict
question: A neuron unit chosen on some dehumanising metaphors (vermin) also fires on unseen ones (disease, machines). Its rate in one side's press about the other side rises before fighting starts.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (A battle of wills). Rival to beat: Dehumanisation word lists; an LLM reading each passage; a probe on sentence embeddings.

title: Do attack messages beat reassuring ones, and for whom?
question: Within one randomised test, the message that attacks an institution wins over the message that defends or reassures. Challengers gain more from attack messages than incumbents do.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (The Meme President). Rival to beat: Sentiment word lists; an LLM labelling each message as attack or reassurance.

title: Do troll accounts invent grievances or echo existing ones?
question: Troll posts carry few ideas new to the target community: their units already appear in that community's earlier posts. The troll posts closest to earlier community content draw the most engagement.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Russian troll farms). Rival to beat: Word overlap and sentence-embedding similarity between each troll post and the community's earlier posts.

title: Does a debunk stop a story, or only its name?
question: After a story is debunked, its named form declines while its name-free form (a lone pilot saving the capital) keeps appearing in later texts without the correction.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Flood the zone). Rival to beat: Keyword search finds the named form. An LLM reader or sentence embeddings must be beaten on the name-free form.

title: Message or money: which predicts a campaign's result?
question: Across many ballot campaigns, the content of each side's printed arguments predicts the result beyond the spending ratio, and adds more than spending does.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Take back control). Rival to beat: Spending ratio alone as the floor; then word counts, sentence embeddings and an LLM rating each argument's appeal.

title: Do winning messages echo what the audience already says?
question: Among a campaign's tested messages, winners share more ideas with what the audience was already saying in its own words than losers do, even where no words are shared.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Take back control). Rival to beat: Word overlap and sentence-embedding similarity between each message and the audience's own earlier text.

title: Are Leave and Trump one family of messages?
question: Leave and Trump campaign texts sit closer to each other in neuron-unit profile than either sits to its own opponent, once place, party and person names are removed.
note: From Mike's 2022 essays (Take back control). Rival to beat: Sentence embeddings; an LLM listing each campaign's themes; word-weight similarity (TF-IDF) after names are removed.

title: A text's sparse code as its read
question: Is 'this unit is among the strongest few per layer at this token' a more repeatable presence call than the study's rule of beating 68 of 69 reference films?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The paper shows one model can run on its top 320 neurons per token and layer. Rival to beat: the study's rule, the unit's own strong range (IN-23), word presence and an LLM reader, on the two-summary stories of IN-25. Only sensible if the dense 8B models turn out to be sparse (IN-32).

title: Mode-level characters on documented adaptations
question: When each unit's firings are split into roles by what drives them, do adaptations share roles with their documented source more than they share whole units, beyond shared words?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The paper finds about half of neuron poles have more than one role, so two unrelated works can share a pole in different roles. Rival to beat: TF-IDF on name-free text, whole-pole units, and poles split by an LLM that only reads each firing sentence. Large: needs input attribution for thousands of firings per unit.

title: Story-turn units against annotated turning points
question: Do units chosen as story-turn detectors place the turning points that human annotators marked in film synopses, once sentence punctuation is removed and stock turn words are reworded?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). Goodfire's public atlas has units labelled for story turns that fire on a full stop, a comma or 'but'. Data: TRIPOD (Papalampidi, Keller and Lapata 2019), film synopses with human-marked turning points. Rival to beat: expected position alone, a list of turn words, and an LLM asked to mark the turns.

title: Causal presence: count a unit where removal matters
question: Is a unit's reading of a text more repeatable and less tied to words when each firing is weighted by how much removing it changes the model's next-word predictions?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The paper weighs firings by their effect on the output, and its Colorado neuron looks clean by effect and messy by count. Rival to beat: activation alone, the unit's own strong range (IN-23), TF-IDF, and the damage from removing random units at the same tokens.

title: Atlas story labels as an outside motif list
question: Do story-level ideas that have a unit in Goodfire's 35B model more often have a passing unit in Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B than matched motifs taken from a human index?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The atlas is a list of ideas another lab's pipeline found inside a different model: a test of P2 at the level of which ideas get a unit. Needs Goodfire's permission first: the atlas states no licence and the site terms restrict copying. Rival to beat: a word classifier, sentence embeddings and an LLM reader on the same passages.

title: Do neurons add anything beyond expert routing?
question: In a mixture-of-experts model, does the record of which experts each token was sent to find a story's documented source as well as the neuron-level reading does?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The router's choice of 8 experts out of 256 per layer is a coarse code that comes free with models like the paper's, and may be what a neuron reading reduces to: topic. Rival to beat: routing counts plus TF-IDF. Needs Qwen3.6-35B-A3B run locally, which the study has not done.

title: A sparsified, fine-tuned reader as the instrument
question: Does a copy of the reader model fine-tuned to run on only its strongest activations give readings that are more repeatable and less word-bound than the original model's?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The paper fine-tunes its model to run with 92.2% of activations zeroed and reports that neurons keep their roles. Rival to beat: the untuned model with the same mask applied only at reading time, which is free. Large: a 100-million-token fine-tune on rented GPUs.

title: Copied layers: a census of duplicate neurons
question: Do the study's models contain neurons that are copies of the neuron at the same index a fixed number of layers away, and how much do such copies inflate unit counts and twin rates inside the Qwen family?
note: From Goodfire's companion paper (10 November 2026). The paper's authors suspect Qwen3-32B was built by copying layers of Qwen3-14B. If so, some agreement inside a model family is inheritance, not convergence. Weights only, under a day. Control: different-index pairs at the same layer gap, and the same census in Llama 3.1 8B.
